items.title: Stiegler, The Re-Enchantment of the World: a study companion
items.text:
Bernard Stiegler & Ars Industrialis, Réenchanter le monde. La valeur esprit contre le populisme industriel (Flammarion, 2006); The Re-Enchantment of the World: The Value of Spirit against Industrial Populism, trans. Trevor Arthur (Bloomsbury Academic, 2014).

A fair-use companion of condensed summaries, short attributed quotations and evaluated third-party accounts. It does not reproduce the book. Read it as a website at lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world.

items.title: The thesis in one sentence
items.text: Consumer capitalism has captured desire and attention through the industries of communication and culture ("industrial populism"). In doing so it lowers "the value of spirit" and turns the promised knowledge society into a reign of ignorance. To re-enchant the world, the same technologies must become "technologies of spirit" that support knowledge, care and individuation, under an industrial politics led by a renewed public power.

items.title: The book in one paragraph
items.text: In 2005 the French employers' federation, Medef, held its summer university under the slogan "the re-enchantment of the world" to promote the knowledge economy. Stiegler and the newly founded association Ars Industrialis "take it at its word". Re-enchantment requires reversing the "drop in the value of spirit" Paul Valéry noted in 1939. That drop is now organized by a libidinal economy in which television and marketing sell "available brain time". The result exhausts desire into drives and proletarianizes producers, consumers and knowledge workers alike, stripping them of savoir-faire, savoir-vivre and theoretical knowledge. Because human memory and knowledge have always been technical (grammatization, tertiary retention), the answer is not to reject technology. It is to invest, publicly and over the long term, in instruments, institutions and practices that let people re-appropriate their technologies of memory. The book gathers the association's 2005 manifesto (and, in English, its 2010 manifesto, which reframes the programme as a pharmacology of care and an economy of contribution), two essays by Stiegler on the "re-foundation of society" and "against the reign of ignorance", and a motion addressed to the 2005 UN summit on the information society in Tunis.

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
Home › Glossary · full entries in concepts/ · cross-reference in INDEX.md

Terse definitions as the book uses the terms. Each heading links to a full concept file with locations, related terms, secondary glosses and disagreements.

Term Definition Spirit (esprit, valeur esprit) Noetic life (attention, memory, judgement, sublimated desire), psychic and collective and technically supported. Valéry's "value" that can fall like a commodity price. Industrial populism Populism produced by the economy: culture industries and marketing levelling attention to drives and selling "available brain time". Political populism follows from it. Libidinal economy The organization of desire. Consumer capitalism captured libido as its energy and, by capturing it, destroys it, reducing desire to drives. Symbolic misery Loss of individuation through losing a part in producing symbols. Leads to "spiritual misery". Hyperindustrial society Not post-industrial. Industrialization extended to services, culture and cognition. Service capitalism controls how ways of life are adopted. Tertiary retention Memory held in artefacts. It conditions perception (primary retention) and recollection (secondary retention). Grammatization Discretization of flows (speech, gesture, perception) into reproducible marks, from the alphabet to the digital. Each stage both enables knowledge and threatens it. Hypomnemata Memory supports. Writing and all mnemotechnics. They can serve care of the self or replace memory. Pharmakon / pharmacology Every technics is remedy and poison. A therapeutic (care) decides which. Explicit already in Ch. 1 (pp. 47–51) and systematized in the 2010 Manifesto. Proletarianization Loss of knowledge to apparatuses: workers' savoir-faire, consumers' savoir-vivre, thinkers' theoretical knowledge. Otium / negotium Studious leisure for existence and self-cultivation, against business for subsistence. Service capitalism folds otium into negotium. Care (soin) Attention to self, others and world, sustained by techniques of the self. "To economize means… to take care." Its opposite is carelessness (incurie). Short-termism The drive's temporality in finance, management and media. It destroys investment, both financial and libidinal. Economy of contribution Industrial model without a producer/consumer split. Positive externalities, capabilities, de-proletarianization. Free software is the model. Associated / dissociated milieu Simondon. A milieu its participants co-individuate (associated), against one individuated by specialists at others' expense (dissociated). Individuation / transindividuation / disindividuation Simondon. Becoming who one is, psychically and collectively. The co-production of a "we". Its breakdown through short-circuits. Disenchantment / re-enchantment Weber's rationalization, radicalized into the destruction of desire and of capitalism's "spirit". Medef's slogan, taken at its word. Technologies of spirit The converged culture, media, telecom and cognitive industries. Psychotechnologies (control) against nootechnologies (the life of the mind). Knowledge vs information Information as a commodity is entropic (value decays). Knowledge is negentropic (lasts, intensifies). Confusing them yields a "reign of ignorance".

items.title: Other terms you will meet
items.text:
• R technologies: relational technologies (Ch. 1, p. 29): telecom and broadcast networks, RFID, chip cards, wi-fi, Bluetooth, biometrics, nanotech, used as technologies of control. See technologies of spirit.
  • Dissociated milieu: a milieu in which production and consumption are separated, so participants lose their knowledge and cannot individuate themselves (Ch. 1, pp. 34–37). See associated milieu.
  • Plane of consistencies / motifs ("the plane that enchants me"): the incalculable objects of desire (works, the beloved, idealities) which "do not exist" but consist, and must be cared for (Ch. 1, pp. 58–60).
  • Discharge: services relieve the consumer of tasks and so of his existence (Ch. 1, pp. 30–31).

  • Meta-transformation: the capacity to transform the way ways of life are transformed (Ch. 1, pp. 44–45).

  • Savoir-faire / savoir-vivre: know-how / knowing how to live. Left in French by the translator. See proletarianization.

  • Available brain time (temps de cerveau humain disponible): Patrick Le Lay (TF1), 2004. See context.
  • Medef: French employers' federation. Its 2005 summer university was titled "Réenchanter le monde". See context.
  • Program industries / program institutions: culture and media industries against schools and universities. See Ch. 2 p. 90.
  • Adoption: the process by which ways of life are taken up. Individuation is adoption. See Ch. 1 §3.
  • General organology: the co-evolution of bodily organs, technical organs and social organizations. See grammatization.
  • Desublimation: loss of the capacity to sublimate drives into desire for singular objects. See libidinal economy.
  • Sursaut ("jumpstart", also rendered "sudden surge", Introduction p. 5): a leap and rupture that re-founds the "human enterprise" (entreprendre de fonder). See Ch. 1 pp. 44–47.

items.title: The French edition, and FR/EN differences
items.text:
1. The 2010 Manifesto is not in the 2006 French first edition. The Introduction's n. 17 (p. 102) says that at the time of the French publication only the 2005 Manifesto existed, and that the 2010 Manifesto was added in the English edition. It was written in 2010 (it refers to the 2007–2010 crisis and Facebook's 500 million users in July 2010). The English edition (2014) therefore adds it. Its vocabulary of pharmakon, care and the economy of contribution belongs to Stiegler's 2008–2010 work and is later than the chapters. Readers should not read those concepts back into Chs. 1–2.
  2. The 2005 Manifesto is in the French edition. French catalogues note "Contient le Manifeste d'Ars Industrialis".
  3. Authorship is presented differently. The French cover reads "Bernard Stiegler et Ars Industrialis". The English title page names Stiegler alone, though the translator's preface speaks of "Stiegler and co.". The two chapters are Stiegler's own texts. The manifestos and motion are signed collectively (Collins, Crépon, Perret, B. Stiegler, C. Stiegler).
  4. French pagination anchor. Ch. 1 §3 ("Les sociétés hyperindustrielles de services comme destruction des processus d'individuation par le contrôle des processus d'adoption") is at French pp. 42–47 (English pp. 31–33). That implies roughly 1.4 French pages per English page.
  5. French Ch. 1 section headings in retailer and catalogue listings: "capitalisme de services", "Les sociétés hyperindustrielles de services comme destruction des processus d'individuation par le contrôle des processus d'adoption", "technologies R" with "appareils de l'esprit" (the English has "new spiritual devices").
  6. The French back cover is a compressed version of the Introduction's opening (Valéry 1939; 45% radio; "temps de cerveau disponible"; "un cerveau sans conscience"; Medef 2005; "ce livre propose de le prendre au mot").
  7. French pagination of the 2005 Manifesto: pp. 27–35 (per the bibliography of de Beer 2012, source). The French front part (Introduction, "Que faire ?") therefore runs to about p. 26, and Ch. 1 begins soon after p. 35.
  8. Opening text titled "Que faire ?": attested by a 2007 English summary (Holmes), which is consistent with the English "What Is to Be Done?".
  9. Editions: BnF FRBNF40245952 (Flammarion 2006, 172 pp.); Champs paperback reissue, 3 Oct 2008, 176 pp. (EAN 978-2-08-121784-3); e-book 2013. See sources/review-bnf-catalogue-records-2006.md.
  10. An earlier partial English translation exists. Two sections were translated by Stephen Barker in New Formations (2012): "Grammatisation and Individuation Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow" (= Ch. 1, p. 47) and "The Risk of Disindividuation as the Increase of Ignorance Rather Than Knowledge" (= Ch. 2, p. 81). See sources/review-barker-new-formations-2012.md.

  • The English section on the sursaut turns on entreprendre: "UNDERTAKE A FOUNDATION (ENTREPRENDRE DE FONDER)" (p. 46). The French subtitle "entreprendre autrement" plays on entreprendre/entreprise (business), which "starting over again" does not carry.
  • The French edition prints the Tunis motion, at FR p. 163 (Ch. 2, n. 6).

  • Ch. 2 n. 20 shows why the French edition is dedicated to Laurence Parisot. Stiegler saw her succession to Seillière at Medef as giving "some hope" for civic responsibility among French employers.

items.title: Reading order note
items.text: The book's order is not the order of composition. Composition ran 2005 Manifesto (spring 2005) → Ch. 2 (Sept 2005) → Tunis motion (Nov 2005) → Ch. 1 and Introduction (2006) → 2010 Manifesto. Chronologically, the book is the founding dossier of Ars Industrialis, framed by a 2006 introduction and updated in 2014 with the 2010 manifesto.

items.title: Overview (L1)
items.text:
Home › Overview · down: Structure · Chapters · Concepts

About a page. The argument arc, where the book sits in Stiegler's corpus, and the Ars Industrialis project. Evaluation is kept out of this file; see reception.md.

items.title: 1. What kind of book this is
items.text:
Réenchanter le monde (Flammarion, 2006; English 2014) is not a treatise. It is the founding dossier of Ars Industrialis, the "international association for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit" that Bernard Stiegler set up in 2005 with George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler. It contains:

  • a polemical Introduction ("What Is to Be Done?", 2006);
  • the association's manifestos (2005, and in the English edition only, 2010);
  • two essays by Stiegler: Ch. 1 "The Re-Foundation of Society" (2006) and Ch. 2 "Against the Reign of Ignorance" (from a September 2005 talk);
  • the motion the association published on the eve of the 2005 UN World Summit on the Information Society in Tunis.

Composition ran 2005 → 2006, plus a 2010 add-on, which is not the printed order. See STRUCTURE.md.

items.title: 2. The argument arc
items.text:
1. Provocation. In 2005 the French employers' federation (Medef) took "the re-enchantment of the world" as the slogan of its summer university, to sell the "knowledge economy". Stiegler takes the slogan at its word. Re-enchantment would require raising the value of spirit, the faculty Valéry saw falling in 1939. The milieu that coined the slogan is the one lowering that value. Its emblem is TF1's boast of selling "available brain time" to Coca-Cola. Stiegler's name for this is industrial populism.
  2. Diagnosis: libidinal economy and its exhaustion. Twentieth-century capitalism organized consumption by capturing desire through the culture industries, a libidinal economy. That capture has turned into its destruction: desire degrades into drives, sublimation fails, and attention is "short-circuited". The outcome is a symbolic misery, and a disenchantment more radical than Weber's.
  3. Mechanism: control of adoption and proletarianization. Hyperindustrial service capitalism controls how people adopt ways of life, and with it their individuation. Knowledge is formalized into apparatuses and services and lost by individuals. Producers lose savoir-faire, consumers lose savoir-vivre, and knowledge workers lose theoretical knowledge. This is generalized proletarianization.
  4. Ground: memory is technical. Human memory and knowledge have always been externalized, through grammatization, tertiary retention and hypomnemata. The problem is not technology as such but whether a society organizes the re-interiorization of its memory technologies. Schools did this for writing. Today the program industries out-compete the program institutions.
  5. Contradiction of the "knowledge society". Commodified information is entropic. Knowledge is negentropic. An economy that reduces knowledge to information risks a reign of ignorance (knowledge vs information).
  6. Remedy: an industrial politics of spirit. The same technologies are technologies of spirit. They could support a new age of individuation if a new public power, working with industry and taking a long view against short-termism, invested in instruments of knowledge, reformed media and education, and championed a European way of life. Already in Ch. 1, and systematically in the 2010 Manifesto, this is framed as pharmacology: every technics is both poison and remedy. It calls for an economy of contribution built on care and associated milieus, and for reconquering free time as otium.

items.title: 3. Place in Stiegler's corpus
items.text: Period Works (FR date) Relation to this book Foundations Technics and Time 1–3 (1994, 1996, 2001); Echographies of Television (with Derrida, 1996) Originary technicity; epiphylogenesis; tertiary retention; TT3 supplies the "prosthetic" synthesis, the adoption theory and the "ill-being" of cinema/TV that Chs. 1–2 rely on. Political turn (2003–06) Acting Out (2003); Symbolic Misery 1–2 (2004–05: "the hyperindustrial epoch", "the catastrophe of the sensible"); Disbelief and Discredit 1–3 (2004–06: decadence of industrial democracies; uncontrollable societies of disaffected individuals; the lost spirit of capitalism); Constituer l'Europe 1–2 (2005); La Télécratie contre la démocratie (2006) The book's immediate context. Its vocabulary of symbolic misery, libidinal economy, the spirit of capitalism, disindividuation, Europe and telecracy is drawn from these, often in compressed form. Ch. 1's notes refer to Disbelief and Discredit 2 and Télécratie. This book Réenchanter le monde (2006) A popularizing, programmatic hinge. It turns the 2004–06 diagnoses into an association and a policy agenda. Care and pharmacology Taking Care of Youth and the Generations (Prendre soin, 2008); For a New Critique of Political Economy (2009); What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2010) Systematizes what Ch. 1 already sets out: care as socio-therapy, the pharmakon (pp. 47–51) and the economy of contribution (pp. 36–37). The 2010 Manifesto (EN edition) belongs to this phase. Late work States of Shock (2012); Automatic Society (2015); The Neganthropocene (2018); In the Disruption (2016); Qu'appelle-t-on panser ? (2018–20) Entropy/negentropy, first sketched in Ch. 2's knowledge/information contrast, becomes neganthropology. The contributory economy becomes the Plaine Commune contributory-income experiment.

items.title: 4. The Ars Industrialis project
items.text:
• Founded spring 2005 in Paris (manifesto; the association was active roughly 2005–2020). Public sessions were held at the Théâtre de la Colline and Centre Pompidou. It later ran working groups ("techniques of the self", "relational technologies", "economy of contribution"), a Vocabulaire, and the summer school pharmakon.fr (from 2010). It worked closely with the IRI (Institut de recherche et d'innovation, Centre Pompidou), which built contributory annotation tools such as Lignes de temps.
  • Self-image: a research collective modelled, by its own account, on the early Frankfurt School, aimed at public power and industry, not at party politics.
  • Political register: European, reformist, interventionist. It calls for a "new spirit of capitalism", not its abolition. Whether that is a strength or a weakness is a matter for reception.md.

items.title: Reception and critique
items.text:
Home › Reception · sources rated in sources/EVALUATION.md

Everything in this file is evaluation, by reviewers, critics or (where marked) us. The summaries in chapters/ and concepts/ deliberately leave it out.

items.title: 1. Publication history and audience
items.text:
• 2006 (FR). Published by Flammarion in October as a short, cheap book co-signed with the new association. It was one of four Stiegler books that year, alongside Mécréance et discrédit 2–3 and La Télécratie contre la démocratie, and it was the most programmatic of them. Reissued in Flammarion's Champs paperback series in 2008, which is the source of the "2008" date that some sites give (Babelio, catalogue records).
  • French reception is thin. It consists of a bookseller note (Charybde), a short web review that finds the book "peu accessible aux non-initiés" (Cherrier), and reader pages. A 2007 review appeared in Spirale. Ars Industrialis's own sessions (2005–07) were the book's main French context (context).
  • Early English circulation came before the translation, via tactical-media and net-art milieus (Holmes 2007), and via two sections translated by Stephen Barker in New Formations (2012) (Barker).
  • South African reception (2012). A pair of Afrikaans articles in Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe: de Beer's enthusiastic review-article and Roodt's Arendtian critique of the manifestos (de Beer, Roodt).
  • 2014 English edition. Reviewed by Patrick Lyons in Critical Inquiry and Christian Lotz in Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015). (Lyons, Lotz).

items.title: 2.1 "Abstract diagnosis, empty remedy"
items.text: Lotz: the positive notion of spirit is expressed through "empty placeholders" ("battle against regression", "conquest of the best over the worst", p. 71). The only concrete example of cooperative knowledge tools is Wikipedia (p. 87). Lyons agrees that the book offers few concrete answers, though he reads it as a "philosophy of hope". Goodreads readers repeat the verdict: strong diagnosis, abstract remedies (Goodreads). - Possible response (labelled interpretation): the book does contain sectoral proposals. These are Ch. 2's "practical consequences" (pp. 91–94: specific instruments for research and education, new editorial functions, delinearized audiovisual objects, societies of authors and readers) and the 2010 Manifesto's seven policy planks (six in the web draft). What is missing is less concreteness than an account of political agency: who carries the programme against whom.

items.title: 2.2 The Marxist objection: proletarianization without class
items.text: Lotz: control of labour "evaporates" into control of consumption. The production/consumption dialectic and the role of money and capital go unanalysed, and the framework is Kantian, Enlightenment and reformist social-democratic. Hutnyk (2012) and Manche (2021) generalize the point. Redefining proletarianization as loss of knowledge sidelines exploitation and accumulation. It yields "good capitalism vs bad capitalism", and the contributory economy risks self-exploitation and co-optation (Hutnyk, Manche). - Primary evidence relevant to the dispute: the book's own section titles ("Making the revolution of capitalism"; "The jumpstart"); Stiegler's 2005 call for an "enlightened capitalism" (Libération); the Tunis motion's "new spirit of capitalism"; and Stiegler in 2010 bracketing the question of whether the new model will still be capitalism (Lemmens interview). The reformist reading is textually well grounded. Whether reformism is a fault is a judgement of framework.

items.title: 2.3 Statism and Europeanism
items.text: The manifestos and motion call for a "new form of public power" with industry, and for a European industrial policy (Beffa, Lisbon). Lemmens (2017) finds this statist, and doubts it can be squared with the decentralized contributory model (Lemmens). Lotz notes the "politics of decentralization" (p. 63) but sees no movement to carry it.

items.title: 2.4 Spirit and its genealogy
items.text:
• Roodt (Arendtian): the 2005 Manifesto invokes Arendt's Life of the Mind, but by treating mind as libido and as a function of economic forces it loses Arendt's distinction between thinking and doing.
  • De Beer: embraces the spirit vocabulary in a quasi-spiritual, Heideggerian register.
  • Abbinnett: a Derridean reading. Spirit must pass through technical memory, against Beardsworth's "futural" reading (Abbinnett).
  • Rossouw: re-enchantment and the "new otium" as Christianity by other means (Rossouw).
  • Cohen: the Valéry genealogy; care as Foucauldian epimeleia (Cohen).

items.title: 2.5 Media-theory reception
items.text: Hansen finds it "curious", even "perverse", that the programme seeks to save libidinal capitalism by re-enchanting it (Hansen). Lyons reads the 2014 book through the pharmakon. Lotz credits it with extending culture-industry critique from content to technological systems.

items.title: 2.6 Decline narrative and empirical claims
items.text: Hutnyk reads Stiegler as a conservative "decline" theorist and contests his claims about television and children. The house glossary's claims about screens and synaptogenesis are asserted without discussion (glossary). Hutnyk also turns the pharmakon on Stiegler: "stupidity too can be pharmacological".

items.title: 2.7 Style
items.text: Almost all readers note difficulty: "excessive use of technical terminology" (Lotz), associative prose and shorthand (Lyons), "peu accessible" (Cherrier). A minority call it "tonique" (Charybde).

items.title: 3. The author's own revision
items.text: In The Neganthropocene (2018), Stiegler cites this book as his analysis of Simondon's associated milieus in the digital age. He also concedes that the algorithmic web has become "a systemically dissociating milieu, because it is hyper-proletarianizing". That partly withdraws the 2005–2010 hope that digital networks are intrinsically contributory (Ross file). By 2019 the programme had become a "contributory economy" against entropy, the Neganthropocene (MACBA podcast).

items.title: 4. Afterlife
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis ran sessions, working groups, the Vocabulaire and the pharmakon.fr school. In 2020 it changed its statutes, becoming the "Association des Amis de la Génération Thunberg" (context).
  • "Available brain time" became a French classroom topic, via documentary rather than this book (fiche).
  • Recent readers find the book prescient about attention economies and AI (Goodreads).

items.title: 5. Errors in circulation
items.text: Claim Where Correct Book co-authored with three people EN Wikipedia Five founders sign the collective texts: George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard Stiegler, Caroline Stiegler Catherine Malabou a co-founder some search summaries Not among the founders in any primary source Motion adopted "at" the Tunis Summit; book includes "an account of the organisation's summit in Tunis" Lyons; bookseller blurbs A motion adopted a few days before the summit; Libération (14 Nov 2005) printed excerpts, and the book prints the complete text (Introduction, p. 9) Stiegler at Centre Pompidou in June 2005 P2P Foundation wiki Still IRCAM director; Pompidou from 1 Jan 2006 Published 2008 some sites 2006 first edition; 2008 is the Champs paperback The 2010 Manifesto is part of Réenchanter le monde implied by the EN packaging Added in the English edition only Same book as Maffesoli's Le Réenchantement du monde (2007) or Landy & Saler (2009) search conflation Unrelated books

items.title: 6. What the book's own text says on these debates
items.text:
Evaluation, labelled. The text of the book bears directly on several of the disputes above.

  • Reformism is explicit, with a hedge. Capitalism "to this day does not have a credible alternative" (Introduction, p. 6). The aim is to make "the revolution of a capitalism that is on the road to collapse" together with "revolutionary capitalists", likened to the French bourgeoisie of the late eighteenth century (p. 53). Public opinion should back industrial capitalism against financier capitalism (p. 7). This supports Lotz, Hutnyk and Manche on the reformist reading. Yet Stiegler also writes of a new spirit of capitalism "while waiting for the replacement of the latter by another form of society" (p. 37), and of no future "of capitalism, or a beyond of capitalism, which is certainly not eternal" (p. 60). His position is therefore post-capitalist in horizon and reformist in strategy, not simply pro-capitalist.
  • "Only Wikipedia" is too strong. Lotz says Wikipedia is the book's only example of cooperative knowledge instruments. Chapter 1 already rests its alternative on open-source software, Linux and the IP network as an associated milieu (pp. 36–37), and the 2010 Manifesto adds free software, smart grids and AMAP.
  • "Abstract remedy" is partly answered. Chapter 1 specifies the agents (a new European public power; enterprising citizens), the model (the economy of contribution) and the danger (financier capitalism and tele-cracy). Its political agency remains thin, as Lotz says: there is no account of how the public power is to be built against the interests that profit from dissociation, interests the chapter itself identifies (p. 40).
  • The labour objection. Lotz says labour control "evaporates". Chapter 1 does address labour: Taylorism as the grammatization of gesture (n. 38); de-industrialization as offshoring to "very poorly remunerated workers, if not… slaves" (p. 29); and the proletarianized producer turned consumer under Fordism (p. 35). But it subordinates exploitation of labour to the loss of knowledge and the exhaustion of libido, which is just what the Marxist critics object to.
  • The decline narrative. Chapter 1's evidence for "spiritual misery" is largely anecdotal and drawn from the press: a Nice crime, Skyblogs, the Durn and Brunerie cases, the November 2005 riots, an Inserm study on attention disorders (pp. 39, 57–58). This bears out Hutnyk's methodological complaint, though it is consistent with the book's genre as an engaged manifesto.
  • The pharmakon reading (Lyons) is supported by the 2006 text itself (pp. 47–51), not just by the 2010 Manifesto.
  • Lotz's page citations are accurate. His references to pp. 1–4, 6–7, 23–24, 33 ("enslaved spirit"), 57 (short-circuiting transindividuation) and 58 ("lost the feeling of existing") all match the text.
  • Property. The complete motion (p. 95) calls knowledge a common good that "does not belong to anyone" and accepts only temporary limits from intellectual property. That is a sharper challenge to property relations than the Marxist reviews allow. Ch. 2 still frames the aim as "the reconstitution of a capitalist future" (p. 67).
  • State and the US model. The motion praises American federal industrial strategy (the internet, the FCC, the State with universities and the military) as a model for Europe (pp. 98–99). This supports Lemmens's charge of statism, but it is a strategic, not a nationalist, statism.
  • Concreteness. Ch. 2 names specific projects (INA 1997, IRCAM, IRI, the 1989–92 computer-assisted-reading prototype, the 1996 Nord-Pas-de-Calais report). The "abstract remedy" charge fits the philosophical framing better than the policy content.
  • Hindsight. The judgement that Lisbon "will have been a total failure" (p. 91) may be a later revision for the English edition.

items.title: 7. Open questions
items.text:
These are open questions the sources leave undecided. They are posed neutrally and are not answered here:

  • Does the knowledge/information (negentropy/entropy) distinction hold up outside its thermodynamic metaphor?
  • Is "loss of knowledge" a deeper or a narrower definition of proletarianization than Marx's?
  • Can an "industrial politics of spirit" be carried by public power and industry, as the book proposes, or does it require a social movement, as its critics say?
  • How should the 2006 hope for digital "new spiritual devices" be read after platform capitalism and the author's own 2018 revision?

items.title: Translator's Preface (Trevor Arthur), pp. vii–ix
items.text: Home › Overview › Structure › Translator's Preface · next: Introduction →

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text: A three-page note by the American translator. It explains two choices that shape how English readers meet the book: leaving savoir-faire and savoir-vivre untranslated, and the inadequacy of "spirit" for esprit. On the way it gives a compact gloss of the book's problem: industrial populism proletarianizes us twice, as workers and as consumers. Its remedy is the value of spirit.

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
• The French is technically easy but syntactically intricate. Long nested clauses are kept where possible.
  • Savoir-faire = the craftsman's, techne-bound knowledge. Losing it to machines is proletarianization.
  • Savoir-vivre = social grace and care for self and others (politesse, heard through polis). Losing it in the role of consumer is a second proletarianization. It is glossed through Simondon's individuation and transindividuation.
  • In consumer society desire is reduced to drives, sublimation is cancelled, and needs and wants are confused. This is the problem of industrial populism.
  • Valeur esprit (no "of" in French). Esprit joins the psychic, social, intellectual and historical. It is where memory and intelligence meet in reflection.

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text: pp. Move vii Difficulty lies in style, not lexicon. Justifies leaving savoir-faire in French: its double sense of general practical wisdom and the specific skill of a techne. The worker "stripped of his savoir-faire" is proletarianized, and service industries now saturate personal life too. viii Savoir-vivre: the consumer relinquishes it and is "proletarianized all over again". Drives versus desire; sublimation; addiction ("addictive and toxic environment"). Introduces "industrial populism" and "the value of spirit" as the book's poles. viii–ix Esprit versus "spirit": common root spiritus (breath). Esprit as a synthesis tied to individuation ("one becomes who he is") and transindividuation ("we become who we are"). The closing image is of the world able to "sing again" through a revaluation of desire over drives and association over discord.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Interpretive (labelled): the preface already frames the book in the later vocabulary of drives, addiction and care. That framing fits the 2010 Manifesto better than the 2006 chapters.
  • The text has small typos ("contra", "le valeur", "Steigler", "savior-faire"). Reviewers such as Patrick Lyons (see reception.md) credit the preface with clarifying "spirit".

items.title: Introduction: What Is to Be Done? (pp. 1–10)
items.text: Home › Overview › Structure › Introduction · prev: ← Translator's Preface · next: 2005 Manifesto →
path: Introduction: What Is to Be Done?

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text: The Introduction gives the book its title and its problem. In 2005 the French employers' federation, Medef, held its summer university under the slogan "le réenchantement du monde" to promote the "knowledge economy". The book "takes Medef at its word". To re-enchant the world through technologies of consciousness requires revaluing spirit in the economy. The obstacle is that the same milieu (Seillière's preface to a book in which TF1's Patrick Le Lay boasts of selling "available brain time") organizes the "drop in the value of spirit" (Valéry, 1939) through an industrial populism. Twentieth-century capitalism is a libidinal economy that, in capturing desire, destroys it. This is a chapter of Weber's disenchantment. The ecological and demographic stakes of the coming decades demand "a new human consciousness". In short, humanity must overcome the age of consumption through a "new, qualitative growth", a "new industrial model" and a new spirit of capitalism.
path: Introduction: What Is to Be Done?

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. The capitalism called "cultural" or "cognitive" is above all an industrial populism that uses every technical evolution to turn consciousness, "the seat of spirit", into a reflex organ. A brain without consciousness becomes a commodity on the audience market whose value keeps falling (p. 1).
  2. Benjamin and Freud saw that communication technologies began a new history of consciousness and the unconscious. They did not see the organization of capitalism around the consumer as a libidinal economy, a channelling of desire. Benjamin saw the aestheticization of politics under fascism but not the aestheticization of the economy through control technologies and the manufacture of consumers (pp. 1–2).
  3. This libidinal economy, by destroying consciousness, destroys desire. That is a chapter of Weber's disenchantment of the world (p. 2).
  4. Medef's 2005 "re-enchantment" (Denis Kessler; Tony Blair's proposal to move EU agricultural funds to cognitive-technology R&D) is ambiguous. It could be a genuine "jumpstart" of spirit, or the industrial production of knowledge without spirit, as one now produces "brains without consciousness" (pp. 2–3).
  5. Ars Industrialis is "an international association for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit" (p. 3).
  6. Humanity faces challenges (ecology, scarcity; Laurence Tubiana, Robert Lyon's "age of less") that require a new human consciousness and overcoming the age of consumption by "new, qualitative growth" (p. 3).
  7. Contemporary capitalism replaces intelligence and responsibility with "the time of gregarious audiences" and nervous systems turned into reflex, i.e. drive, systems; consumerism has reached a "mortally toxic limit" (p. 4). Only a fight against industrial populism can re-enchant the world by making it desirable again and restoring reason as a motive for living (p. 5).
  8. Medef's slogan alludes to Weber: capitalism unleashed disenchantment through a stroke of enchantment (the Protestant spirit, itself tied to the printing press, a "techno-logy" of spirit). Rationalization is then a new spirit that lowers the value of spirit. The present low point calls for a sursaut ("sudden surge") and a new spirit of capitalism (p. 5).
  9. Capitalism, which "to this day does not have a credible alternative", can survive only by raising the value of spirit against industrial populism. That is why Ars Industrialis was founded (p. 6).
  10. Spirit is a modality of psychic and collective individuation (Simondon). Knowledge is "the treasure bequeathed by those who are dead". The conditions under which a technology of spirit elevates rather than degrades spirit are a question of political economy, not to be left to shareholders. Public opinion must side with industrial capitalism against financier capitalism, "the true underwriter of industrial populism" (p. 7).
path: Introduction: What Is to Be Done?

items.title: Argumentative moves
items.text:
• Taking the adversary at its word. The book does not reject the business slogan "re-enchantment". It radicalizes it, and turns it against those who coined it.
  • Juxtaposition as proof. Seillière's knowledge-economy rhetoric and Le Lay's "brain time" appear in the same book (Les Dirigeants face au changement, 2004). Stiegler treats this co-presence as revealing the system's contradiction.
  • Genealogy by great names. Valéry (value of spirit), Benjamin and Freud (technology and the psyche), Weber (disenchantment) and Derrida (Echographies of Television, 1993) locate the present as an unforeseen stage.
  • From culture critique to political economy. The question "what is to be done?" is answered by founding an association and calling for an industrial politics.
path: Introduction: What Is to Be Done?

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text:
The Introduction has no internal headings. It is divided by asterisks.

pp. Content (paraphrase) x Epigraph, Ulrich Beck. What industrial capitalism disenchants is pre-capitalist tradition, which keeps regenerating. Beck adds that this holds only until the 1950s. 1 Valéry 1939. "Drop in the value of spirit" on the eve of Nazism's catastrophe. Derrida–Stiegler 1993 did not foresee "libidinal television": reality TV soliciting the "scopic drive" (voyeurism/exhibitionism). 1939 → 2000s: 45% radio listenership, no TV, to communication objects chasing "available brain-time" day and night. Cultural/cognitive capitalism = industrial populism; consciousness reduced to a reflex organ ("a slug's" neurons); brain time sold ever cheaper. 1–2 Benjamin and Freud. They saw the new history of consciousness and the unconscious but missed capitalism's reorganization around the consumer as a libidinal economy. They were preoccupied with fascism. Benjamin missed the aestheticization of the economy. 2 Libidinal economy as disenchantment. The organization of desire, which turned into its destruction by destroying consciousness, is a chapter of Weber's disenchantment. Medef's 2005 summer university was titled "The re-enchantment of the world": Kessler, cognitive capitalism, Blair's proposal on agricultural funds. To re-enchant through technologies of consciousness means revisiting the role of spirit in the economy. 2–3 Seillière and Le Lay. Seillière's preface to Les Dirigeants face au changement takes Kessler-like positions on the knowledge economy, and it introduces the very text in which Le Lay describes selling available brain-time, i.e. organizing the drop in the value of spirit, "the reign of stupidity". Dilemma: a jumpstart of spirit, or knowledge without spirit? Is knowledge possible without spirit at all? 3 Ars Industrialis defined. Stakes: humanity needs unprecedented intelligence and responsibility, or humans become "inhuman" (Jarry). Tubiana: the necessary change is so deep it seems unimaginable. Lyon: "the age of less", being rather than having. Survival requires overcoming the age of consumption through qualitative growth, not mere reduction. 4 To survive, humanity must raise the level of intelligence. Mental regression, moral debasement and the anaesthetizing of intelligence and will now govern the hyperindustrial world and the discourse of would-be governors. Program industries replace intelligence with "gregarious audiences" and drive-based reflexes for marketing. The consumerist model is suicidal. 5 Nearly all social life is controlled by the industry of available brain-time. Only a fight against this industrial populism can re-enchant the world, i.e. make it desirable and restore reason (Aristotle's logos and noûs, Valéry's "spirit") as the motive and orientation of existence. Weber: capitalism unleashes disenchantment through a stroke of enchantment (Protestantism, born of the printing press). Rationalization (reason as ratio, calculation) lowers the value of spirit and reifies reason (Lukács, Adorno, Horkheimer, Habermas). The extreme low calls for a rebound, a sursaut, i.e. "the invention of a new spirit of capitalism" (n. 10–11: against Boltanski & Chiapello, Le nouvel esprit du capitalisme; see Mécréance et discrédit). 6 Capitalism will not survive without a new spirit and must fight what in itself secretes industrial populism. It "does not have a credible alternative", so it must open itself to an increase in the value of spirit. Since 9/11 television has become largely drive-based, with potentially tragic geopolitical effects. Against industrial and political populism, fanaticism and regression, and for a new industrial model with the value of spirit at the centre of its libidinal economy, Stiegler founded Ars Industrialis with George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler. Radio, TV, computers and the internet are "spiritual instruments" (Mallarmé on the book): hypomnemata, which supported the "writing of the self" (Foucault) but also the sophists' manipulation of opinion. Philosophy was born fighting that and must now wage a new battle. 7 Ars Industrialis exists to find new philosophical "weapons" and political actions. Spirit, which always presupposes technologies of spirit, is a modality of psychic and collective individuation (Simondon). Knowledge, inherited from the dead, lets a society project and desire a future. When a technology of spirit elevates rather than degrades spirit is a question of political economy, "life or death for humanity", and must not be left to shareholders. Public opinion should back industrial capitalism against financier capitalism. Politics should frame economic initiative through social rules and public investment, via a new form of public power. A seminar, Trouver de nouvelles armes, ran at the Collège International de Philosophie from autumn 2005. 8 Founding story: asked "what is to be done?" at the Schaubühne, Berlin, in January 2005, Stiegler announced an association for 15 April 2005, ahead of the 29 May referendum on the European Constitution. The five founders shared an analysis of the constitution but disagreed about how to respond to the referendum. The website opened on 15 April 2005; the first plenary was held at the Théâtre national de la Colline on 18 June, where the 2005 Manifesto was presented. Later sessions covered cognitive technologies, the Tunis summit, psychic suffering from addictive consumption, and television. The two chapters are "reformulations and elaborations" of papers from the first two working sessions after the inaugural one. 9 The book closes with the complete text of the motion adopted a few days before Tunis, of which Libération published excerpts. Sessions resumed in October 2006 (a new public power; reorganizing education "from top to bottom"). At the same time Stiegler published La Télécratie contre la démocratie. Lettre ouverte aux représentants politiques, with proposals in his own name for the coming French election campaign. At stake is the role of France and Europe in "the survival of mankind". 10 Blank.

items.title: Context you need
items.text:
• Medef: Mouvement des entreprises de France. Ernest-Antoine Seillière was president until July 2005, succeeded by Laurence Parisot (to whom the French edition is dedicated). Denis Kessler was a leading Medef ideologue. See the context files in sources/.
  • Patrick Le Lay: TF1 chief executive. His statement, in Les Dirigeants face au changement (Éditions du Huitième jour, 2004), that what TF1 sells Coca-Cola is "temps de cerveau humain disponible" became proverbial in France.

items.title: Ars Industrialis: 2005 Manifesto (pp. 11–16)
items.text:
Home › Overview › Structure › 2005 Manifesto · prev: ← Introduction · next: 2010 Manifesto →

The text. pp. 11–15 (p. 16 is blank), with notes on p. 102. The association also published English and French versions on its website (source). The text numbers ten "motifs" and then lists the association's goals.

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text: This is the founding text of Ars Industrialis (spring 2005), signed by George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard Stiegler and Caroline Stiegler. Digitization is merging the culture industries, media, telecoms and cognitive technologies into one sector the manifesto names technologies of spirit. Submitted only to market criteria, these serve control. Their control of desire destroys libidinal energy, the very energy twentieth-century capitalism ran on. "This capitalism is self-destructive" and heads for an unprecedented crisis. The remedy is an industrial politics that is also an industrial ecology of spirit. It would be carried by a new form of public power and would invent new practices of these technologies understood as hypomnemata. The manifesto ends with ten "motifs and motives" and a programme of meetings, including one on the Tunis WSIS.

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. The "life of the mind/spirit" (Arendt) faces total subjection to market imperatives through converging culture, program, media, telecom and cognitive industries.
  2. These technologies of spirit could found a new age of spirit. Under market criteria alone they serve societies of control (Burroughs/Deleuze) and short-term profit.
  3. Control of desire destroys singularity, and with it existence. Capitalism harnessed libido to absorb surplus production. That capture now destroys libido, which "leads, inevitably, to an unprecedented global crisis".
  4. The ruin of desire is the ruin of sublimation and of the super-ego, and has psychic, social, political and geopolitical consequences.
  5. Desire's objects are singular (incalculable). Industrial fabrication of desire categorizes singularities. ICTs are hypomnemata (Foucault, Plato) and so call for new practices and social organizations, not just user manuals and marketing.
  6. The task is to "give a boost to desire", not consumption. That requires a new public power uniting all kinds of competence.

items.title: Argumentative moves
items.text:
• Thesis by naming. Coining "technologies of spirit" makes media, telecom and IT one political object.
  • Freud applied to macro-economics. Libido as capitalism's energy source; its exhaustion as systemic risk.
  • Hypomnemata argument. Placing ICTs in the lineage of ancient memory supports (Stoic/Epicurean/Christian hypomnemata) shows they can support care of the self. What is at stake is practice, not the technology itself.
  • Prediction. "Unprecedented global crisis" is a falsifiable claim that the 2010 Manifesto later presents as confirmed.

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text:
The web text is a continuous series of "motifs and motives" followed by objectives. Correspondence with book pages is approximate.

pp. Motif (paraphrase) 11 §1 Threat to the "life of spirit (the mind)" (Arendt, n. 1). It is wholly subjected to market imperatives and to returns on investment in the culture industry, program industry, media, telecoms and cognitive technologies, which are converging through digitization. Ars Industrialis names this ensemble the technologies of spirit, "spirit" to be understood also as English "mind", despite the word's metaphysical baggage. These technologies have so far aggravated control, but "can and must become a new age of spirit". §2 Industrial politics = industrial ecology of spirit. Market-only criteria keep these technologies in the function of control ("societies of control": Burroughs, Deleuze, n. 2), systematizing calculation and communication for mass short-term profit and blocking original social practices. 12 §3 Control of existence destroys desire. Twentieth-century capitalism harnessed libido to absorb production, and that harnessing has finished by destroying libido, which leads "inevitably and eventually to an unprecedented global economic crisis". §4 The ruin of desire is the ruin of sublimation and of the super-ego; beyond economic disruption, it brings geopolitical, political, social and psychic disorders, problems for an "industrial ecology of spirit and desire". 13 §5 Singularity, calculation, hypomnemata. ICTs are spiritual technologies and raise again the question of memory techniques: Foucault's "writing of the self" (n. 4), Plato's hypomnēsis. As new hypomnémata they call, like those of the Stoics, Epicureans and early Christians, or the Roman practice of otium that succeeded Greek skholē (n. 5: J.-M. André, L'Otium…), for new practices and new social organizations. They should not be limited to user manuals and marketing designed for "two-figure returns", never below 15 percent. §6 "This capitalism is self-destructive"; the association will invent practices that reconstitute objects of desire and experiences of singularity. §7 Revive desire, not consumption. European technocratic measures aggravate the problem. Spiritual industries (broadband, wi-fi, tomorrow nanotechnologies) must not grow at the expense of social cohesion. The general interest is symbolic, so a new form of public power is needed. 14 §7 (end): it is to associate competences of every kind, up to local and territorial authorities. §8 Paris-based but above all European, and international. §9 A network of meeting places in French cities. §10 Use of all means of communication; public and private support. Goals: collective, transdisciplinary reflection; publication; motions; preliminary studies and experiments; defence of members' collective interest. Meeting themes (n. 6: Saturday sessions every two months at the Théâtre national de la Colline; seminar Trouver de nouvelles armes): European policy on spiritual industries; Google's digital library initiative; 15 …scientific research; the UN Tunis summit (Nov 2005); marketing and advertising; art and industrial society; European languages and idiomatic difference; psychological disorders and public health; industrial property; views from the US, Latin America, China and Japan on an international public power. Signed George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard Stiegler, Caroline Stiegler.

Notes (p. 102), complete gloss. n. 1 Arendt, The Life of the Mind (1971); n. 2 Deleuze, Pourparlers (1990), p. 242, on control societies; n. 3 thanks to Pierre Sauvanet for the Claudel reference; n. 4 Foucault, "L'écriture de soi", Dits et écrits 2, p. 1234; n. 5 J.-M. André, L'Otium dans la vie morale et intellectuelle romaine (1966), with thanks to Ludovic Duhem; n. 6 public meetings on Saturday afternoons every two months at the Théâtre national de la Colline (thanks to Alain Françon, Alain Herzog, Anne Goalard, Élodie Regibier), with recordings online, plus the seminar Trouver de nouvelles armes at the Collège International de Philosophie, co-led by Georges Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Bernard Stiegler.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Absent here: pharmakon, care (soin), economy of contribution, proletarianization. All appear in the 2010 Manifesto, and the first three are already developed in Ch. 1 (2006, pp. 36–37, 47). Otium, by contrast, is named in the 2005 text in the book (p. 13). That contrast is the clearest measure of how Ars Industrialis's vocabulary developed between 2005 and 2010.
  • Labelled interpretation: the manifesto's politics is reformist and Europeanist ("new public power", partnership with investors). Marxist reviewers such as Lotz criticize exactly this. See reception.md.

items.title: Ars Industrialis: 2010 Manifesto (pp. 17–28)
items.text:
Home › Overview › Structure › 2010 Manifesto · prev: ← 2005 Manifesto · next: Chapter 1 →

The text. pp. 17–28, with notes on pp. 102–104. The Introduction's n. 17 (p. 102) says this text is absent from the 2006 French book and was added for the English edition. The association also published it on its website (source). Sections start on p. 17 (§1), p. 18 (§2–3), p. 19 (§4), p. 22 (§5), p. 23 (§6), p. 25 (§7), p. 26 (§8–9) and p. 28 (§10).

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text: Written five years after the founding and three years into the global financial crisis, this manifesto claims the 2005 diagnosis is vindicated. The crisis is that of the consumerist model as a whole. That model instrumentalized desire (Bernays) and so destroyed it, together with every form of investment. Speculator and consumer share a drive-based, short-termist behaviour. Disposability produces an addictogenic society of carelessness (incurie), so "to economize means first of all to take care". The alternative industrial model is the economy of contribution: free software, contributors rather than producers and consumers, associated milieus. Digital technologies are pharmaka and can either deepen or end generalized proletarianization. Public power must act through seven national policies (industrial, financial, educational, fiscal, cultural, health and media) and through territorial politics.

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. The 2007– crisis is a crisis of consumerism, not only of finance. Destroyed desire means disinvestment and "systemic stupidity".
  2. Disposable objects make subjects feel disposable. Consumer society is toxic environmentally and psychically, addictogenic, and a society of carelessness.
  3. Care must be at the heart of political economy: economizing is taking care.
  4. The consumerist model is obsolete. It must give way to the economy of contribution, which produces positive externalities and capabilities (Sen). On digital networks, contributors form an associated milieu (Simondon).
  5. Digital networks also breed hyper-consumerist behaviour because all hypomnemata are pharmaka (Plato). Without a therapeutic (care, technique of the self) a pharmakon turns toxic. Politics is a system of care, and culture cultivates a caring relation to pharmaka.
  6. Culture industries (new hypomnemata) competed with program institutions (schools) and replaced reason with rationalization. Marketing seized digital relational technologies. Public power has abdicated since Thatcher and Reagan.
  7. Politics must secure the short term in order to reverse it in the long term, moving from disapprenticeship to the development of capabilities.
  8. Proletarianization is defined as the loss of knowledge formalized in an apparatus. It struck workers (savoir-faire), then consumers (savoir-vivre), and now cognitive workers (theoretical knowledge; Greenspan). Free software shows de-proletarianization. Psychotechnologies must become nootechnologies.
  9. The model generalizes: smart grids, community-supported agriculture (AMAP), contributory firms. "Light time" replaces "carbon time". Relational technologies re-territorialize and lead to post-globalization.
  10. National policy has seven planks in the book (the web version has six; the book adds the rebuilding of financial systems against speculation), and Ars Industrialis adopts a programme to match.

items.title: Argumentative moves
items.text:
• Vindication. The 2005 prediction is presented as fulfilled.
  • Psychoanalytic economics generalized. Drives against desire; disinvestment; addiction.
  • Pharmacological turn. Technics is neither good nor bad but needs therapeutics. This replaces the 2005 opposition of control to spirit with a single ambivalent object.
  • Positive model. Free software and peer production become the paradigm of a whole industrial model, the "economy of contribution".
  • Programmatic close. A list of policies, as in a party platform.

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text:
pp. 17–28. The rightmost column notes where the book's text differs from the association's web version.

§ pp. Content (paraphrase) Book vs web version preamble, 1 17–18 Five years after its founding and three years into the crisis, Ars Industrialis publishes a new manifesto. The 2005 prediction (desire diverted to commodities leads "inevitably, sooner or later" to an unprecedented crisis and shows capitalism to be self-destructive) is confirmed by the 2007 subprime collapse. Speculative finance played the short term against the long term, but the deeper crisis is that of the consumerist model built on Bernays's instrumentalization of desire (via Freud, his uncle), which destroys desire and so all investment (economic, political, social). Speculator and consumer are linked as drive-based; disinvestment is the effect of neoliberal short-termism. The consumer's relation to objects is destructive, a loss of fidelity to objects of desire, producing "systemic stupidity" (n. 2: generalized loss of knowledge, replaced by information). same argument; the book adds the preamble sentence 2 18 Disposable objects sustain innovation cycles (Schumpeter) and colossal waste. The subject who disposes feels disposable. Consumerist society is toxic for the environment and for psychic apparatuses: addictogenic (French toxicology and addiction congress, 2009: "Addictogenic Society"). The addicted no longer take care of self, others or world. This makes a society of carelessness (incurie; n. 3: BP as "Beyond Petroleum", the pharmaceutical "treatment" of attention problems, an "industry of carelessness"), i.e. a dissociation. Care must return to the heart of political economy. Axiom: to economize means first of all to take care. same; n. 3 is book only 3 18–19 The consumption model, devised to overcome the limits of nineteenth-century productivism, is broken by its negative externalities: toxic assets, pollution, resource exhaustion, destruction of the life of spirit, attention disorders, irresponsibility and incivility, generalized lying, trickery and corruption (n. 4: Atlan), and the becoming-mafioso of capital, which Keynes sensed in the 1930s (n. 5: Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren, on a "generalized nervous depression"). Its successor is the economy of contribution: positive externalities, i.e. care for self and others, Sen's capabilities. It has been developing for about 20 years (open source); on the internet there is no division of producers and consumers; contributors form an associated milieu (Simondon) that reconstitutes sublimation and responsibility. book adds lying/trickery, Atlan and Keynes 4 19–21 Social networks spread fast and show hyper-consumerist, addictogenic behaviour more violent and mimetic than the culture industries'. (4.1) Digital technologies are hypomnemata, hence pharmaka. (4.2) All technics is pharmacological; without a therapeutic (melete, epimeleia; n. 6: the "Techniques de soi" group) a pharmakon turns toxic; politics is a system of care; culture cultivates a caring relation to pharmaka. (4.3) Writing, then print and the Reformation, founded Western savoir-vivre, spread by Jesuit missions ahead of industrial markets. (4.4) Culture industries, new hypomnemata (Benjamin understood this, the Frankfurt School did not), compete with program institutions; reason gives way to rationalization. (4.5) Digital hypomnemata could overcome this, but marketing seized these relational technologies (n. 8: poison if left to marketing, cure if made the object of an "inquisitive" politics in Bossuet's sense). (4.6) Since Thatcher and Reagan public power has given up its role: making technical development a social future. (4.7) This carelessness risks a politico-military-ecological catastrophe. Public power, weakened by neoliberal dogma, is instrumentalized by twentieth-century economic powers. same; notes book only 5 22–23 Political forces must take a position. A new role for public power: support the emerging economy of contribution. Consumerism is hegemonic at its limit. True political action, the application of new political and economic knowledge, means "guaranteeing the short term in order to reach the long term" and reversing it. Each of us is both a dependent, unhappy consumer and a citizen. Consumerism, "founded on disposability, waste, carelessness, and blindness", contradicts the future of the 100 million babies born each year. Neoliberalism entrusted development to marketing and demoralized the young. A critical path, negotiated and not monopolized by lobbies, toward a new industrial economy founded on care: not green consumerism but a new savoir-vivre. Move from "disapprenticeship" (Madoff as symptom of systemic stupidity) to the development of all capabilities and forms of knowledge. The digital is a pharmakon that can aggravate proletarianization; Facebook is cited. same 6 23–25 Proletarianization defined: knowledge formalized in a technique, machine or device escapes the individual. Workers lose savoir-faire (Smith, Marx); in the twentieth century consumers lose savoir-vivre to devices and services (TV "takes care" of children, producing "available brain time"), with loss of recognition, sociability, existence; cognitive workers lose theoretical, critical knowledge (Greenspan before the House; Madoff at Nasdaq). Free software breaks with generalized proletarianization by socializing technical possibilities through "social innovation" rather than disposable "innovation". Psychotechnologies must become nootechnologies; de-proletarianization as a principle (free-software workers inventing a new organization of work). same 7 25–26 The model generalizes beyond the digital, which it still needs as a "technogeographical associated milieu" (n. 10: Pour en finir avec la mécroissance; n. 11: Simondon). "Light time" replaces "carbon time"; servers replace centre and periphery; isonomy and autonomy. Transmitter, central power station and buying office give way to smart grids and cooperative arrangements (AMAP, n. 12): no separate energy producers and consumers. Contributory businesses whose ethic (Weber) is care as political economy must learn from the failure of Charles Gide's and Marcel Mauss's cooperative movements. A pharmacology of relational technologies and Sen-style "capacitation" (n. 13) become priorities for local and territorial authorities. book adds Gide and Mauss 8 26 Relational ecology and a new territoriality. Relational technologies are territorializable and localizable (GPS, Google Earth); with post-consumerism this opens post-globalization. The end of consumerism ends globalization as dis-integration of territories. Territory is a space of known externalities and the privileged terrain of political de-proletarianization against the citizen-as-consumer (and against "mediocre electoral products"). Post-globalization is the inscription of territory in planetary reticularity: "hyper-learning" (n. 14: Veltz). same 9 26–28 A politics of digital territories, supported nationally (not territories in competition) and at European level, consisting of seven planks: (1) a scientific, technological and industrial politics for the new digital system and a reasoned break with consumerist capitalism (n. 15: territories and the critique of the "creative economy"); (2) rebuilding financial systems for an economy of investment protected from speculation, ending a consumerist model kept alive only by public and private debt under transnational financial players (n. 16: Jorion; n. 17: Lordon); (3) education and universities using digital hypomnemata to reconfigure written knowledge, not to proletarianize; "digital natives", parents and teachers are left to the market; (4) fiscal and territorial policy rewarding positive externalities, with labour time and new forms of work distinct from "employment"; (5) culture as social investment and "capacitation" (n. 18: Sen), new forms of care and techniques of self and "we"; (6) a health politics of psychotechnologies and non-drug addictions, read pharmacologically after Plato; (7) a new media politics against industrial populism, restoring press and program industries to their role in public space against carelessness and the destruction of attention. book has 7 planks; the web version has 6 (no financial-systems plank) 10 28 Means: working groups on "techniques of self"; contributive technologies with subscribers (Conseil Régional d'Île-de-France; Lignes de temps software); work with territories (Nantes Métropole, Nord-Pas-de-Calais); research on the model of the Frankfurt School's Institute for Social Research. same

Notes (pp. 102–104), complete gloss. n. 1 the 2005 Manifesto online (node/1472); n. 2 systemic stupidity as generalized proletarianization, the loss of knowledge replaced by information; n. 3 the society of carelessness; n. 4 Atlan, De la fraude (2010); n. 5 Keynes; n. 6 the Techniques de soi group (Cabantous, Gautier, Giffard); n. 7 Pomeranz, La Force de l'empire (coal and colonial cotton behind British industrialization); n. 8 relational technologies as poison or cure; n. 9 Cormerais, the economy of contribution; n. 10 Pour en finir avec la mécroissance (2009); n. 11 Simondon, Du mode d'existence des objets techniques; n. 12 the AMAP network; n. 13 Sen, The Idea of Justice; n. 14 Veltz (1994); n. 15 territories and the critique of the "creative economy"; n. 16 Jorion, L'implosion (2008); n. 17 Lordon, La crise de trop (2009); n. 18 Sen, L'économie est une science morale.

Highlights: - n. 3: the "society of carelessness": BP rebranded as "Beyond Petroleum" before the Gulf of Mexico spill; the pharmaceutical industry "treating" attention problems produced by program industries; an "industry of carelessness". - n. 5: Keynes, Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren: without a cultural mutation to match the technical one, "a generalized nervous depression". - n. 8: relational technologies are poison if left to irresponsible marketing, cure if made the object of an "inquisitive" (curieuse) politics in Bossuet's sense. - n. 9: the concept of an economy of contribution was suggested by Franck Cormerais. - n. 10: Pour en finir avec la mécroissance (Ars Industrialis, 2009). - n. 13, 18: Sen; n. 14: Veltz; n. 16: Jorion; n. 17: Lordon.
