items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Chronology (corrected). This text was added in 2014 but written in 2010. Pharmakon, associated milieu and the economy of contribution are not new here: Ch. 1 (2006) already develops them (pp. 36–37, 47–51). What is new in 2010 is their systematic use: care as the axiom of political economy, Sen's capabilities, territories and smart grids, and the seven policy planks. Earlier versions of this file said these terms were "at most embryonic" in the chapters; that was wrong.
  • Labelled interpretation: this manifesto is the book's most concrete answer to the charge (Lotz) that Stiegler offers no positive programme. Reviewers who stress abstraction tend to under-weight it.

items.title: Chapter 1 — The Re-Foundation of Society (pp. 29–60)
items.text:
Home › Overview › Structure › Chapter 1 · prev: ← 2010 Manifesto · next: Chapter 2 →

Provenance (from the Introduction, p. 8). Chapters 1 and 2 are "reformulations and elaborations" of papers Stiegler gave at the first two Ars Industrialis working sessions after the inaugural meeting of 18 June 2005. Chapter 1 was updated to spring 2006: it cites events and press from April 2006.

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text:
Chapter 1 argues that society must be re-founded, and that this requires a revolution of capitalism.

  • Diagnosis. We now live in a hyperindustrial society, with no way back from industry. Its form is service capitalism. Services, delivered through "R technologies, that is, relational technologies" (p. 29), take over the activities through which people once shaped their own lives. They "discharge" the consumer of his existence.
  • Mechanism. Individuation proceeds by adopting ways of life. When service capitalism controls adoption, it destroys individuation and generalizes proletarianization. Producers lose savoir-faire and consumers lose savoir-vivre. The world becomes insipid and the spirit "servile".
  • Associated vs dissociated milieus. The root problem is the dissociated milieu, in which producers and consumers are split. Stiegler draws on Simondon's associated milieu and argues that the internet is the first industrial technical milieu that is structurally associated. That makes possible an economy of contribution modelled on open-source software. This is the remedy, provided public power keeps the internet from being turned into an instrument of control.
  • Libido and the drives. Capitalism is a libidinal economy. Libido, not oil or coal, makes it run. By exhausting libido it becomes a capitalism of drives, heading toward barbarism.
  • The jumpstart. Against this Stiegler calls for a jumpstart (le sursaut), an "undertaking to found" (entreprendre de fonder). It is to be understood through the long history of grammatization: writing, like every pharmakon, can found individuation (the Greek polis) or ruin it (the sophists).
  • Europe. The programme is European: a European public power and a European way of life that put consistencies back at the centre of a new industrial model.
  • The plane that enchants me. The closing section describes the plane of consistencies or motifs, the incalculable objects of desire. Stiegler calls it "the plane of enchantment" (p. 58). Capitalism must take care of it if it is to have any future.

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. There is no alternative to an ever more industrial world. "De-industrialization" is a new international division of labour, not an exit from industry (p. 29).
  2. Hyperindustrial service capitalism controls attention and behaviour across every segment of existence through relational (R) technologies: telecoms and broadcast networks, barcodes, chip cards, RFID, wi-fi and Bluetooth, biometrics and nanotechnologies (p. 29).
  3. Services discharge the consumer of productive tasks, and so of the chance to decide their own way of living (façon de vivre). This is a debilitating reversal of Hegel's master/slave dialectic (pp. 30–31).
  4. Individuation is adoption. Adoption has a future only if adopters can individuate themselves "otherwise, and by themselves", which intensifies their singularity, their negentropy. Service capitalism controls adoption down to primary and secondary identification, and so destroys individuation (pp. 31–32).
  5. Generalized proletarianization. Producers lose savoir-faire and become labour power. Consumers lose savoir-vivre and become purchasing power. Cognitive capitalism liquidates knowledge, producing entropy and distaste and an "enslaved", servile spirit (pp. 32–33).
  6. Re-enchantment requires leaving dissociated milieus behind. These are milieus where marketing's "modes of employment" replace practices and design short-circuits practical time. Dissociation is "capitalism, which needs a spirit" yet destroys it (pp. 34–35).
  7. The internet, unlike earlier industrial apparatuses, "structurally constitutes an associated milieu" (p. 37). Open source shows an economy of contribution that should replace the service economy. It can still be captured by user profiling. Whether it is depends on a new public power (pp. 36–37).
  8. R technologies are themselves hypomnemata, so they are technologies of spirit. They currently serve disindividuation, but they could support individuation. Recorded music shows both sides: loss of listening skills on one hand, jazz on the other (pp. 37–38).
  9. The first service is leisure: taking charge of people's time and distracting them, as the jester distracted the king. Patrick Le Lay and the "client-king" are the examples. Diverting children's primary identification toward television amounts to desublimation (pp. 38–39).
  10. Capitalism runs on libido. Libido is sublimated drive energy that projects consistencies (love, knowledge, art). Industrial exploitation exhausts it. Motivation turns into de-motivation, philia and the "we" are destroyed, and capitalism becomes drive-based and barbarous, "denuded of spirit". This links 9/11, Richard Durn (26 March 2002), and the National Front vote of 21 April 2002 (pp. 39–43).
  11. The jumpstart is the re-founding of the "human enterprise". It means maintaining the conditions of meta-transformation: the capacity to transform how we transform, against the temptation of the worst (Simondon). The American way of life is exhausted and toxic, even though America leads in associated milieus such as the web (pp. 44–47).
  12. Grammatization history. Hydraulic empires used writing to control. The Greek polis turned literal writing into an associated milieu, and so into citizenship. Plato's Phaedrus stages the fight over this pharmakon. Nora and Minc (1978) foresaw the convergence of audiovisual, telecom and computing, but missed "tele-cracy" (Berlusconi) and the industrial politics of technologies of spirit (pp. 47–51).
  13. Making the revolution of capitalism. Re-founding must come from enterprising citizens supported by a new public power, on the model of the revolutionary French bourgeoisie of the late eighteenth century. The alternative is financier capitalism and a "tele-cracy" that restores autocracy (pp. 51–53).
  14. A European way of life. Europe must become a European public power. The French "no" to the 2005 constitution expressed a feeling of public powerlessness. Saturation by automobiles, information and RFID chips shows where dissociated milieus lead. Young people who have "lost the feeling of existing" (Durn, Brunerie, the November 2005 rioters) mark the limit (pp. 53–58).
  15. The plane that enchants me. Desire aims only at the incalculable and singular: works of art (Kant's reflective judgement), the beloved. These consistencies "do not exist" and must be cared for. A libidinal economy is an oikos-nomos of care. Without such care there is no future "of capitalism, or a beyond of capitalism" (pp. 58–60).

items.title: Argumentative moves
items.text:
• Etymological arguments. Sapere gives savour, so knowledge makes the world "sapid". Service recalls the serfs once charged with chores. Entreprendre combines apprendre, comprendre and surprendre (to learn, understand, surprise). Intelligence is inter-legere, "being-among". Économie is the nomos of the oikos.
  • Simondon applied to industry. Individuation, transindividuation, the associated milieu (the Guimbal turbine) and the "temptation" toward a lower level of individuation are all carried over into a critique of the service economy.
  • Freud reread economically. Libido is the energy of capitalism. Its exhaustion explains motivation crises and acting out. Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents is said to anticipate Nazism.
  • A deep history of technics as the frame for policy. The chapter runs from Sumerian tablets to RFID implants, so that the digital appears as a new stage of grammatization: both poison and cure.
  • Dated case studies (2005–06). A Nice rape filmed on a phone; Skyblogs; Applied Digital Solutions' implantable chip; INRIA/JCDecaux; Microsoft Research's "Intelligent Environments" symposium (Cambridge, 5–7 April 2006); the Béarn hunger strike; Seillière and Le Lay.
  • Reformist framing. "Revolution of capitalism", led by "revolutionary capitalists". But Stiegler also writes that capitalism "is certainly not eternal" and speaks of a possible "beyond of capitalism" (pp. 37, 60).

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text: pp. Section Content (paraphrase) 29–30 The hyperindustrial epoch as service capitalism There is no future except in a more industrial world. In hyperindustrial society all forms of life become objects of rationalization, investment and service. This continues a process of grammatization, defined in note 2 as the discretization of human behaviours that makes them reproducible. Its new hypomnemata are both control technologies and potential supports of "a new age of spirit", a hope voiced by UNESCO (n. 4) and by business. De-industrialization relocates production; service capitalism is just as industrial. Cheap personal apparatuses make all of existence an object of permanent control of attention and behaviour through "R technologies," that is, relational technologies (p. 29; n. 5 cites Rifkin, The Age of Access): telecom and broadcast networks, barcode and chip-card readers, RFID (n. 6), wi-fi, Bluetooth, biometrics, nanotechnologies. Service enterprises thus become the main actors of public life, and steering how ways of life evolve becomes a matter of taking control. 30–31 The consumer discharged of his existence Every epoch's social dynamism is the permanent transformation of ways of life, that is, psychic and collective individuation (n. 7: individuation is not individualization; Simondon). Humans cannot merely subsist; they "ex-sist" by transforming themselves. Societies are systems of cooperation and competition (Greek eris), now co-piloting their individuation at planetary scale. Service industries transform ways of life but short-circuit transindividuation: one's existence changes without one's participation. The consumer, relieved of productive tasks, is "relatively disaffected". The relief is sold as a "discharge" (as serfs were once "charged" with chores), but it divests the person of their existence and of the power to choose a way of living. Stiegler calls this a reversal and a debilitation of Hegel's master/slave dialectic (n. 9). 31–33 Hyperindustrial service societies as the destruction of processes of individuation through the control of processes of adoption Nobody decides how they live; we reproduce or adopt ways of life (family, education, foreign cultures, merchandise, evangelism, culture industries). "The process of individuation is essentially a process of adoption" (n. 10: Technics and Time 3). Civilizations form by inventing and adopting: China, whose characters are an Asian hypomnematon; Alexander's mutual religious adoptions in Egypt. Adoption has a future only if adopters can individuate "otherwise, and by themselves", raising their singularity or negentropy (n. 12). By controlling adoption down to primary and secondary identification (n. 13: disidentification; Télécratie), hyperindustrial capitalism destroys individuation. Using information and communication technologies (ICTs) as control rather than individuation technologies, it generalizes proletarianization: producers lose savoir-faire and become labour power; consumers lose savoir-vivre, which becomes a "mode of employment", and are left as purchasing power. Life loses its savour (sapere/sapid). Cognitive capitalism (Negri to Seillière) and the knowledge society (Blair, UNESCO, Serres) are announced just as capitalism liquidates knowledge and produces entropy and distaste. Marc Jimenez's "mystification of the masses" (n. 14) lacks an account of grammatization and a general organology (n. 15: co-evolution of physiological, technical and social organs). The result is an "enslaved spirit" serving service societies (p. 33): general ill-being, with hyperconsumption as only one symptom (n. 16: the Ars Industrialis session "Suffering and Consumption", 25 Feb 2006; against Lipovetsky). Civilization's discontent has become the discontent of consumption, "particularly in France". 33–37 Re-enchanting the world faced with the unhappy destiny of consumption There was a happy postwar age of consumption, though Debord in the 1950s already announced its unhappy destiny. That destiny arrived with the generalized service economy. The industrial economy supplied material goods (appliances); the service economy destroys the social game itself, i.e. individuation as a participatory process (Simondon, IPC p. 18). Language is the model of a participatory milieu: speakers individuate themselves and the language at once. One does not "use" a language, any more than one "uses" a piano (n. 19; Crépon). The service economy rests on designers controlling consumers' behaviour, so consumers find no material through which to individuate and become disindividuated ("life time value", n. 20). Re-enchantment requires leaving dis-sociated milieus: there, design upstream of production short-circuits practical time and marketing's uses replace practices. Consumers are proletarianized as producers were. Fordism generalizes this; when it reaches symbolic milieus it causes great suffering. Dissociation is capitalism, "which needs a spirit" and is destroying it (n. 21). Associated milieus (pp. 36–37): Simondon's concept, illustrated by the Guimbal turbine cooled by the very water that drives it. Digital hypomnemata form technical and industrial associated milieus in which addressees are in principle in the position of designers. The internet, an associated, participatory and dialogic milieu since 1992, makes possible "the economy of contribution typical of open-source software" (Linux; users as practitioners). This is the basis of a new industrial model to replace dissociated milieus, which are "ANTISOCIAL". Any associated milieu can be turned toward control (user profiling, n. 23). What is new is that the internet "structurally constitutes an associated milieu" (p. 37). That novelty must become the object of a public politics, so that the associated digital milieu is not "instrumentalized by R technologies" and so that a new spirit of capitalism can emerge, "while waiting for the replacement of the latter by another form of society". 37–39 R technologies and the new spiritual devices Individuation needs cultivated, associated social milieus and develops all three forms of knowledge (savoir-vivre, savoir-faire, theoretical). Control devices are also hypomnemata. Cognitive and cultural industries currently use them in dissociated milieus as control or R technologies (n. 24), yet they remain technologies of spirit and could become supports of individuation. Music shows both sides: with Nicolas Donin, the "machinic revolving of the sensibility" (n. 25) lost listeners their musical knowledge, yet the same recording devices produced jazz as a new form of writing and individuation. The canalization of attention by culture industries was the first service: taking charge of people's time and distracting them, like the jester distracting the king. Patrick Le Lay confirms the point, and "to distract" also means to steal: the "client-king's" attention is hijacked for prescriptions of consumption, replacing free judgement with systematic conditioning. Children become helpless, herd-like, impulsive, overinformed and disaffected. Counter-tendencies (the web, blogs) are hijacked too (Skyrock's Skyblogs), leading toward "the war of all against all". Spiritual misery: a rape in Nice at the end of 2005 was filmed on a phone by the aggressor (n. 26). This tendency leads to the capitalism of drives. Television diverts the primary identification by which children inherit from parents. Dissociation becomes desublimation, liquidating the family and the psyche. 39–44 Overcoming the capitalism of drives and fighting its becoming-barbaric The promised knowledge-based "cognitive" or "cultural" capitalism will not happen while the model of dissociated milieus endures. Firms profit from dissociation in the short term and are self-destructive in the long term. Capitalism has rested on controlling concepts and affects through R technologies, the "control" Deleuze named, with television as its principal instrument (n. 27: Deleuze, letter to Serge Daney). Control destroys public space and time and breeds uncontrollable societies. Libido is socialized, sublimated sexual energy; societies are apparatuses for canalizing it into roles, civilities and savoir-vivre. It projects consistencies (love, sophia, science, art), i.e. objects that "do not exist". The libidinal economy economizes: it defers satisfaction (Derrida's différance; pleasure is not jouissance) and binds life and death drives (Freud after 1920; Civilization and Its Discontents foreshadows Nazism). Libido, "neither oil nor coal" nor any other energy, makes capital function. Motivation (Bergson's "gods") is produced under conditions that now invert it into de-motivation: indifference, disaffection, disgust, hate (n. 30). Exhausting libido destroys the "we", philia and affectio societatis; financierization accelerates this. Capitalism becomes barbarous, "denuded of spirit", with no "desire for the future". This connects 9/11, Richard Durn (Nanterre, 26 Mar 2002) and the National Front vote (21 Apr 2002). Traditional societies took care of this energy under names such as philia, eros, agape, caritas, mana. The man of hyperindustrial society of control is infantilized and stripped of initiative. When "discharge" becomes capital's main revenue source it becomes disindividuation, eliminating experience (n. 31: the self-driving car whose freed time is sold as "available brain"; Rifkin's "marketization of experience"). 44–47 The jumpstart (le sursaut): starting over again Opposing foreign ways of life is not the point; societies leapt forward by adopting them. The question is the conditions under which new ways of life form, i.e. meta-transformation: knowing how to transform how we transform. Transformation can lead to the best or the worst (dissociating, drive-based, barbarous). Simondon describes the "fundamental temptation" in individuation, a regression to a lower level (n. 32). Meta-transformation is the function of primary parental identification and of a superego produced through criticism of the inherited one. America invented a style of transforming ways of life ("the American way of life") that is now exhausted and toxic (n. 33): it substitutes the police society (société policière) for civil society (société policée) and provokes fundamentalisms. Yet America also revived associated milieus with the web, exploiting European public research while Europe imitated and subsidized it. The fashionable talk of "winners and losers" ignores that everyone loses from carelessness: Chernobyl's cloud "stopping" at the French border; a "lose/lose" tendency toward disindividuation. Hence the need for a jumpstart, a public good and a rupture. Enterprise needs a spirit of enterprise, not a "debilitated", "rotten" or "servile" spirit. Humans are spontaneously enterprising (entreprendre, apprendre, comprendre, surprendre), so the task is to "UNDERTAKE A FOUNDATION (ENTREPRENDRE DE FONDER)" (p. 46). When enterprises and societies hit a limit they must take a leap (sauter un pas): a jumpstart is a rupture (p. 47). 47–51 Grammatization and individuation—yesterday, today, and tomorrow The drop in the value of spirit is caused by technologies of spirit reduced to control (n. 34), and it can be fought only with the same technologies. The poison is the remedy: the pharmakon (Plato, Derrida, n. 35), reanalysed in Mécréance et discrédit 3 as a question of socio-therapy, of care for individuation, "the political question par excellence", which passes through industry. Technologies of spirit result from grammatization (n. 36), which over millennia lets civilizations re-found themselves when they reach their limits. Ancient Greece: the founders of cities (nomothetes: Thales, Solon) invented a new psychic and collective individuation, the polis. Hydraulic empires (Egypt, Mesopotamia) had used writing to control floods, merchandise and slaves under royal scribes. Via the Phoenicians, literal writing became in Greece a new relation between the psychic and the collective: the citizen. Nora and Minc (1978, n. 37) compared informatics to the Sumerian invention of writing. Remarks: (1) literal writing turned the associated milieu of language into a principle of association: the logos overturned the dynastic principle. (2) The Phaedrus makes writing a pharmakon: the tekhnè tou biou (art of living) of the citizen, and also the sophists' instrument for manipulating opinion, leading to stasis (civil war). (3) Today industrial populism and tele-cratic television form a process of disindividuation. Nora and Minc foresaw convergence but missed "tele-cracy" (Berlusconi, Giscard d'Estaing) and the alternatives opened by the ambiguity of these pharmaka. (4) The stakes are the same as Plato's: (a) founding and (b) caring for individuation against the disindividuation every pharmakon carries. Machines (n. 38: Taylor) and then appliances (n. 39) exteriorize knowledge into modes of employment, which is proletarianization. (5) The foremost task is the re-foundation of the human enterprise: digital technology is the pharmakon that opens the reconstitution of associated milieus, an ecology of spirit. 51–53 Making the revolution of capitalism Political re-foundation rests on re-socializing an industrial technology and inventing a new type of economic enterprise of services. That can be done only by "enterprising citizens", aroused and supported by a public politics of industrial development of technologies of spirit, led by a new form of public strength (puissance) that associates public authorities, private economic powers and "the public". Television has been absorbed into a larger convergence with digital hypomnemata. It has become drive-based, "the secular arm" of a capitalism grown barbarous, irresponsible and financialized; industrial democracy risks collapsing into a tele-cracy that restores autocracy for deterritorialized financial oligarchies. To be enterprising today is to look after the possibility of being enterprising tomorrow. The Greek polis was also a new economy, arousing eris (rivalry) limited by dikē (justice) and aidōs (shame) (n. 41). Economy is never just subsistence; it is also a libidinal economy of existence that projects "planes of consistency". Hence the call to make, "along with revolutionary capitalists (like the French bourgeoisie of the end of the eighteenth century)", the revolution of a capitalism "on the road to collapse" (p. 53). 53–58 A European way of life The polis opens public space and time where public power serves a public good on which interests converge. That convergence is itself an associated milieu. Europe must become a European public power and not a "space of mere police" where merchandise and consumers circulate under surveillance. The 2005 constitution was rejected because it seemed to offer public powerlessness: Béarn deputy Jean Lassalle's hunger strike against a Japanese firm while Chirac, Villepin and Sarkozy competed for attention (n. 42). Public power must fight tendencies toward dissociation, incivility and barbarism, and must be international, because grammatization is global. Only public action can resolve the contradiction in which Seillière praises cognitive capitalism while, in the book he prefaced, Le Lay sells "available brain time" (n. 43). The answer is a new industrial model, "a European way of life". Intelligence is social (inter-legere). Weber's spirit of capitalism has been lost to the control of affects: libido becomes drive, and affective saturation leads to disaffection. Saturation problems follow: cars, cognitive overload online, the senses, and soon the skin, through RFID implants (Applied Digital Solutions' rice-grain chip; INRIA/JCDecaux bus-shelter messaging; AFP, 11 Mar 2005, on Australia) and Amazon-style profiling that grammatizes singularities into calculable particularities. "Invasive informatics": Microsoft Research's "Intelligent Environments" (5–7 Apr 2006), transreality games, otaku. Hyper-solicitation short-circuits transindividuation: dis-identification, loss of attention, "incivility" (Finkielkraut), attention-deficit disorder. These are technologies of spirit put in the service of control; they breed the uncontrollable and the reign of stupidity, despite UNESCO's rhetoric at Tunis. Aesthetics has served production and consumption for a century, yielding symbolic and spiritual misery. People who have "lost the feeling of existing" (Durn; Maxime Brunerie, who attempted to assassinate the President on 14 July 2001; young people arrested in the November 2005 riots, per psychiatrist Cyril Canetti) show the stakes. A new European way of life must put back the consistencies that support existence, an industry that intensifies the incalculable: "the plane of motifs, which, like the horizon of the Muses, is the plane of enchantment" (p. 58). 58–60 The plane that enchants me Capitalism needs motivation, a kind of enchantment; if nothing changes it will destroy that and us. Singularity alone is the object of libido. Since Newton everything can be calculated, but desire knows only the incalculable, "a plane other than that of the calculable". Mathematicians' idealities and axioms belong to it too. The work of art is singular: Kant's reflective judgement ("this is beautiful") cannot be proven, only experienced (éprouvé). Its universality is "by default". Singularity "does not exist" but consists in my existence and my participation in collective individuation. Likewise with the beloved: however profilable her behaviours (loyalty cards, RFID, Amazon), love is not drive. These consistencies are "the plane that enchants me", and they must be treated "with the greatest care". A libidinal eco-nomy (nomos of the oikos) is what takes care of them. Capitalism has left this care, called culture, in ruins while calling itself "cultural" and "cognitive". Hence the need to revolutionize it: there will be no future "of capitalism, or a beyond of capitalism, which is certainly not eternal" unless that future takes care of the future of the objects of desire (p. 60).

Provenance. The Introduction (p. 8) calls this chapter a "reformulation and elaboration" of a paper from the second Ars Industrialis working session. That paper is Stiegler's talk of 24 September 2005 at the Théâtre de la Colline (source), whose section headings the chapter keeps in order. The chapter is substantially rewritten and expanded; see "What changed from the 2005 talk" below. The chapter ends at p. 93, and p. 94 is blank.

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text:
This is the book's long policy essay on the "information society". It was written to shape Ars Industrialis's intervention at the 2005 UN summit in Tunis and is addressed to executives, CEOs and politicians (p. 70).

History. It opens with an industrial-political history of networks: the French Minitel, which followed the Nora–Minc report, and the Clinton–Gore internet. Both were "regal" acts of public industrial strategy. Minitel in fact opened "the age of associated milieus founded upon an industrial technology" (p. 61). Every new medium is a stage of grammatization and can produce either an associated milieu or an aggravation of control. Television in the hands of Giscard, Mitterrand and Berlusconi produced tele-cracy, "the perfect accomplishment of the dissociated milieu", which leads to populism (p. 62).

Ideology. The European Commission's ideology of the "information society", with its demand that everyone "adapt", fused with neoliberalism. Adaptation, as Medef's Seillière preaches it, is entropic: it demotivates and leads to dissociation and to the "loss of the spirit of capitalism" (p. 67). Patrick Le Lay's sale of "available human brain time" is its clearest expression. Such an economy makes knowledge into information. Information as a commodity is entropic, while knowledge is negentropic (knowledge vs information).

Memory and education. Against Plato and Michel Serres, Stiegler holds that memory has always been exteriorized. The danger is exteriorization without re-interiorization, which leads to disindividuation and a new "reign of ignorance". The school, built on alphabetic writing, is the model institution of re-interiorization. It is now in crisis before the program industries, because modern education never understood its own technical basis.

Remedy. The remedy is an industrial politics of technologies of spirit: new instruments of knowledge for research and higher education, a new publishing industry, audiovisual objects that break up mass audiences, and cooperative "societies of authors and readers". Wikipedia and Web 2.0 show that these are possible. All this should be backed by a long-term European public power that fights financierization, and should be debated at "a new summit" (p. 93).

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. Big public industrial strategies, from Minitel after Nora–Minc (1978) to the Clinton–Gore internet (1993), are what open new technical epochs. France abandoned such strategy after Giscard; Mitterrand conceded a TV channel to Berlusconi (pp. 61–62).
  2. Each network technology is a stage of grammatization whose social meaning outstrips its makers' intentions. It is revealed only through "economic, political, and social, but also spiritual, battles", the "epokhal double redoubling" (p. 62; n. 4).
  3. Tele-cracy is the "perfect accomplishment" of the dissociated milieu and leads to populism. The internet is at once a rupture (an associated milieu) and a new stage of control (R technologies) (p. 62).
  4. Decentralization under Mitterrand, plus the European Commission's takeover of research policy, fed a libertarian then neoliberal abandonment of public responsibility. Europe piggy-backed US industrial policy (pp. 63–64).
  5. The EU's "information society" ideology produced the "calamitous and caricatured" Tunis summit, entrusted to Ben Ali, and an infrastructure favouring short-term market criteria for social change (p. 64).
  6. Cognitive capitalism arises from four things (p. 65): diffusion of cognitive technologies, the service economy, externalized production controlled through marketing, and the convergence of cultural and cognitive technologies. Used as R technologies, these lower the value of spirit, which amounts to desublimation.
  7. The stake is "spirit understood as the power to sublimate" and socialization as sublimation within a libidinal economy (p. 65). The appearance of technologies favourable to associated milieus makes a "reversal" possible.
  8. The firm is the main obstacle to change, because it drives dissociated milieus. Adaptation is "deeply entropic and demotivating" (p. 67).
  9. Only associated milieus let "the life of the spirit … blossom". Building them needs long-term action by "a new international public power" against financierization, for the sake of "a capitalist future" (p. 67).
  10. Le Lay's "available human brain time" is "a remarkably clear and concise formulation of dissociation" (p. 67). It amounts to the systematic organization of the drop in the value of spirit and to "décervelage" (Ubu's brain-removal) (pp. 68–69).
  11. Spirit cannot be "adapted". One learns a theorem by re-living its genesis (methodos), so controlling spirit destroys it (p. 69).
  12. Against TINA ("there is no alternative", Chomsky): "there is no alternative to a change in the industrial model" (p. 69).
  13. Knowledge is critique, and so it contradicts adaptation (p. 72). The losses of savoir-faire and savoir-vivre in recent decades are losses of individuation, singularity and desire (p. 72).
  14. All knowledge needs instruments. The issue is instrumentalization, as with the old Paris bookshop sign "Instruments of thought". Control technologies can become technologies of individuation (pp. 73–74).
  15. Hyperindustrialization is unavoidable. The real alternative is associated milieus, the "a priori condition of any society worthy of the name" (pp. 74–75). The common limit of all present crises is dissociation (p. 75).
  16. Information as a commodity is entropic; knowledge is negentropic and "constitutes the time of existence" (p. 77). Lyotard and Portella are cited on knowledge produced to be sold (p. 78).
  17. Against Serres: the exteriorization of memory is "the very origin of man". Memory is always already "collective and objective" (p. 79).
  18. The threat is exteriorization without interiorization. A knowledge society that fails to organize the social appropriation of new memory technologies becomes a "reign of ignorance" (p. 80).
  19. Individuation is psychic and collective, and knowledge exists only when shared. The convergence of TV with the IP network can reintroduce dissociation through "push" logic. "Pull" makes the receiver a sender (pp. 81–82).
  20. "Knowledge management" is managerial, not cognitive. Investment in instruments of knowledge has been absent, giving disappointing e-learning, whereas Wikipedia shows the power of participatory associated milieus (pp. 83–87).
  21. Memory is selection. An instrument of knowledge produces its own selection criteria, and an ecological crisis of spirit is possible (pp. 87–88).
  22. Technoscience has abandoned the ontological project of knowledge. The school, once "the matrix … of society as an associated and sapid milieu", risks becoming an institution of dissociation (p. 89).
  23. Education was never thought from originary exteriorization. Kant ignored the "prosthetic synthesis", so the crisis of spirit appears first as a crisis of education (pp. 89–90).
  24. Practical consequences: instruments of knowledge must be specific, hierarchical and reversible. Two tasks follow, new instruments for research and a new editorial industry. Three conditions make this feasible (pp. 91–93).

items.title: Argumentative moves
items.text:
• Industrial-political history as argument. The chapter treats Minitel, TCP/IP and the Commission's information-society programmes as proof that technical epochs are politically opened or squandered.
  • Turning the adversary's text against him. Seillière's preface and Le Lay's interview, "some dozen pages" apart in the same book, are read as a single logic of adaptation (p. 67).
  • Thermodynamic contrast. Entropy (information, adaptation, dissociation) is set against negentropy (knowledge, association, individuation). This is the axis of the whole chapter.
  • Anti-Platonic theory of memory. Hypomnesis is the condition of anamnesis (Phaedrus; Husserl's Origin of Geometry; Leroi-Gourhan; Goody).
  • Phenomenology of the instrument. Mallarmé's "The Book, a spiritual instrument", Husserl's "spirit-invested objects", and the library as an associated milieu (pp. 84–86).
  • From philosophy to industrial specification. The chapter ends with design principles and Stiegler's own projects at INA, IRCAM and Centre Pompidou's IRI.

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text: pp. Section Content (paraphrase) 61–64 From the "informatization of society" to the "society of information" The internet's worldwide growth dates from Clinton and Gore's 1993 decision to make it the spearhead of their politics. This was a public industrial strategy and a "regal gesture" repeating France's Minitel, which followed the Nora–Minc report via the DGT under Gérard Théry. Minitel socialized micro-computing (n. 1: the exhibitions Les Immatériaux, 1985, and Mémoires du futur, 1987) and "inaugurated the age of associated milieus founded upon an industrial technology", even if it began with the messageries roses (adult chat services). ARPANET was demilitarized, there was Berners-Lee's work at CERN, and broadband followed. France's last great industrial project was Giscard's. Mitterrand created a pay channel and conceded a channel to Berlusconi (with Ricardo Freccero). Tele-cracy is the "perfect accomplishment of the dissociated milieu" and leads to populism. The internet is both rupture and a new stage of control by R technologies. Like the alphabet, printing press, machine-tool and TV, it is a stage of grammatization that outstrips its actors' intentions, the "epokhal double redoubling" (n. 4). The internet is decentralized and terminal-agnostic. The French critique of "Jacobin" Minitel missed that Clinton–Gore were just as regal. Mitterrand's decentralization and the Commission's takeover of research policy produced a "double de-centering" and then libertarian and neoliberal ideology. Europe piggy-backed US policy despite its own labs (GSM). The Commission christened the "information society" and demanded "adaptation". The IRISI programme was read through e-commerce and tax exemptions; n. 5 refers to Stiegler's own 1996 report for Nord-Pas-de-Calais. Convergence, anticipated by Nora–Minc, became deregulation and privatization. The ideology led to the "calamitous and caricatured" Tunis summit, entrusted to Ben Ali, and to Boltanski–Chiapello's "remote control", favouring short-term market criteria for meta-transformation. 64–66 From the "information society" to "societies of knowledge"—or, on the possibility of "re-enchanting the world" TCP/IP, digitization and convergence are the origin of "societies of knowledge". Tunis presented itself as transitional. The economy became hyperindustrial or "cognitive" through four factors: cognitive technologies; the becoming-tertiary of services; capitalism externalizing production to control "conceptual and behavioral apparatuses" by marketing; and the convergence of cultural and cognitive technologies into what ought to be technologies of spirit. As R technologies these lower the value of spirit, i.e. desublimation (Marcuse 1955; n. 9: "I do not share", even "frankly opposed"). The "Save Research" movement shows the stake is knowledge, not information. The stake is "spirit understood as the power to sublimate", socialization as sublimation in a libidinal economy, through hypomnemata. Technologies favourable to associated milieus make a "veritable reversal" possible, as Kessler wished in commenting on Medef's 2005 "re-enchanting the world". Kessler cited Blair's proposal to redirect CAP funds to cognitive technologies. Seillière's preface: the end of the West's "rente technologique" and the turn to human capital (n. 10). The question is geopolitical (India, China, Japan) and is also about re-enchanting the European project, not just firms steered by financier capitalism's short-term returns. 66–70 Enterprises, public power, and industrial populism The firm drives dissociated milieus and is the main obstacle, against Medef's "head in the global, feet in the local". Adaptation is "deeply entropic and demotivating", the "abandonment of any vision of the future" (Seillière, ex-Medef and president of Marine Investment). It leads to dissociation, desocialization, disindividuation and demotivation, the loss of the spirit of capitalism (p. 67; n. 12). Only associated milieus let the life of spirit blossom. A new international public power of public and private actors must found a new industrial civilization and fight financierization for "a capitalist future". Seillière's adaptation leads to nihilism (Nietzsche). Le Lay's declaration, "some dozen pages" later in the same book under the title "TF1—The School of Reactivity", is a clear formulation of dissociation. Selling brain time makes "a total absence of thought" into a standardized product (p. 68; n. 13). Adaptation generalizes the availability of brains, including executives' own, under fatalism, which the Enlightenment fought. It breeds social and moral regression and suicidal extremes, and amounts to décervelage. Spirit cannot be adapted: one learns geometry by re-making the theorem (methodos), so control destroys spirit (p. 69). Chomsky's TINA: the reality is "no alternative to a change in the industrial model". The information society is a society of control by R technologies; the knowledge society is "the generalization of associated milieus". The dissociated model leads to industrial populism, ruinous for society and eventually for firms, and to "generalized debasement". Stiegler addresses executives and politicians in charge of society as public space and time, an "as-sociation" (p. 70). 70–71 Changing the industrial paradigm Available brain time is neither knowledge nor information: Pavlovian conditioning makes judgement unavailable. It is the worst case of the society of control (Bradbury and Truffaut's Fahrenheit 451). Le Lay boasts that TF1 "knows" its clients after 24 hours, and calls Star Academy (n. 15: TF1's softer answer to M6's Loft, with Endemol) "controlled reactivity", worthy of Papa Ubu. A knowledge society requires producers, consumers, entrepreneurs and governors to rise "toward ever more refined forms of the life of the spirit", "a conquest of the best over the worst", a "battle against regression", through the creations of sublimation (p. 71). Seillière calls for social intelligence while prefacing Le Lay. These contradictions express industrial society's "intrinsic debility". Overcoming them means changing axioms: the UN's and Commission's prose, Tunis and Lisbon (n. 16) must move from dissociated to associated milieus. 71–73 Information society, disenchantment, demotivation, and the control of forms of knowledge Medef can speak of "enchantment" because the economy is libidinal. Questions of spirit are first questions of motives, projected onto "the plane that enchants me" (n. 17, back to Ch. 1), i.e. psychic and collective individuation. Cognitive capitalism carries R technologies' dissociation to its climax, Weber's disenchantment. It is a stage of grammatization: control of knowledge of production and consumption by R&D, design and marketing. This control makes knowledge adaptive and entropic, but knowledge is "intrinsically contradictory to adaptation": it is critique (p. 72). Theses: (a) an entropic tendency against the "consubstantially negentropic structure of knowledge"; (b) losses of savoir-faire and savoir-vivre over a few decades; (c) these are losses of individuation, singularity and desire, the reality of the "information" society; (d) hence an industrial political economy of technologies of spirit, an "industrial ecology of spirit" (p. 73). 73–77 The re-instrumentation of forms of knowledge and the future of hyperindustrial society All knowledge presupposes instruments, a "techno-logy". A Paris bookshop on Boulevard Bonne-Nouvelle had the sign "The instruments of thought". Printing and account books opened rational capitalism (Weber; Foucault's hypomnemata, n. 19), the Republic of Letters and Enlightenment, and critique "in Kant's sense". Today's digital instrumentation becomes instrumentalization, proletarianizing researchers and dissociating cognitive milieus. A right must be opposed to this fact. Control technologies, like Mesopotamian and Egyptian ones that became Greek hypomnemata, are the condition of individuation (p. 74). Hyperindustrialization is ineluctable, but if it rests on dissociation society will "come up against a wall". The alternative is "a refoundation of the human enterprise" as civic enterprise (n. 20: Gandois, Seillière and "some hope" from Laurence Parisot). Associated milieus are "the a priori condition of any society worthy of the name". Saturations (urban, physiological, cognitive, affective) mark the limits, in René Passet's sense (n. 22). Thesis: "the common limit to all of the limits is dissociation". Associated milieus offer a rebirth of knowledge and of industrial democracy, which has "collapsed into telecracy, … the Italian name for industrial populism" (p. 75). Only an elevation of collective intelligence (Husserl's "reactivation") can face demographic and energy limits: caloric use from 2,000–3,000 kcal for early humans to 150,000 (Europe) and 230,000 (US); population doubling times falling from 1,500 years to 37 (p. 76). Lévi-Strauss's pessimism (n. 24). Against Seillière's TINA "fatalism": think hyperindustrial knowledge in its necessity (a stage of grammatization) and its limit (dissociation by R technologies), toward "the lasting development of spirit" and a "digital instrumentality … of the intellect" (p. 77). 77–79 Knowledge (Savoir) and information Information as commodity is "in its essence entropic": its value decreases with time (n. 25: Collins on the value of spirit and Walras). Knowledge is "in its essence negentropic". It intensifies (intensive magnitudes: Kant, Thom) and "constitutes the time of existence". Knowledge societies must open digital technology onto new associated milieus or remain fragile. Lyotard (1979): knowledge produced to be sold loses its use-value (n. 26–27). Portella: a "dangerous return to positive … knowledge", "know-how" without knowledge (n. 28). The information-commodity is entropic, knowledge negentropic: an internal contradiction caused by dissociation. Associated milieus are negentropic; dissociated societies homogenize. A critique is needed through analysis of grammatization: a "reversal of the entropic effects of information" (p. 79). No spirit without material milieus (Husserl, Leroi-Gourhan, Goody). The passage from mnemotechnical to mnemotechnological society is not, as Serres claims (n. 29), loss of memory for gain of knowledge. Exteriorization of memory is "the very origin of man" and the condition of knowledge, "collective and objective": grammatization. 79–81 Knowledge and memory, or reign of ignorance? Plato's Phaedrus need not bind us. Living memory exceeds its "retentional finitude" by projecting itself outside, which allows transmission between generations (n. 31). The threat is exteriorization without correlative interiorization (= individuation), which induces "losses of knowledge". The school (Greek or modern) lets one adopt the past of knowledge as a future (n. 32). A knowledge society that ignores the need to organize anamnesic capacity through social appropriation of new hypomnesic apparatuses, by a politics of technologies of spirit implemented by "a new public power on the European level", would be a society of non-knowledge. That means neither Socratic ignorance nor Charles Lenay's "cognition of ignorance" (Compiègne), but "a new age of the reign of ignorance" (p. 80). Anamnesic capacity = knowledge's negentropy, its "revenance" (Euclid in Lobachevsky; Husserl's reactivation, n. 33). Memory is anamnesic insofar as it is an associated milieu (transindividuation); grammatization can dissociate (entropy) or associate (negentropy). Hence a politics at once of research instrumentation, industrial politics of knowledge instruments, transmission and education, editorial industries, and of television as a program industry, with research "subject to new types of obligations" (p. 81). 81–83 The risk of disindividuation as the growth of ignorance rather than knowledge Informationalization threatens dissociation, a "society" of ignorance. It is also a chance for a qualitative leap (saut) of knowledge as psychic and collective individuation. Digitization integrates conception, production and consumption into one cognitive system, with TV and mass media as actors in all three. "Available brain times", starting with children's, are absorbed by dissociated milieus, while the IP network and Web 2.0 open possibilities of association. The question of knowledge societies is first that of television: its relation to digital media and public policy. The convergence of mass media with the IP network risks reintroducing dissociation through "push" (a new overflow valve, déversoir, of programmes). "Pull" is associative: the receiver becomes a sender and individuates himself while individuating the milieu (p. 82). Individuation is psychic and collective, so knowledge must be shared. Serres "belatedly" discovers Leroi-Gourhan (n. 34: losses of individuation in the West, De la misère symbolique 1). The risk is a weakening of individuation through conflict among the psychic, the collective and the machinic. Global financier capitalism blocks individuation and "has come undone", yet capitalism maintains its "perpetual returns". The task is re-appropriation through techno-logical equipment, i.e. "true societies of knowledge". 83–87 Cognitive saturation and "knowledge management" "Cognitive overflow syndrome": information paralyses decision instead of becoming knowledge. Knowledge management is managerial ("cognitive" = decision-supporting), not scientific. Instruments of science and research are secondary effects of tertiary-sector software and services. Informatics went from scientific to managerial to bureaucratic. Nora–Minc saw a large public market, but the logic reversed to short-term profit, non-research applications and video games. The milieu could still "syncrystallize" (Simondon) a new associated milieu. Mallarmé: "The Book, a spiritual instrument" (n. 35), an antithesis in which spirit overflows its instrument. Valéry on the mortality of civilizations and the fragility of spirit. Frazer, the return of the dead; Pascal and Comte: humanity "composed more of the dead than of the living" (p. 84). Husserl's "spirit-invested objects", book and spoon (n. 36), and the Origin of Geometry. The instruments of spirit are dead and need the living, and so need care (therapeuma). Digital hypomnemata are "new spiritual instruments". Google's library digitization and the BnF president's call for a "European Google" merely mimic search engines, whereas the BnF had posed the question of "spiritual navigation" (n. 37: Stiegler's 1989–92 computer-assisted-reading working group with Giffard and Gattegno; the AIS-Berger Levrault prototype cut by the Balladur government in 1993). The library is a place of production and genesis, of "spirit-invested objects", now digitized as a network (p. 85). Spirit is finite; it retains the trace through instruments, the "demiurgic factor" of technique, too often forgotten when instruments become industrial. That is the oblivion of the value of spirit (n. 39: Google; Brzezinski's "soft power"). Spirit has always placed itself "outside the living". The library is an associated milieu "par excellence"; the network can be too. To read is already to write; Jules Ferry made the letter the basis of the Republic. Without investment in new spiritual instruments, e-learning and educational software have been "disappointing, … deeply regressive" (p. 86). Meanwhile Wikipedia, "the cooperative and free encyclopedia", is an "extraordinary success" showing that the participatory logic of associated milieus is "an extremely new and powerful dynamic". Knowledge markets are insolvent in the short and medium term, so there is a case for mutualized public investment at European level. The insolvency concerns not just the two billion people without electricity but research labs' basic instruments (p. 87). 87–89 Instruments of knowledge and the criteria of selection that they produce The alphabet is grammatization preceding all logic and grammar (n. 40: Auroux; the English bibliography misattributes his book). The third industrial revolution moves from mnemotechnical to mnemotechnological society, delegating cognitive functions to devices and absorbing or eliminating "the clerks" (n. 42). Memory, including information about the immediate present, becomes the object of vast industries of memory and imagination that separate producers from consumers. Memory is retention, hence selection, and its industrialization defines new criteria of selection (Google, "a poor example"). An instrument of knowledge "produces through its practice its own criteria of selection" as its practical rules. Such practices must be encouraged by public and private powers, not reduced to "cultural politics" but carried by an industrial politics: an eco-logy of the milieu of spirit. Spirit is originally exteriorized, so it is industrially exploitable. ICTs can reduce practical rules to procedural uses (R technologies), making "a major ecological crisis of spirit conceivable, and even probable". Future knowledge societies would subject the organization of information to the imperatives of knowledge, through "a politics of the regulation of new spiritual milieus" favouring their associative over their dissociative tendencies (p. 88). 89–90 Being and becoming in "technoscience" Technoscience is "the industrial epoch of science" (Mallarmé's Crise de vers): a calling into question of being and of knowledge, an abandonment of knowledge's ontological project. The crisis of knowledge, of which schools are the theatre (n. 43: Technics and Time 3, ch. 4), comes from teaching that knowledge formalizes being when it explores becoming, with a new instrumentality not appropriated by schools. The school, "the matrix, par excellence, of the production of society as an associated and sapid milieu", is becoming an institution of dissociation that makes knowledge "nothing but a merchandise". Technoscience brings chronic instability, calculation at light speed, axiomatic and axiological crises (biology), and impossible transmission: teachers lag behind what pupils meet daily. Condorcet, Guizot and Ferry did not think from originary exteriorization, although the school consists in interiorizing techniques of exteriorization, "numbers and letters" (n. 44). 90–91 The crisis of education The organization of knowledge rests on obscuring originary exteriorization. In Stiegler's reading of Kant's transcendental deduction, Kant ignored "the fourth synthesis of the transcendental imagination, or the prosthetic synthesis" (n. 45). So program institutions (education systems) are "completely divested" before program industries. Together with informational entropy and science's changing meaning, this makes a crisis of education necessary: "the ecological crisis of spirit translates itself in the first place as a crisis of education" (p. 90). Institutions that produce knowledge are in crisis too. A new instrumental chain of knowledge (digital instrumentality) is forming and can be oriented: the crisis "is not hopeless", but socialization as sublimation is threatened "at its very core". Public policy is required. Tunis should have debated this, but France and Europe, "left speechless by the very liberal 'Lisbon strategy'", stayed silent (p. 91). 91–93 Practical consequences The chain of production and diffusion of knowledge currently works through "instrumental functions" of dissociated milieus (control, KM, R technologies). It must be specific, hierarchical, and reversible. (1) Instrumental functions of knowledge cannot be sub-domains of bureaucratic tools, document management, information systems and KM, as long as knowledge activities are not solvent markets and public power gives no long-term support. (2) Production instruments must be specified by users' qualifications and research practices, not by "broken models of use" from consumption (n. 46). (3) Diffusion instruments must implement the same primitive functions in simplified form, respecting the "communitization" of knowledge communities as associated milieus. Following Husserl, the recipient must be able to "retrace" a statement's genesis "techno-logically". An editorial industry should serve the institutions that prescribe programmes, which presupposes new production instruments defining norms of appropriation (a transductive relation between exteriorized knowledge and users' practices). Two tasks: new instruments for research and higher education; an editorial industry creating new functions for instruction and training. Feasible because (1) computer-assisted intellectual work (analysis, critique, argumentation, indexing, synthesis) is technically adequate; (2) program industries can make discretizable, delinearizable audiovisual temporal objects that de-massify audiences (INA hypermedia studio, 1997, n. 47; IRCAM music education with the Ministry; Centre Pompidou's IRI); (3) instruments applied at the source as supports of labour, cooperation and collective thought, "cooperative instruments of forms of knowledge", allow "societies of authors and readers" (n. 48) contrary to dominant business models and so "insolvent", "even if Web 2.0 is infrastructure that anticipates a new industrial model". Close (p. 93): these questions, unexamined at Tunis, should be the object of a new summit preceded by debate at EU level. Only then can a European project be built, which "can only be a European project of spirit: the spirit of Europe in the age of technologies of spirit".

items.title: What changed from the 2005 talk
items.text:
Compared with the Colline talk of 24 Sept 2005 (source), the chapter keeps the section skeleton and the core theses: entropy/negentropy, reign of ignorance, crisis of education, practical consequences. It adds:

  • a new opening history: Minitel, Nora–Minc, DGT/Théry, Clinton–Gore, Giscard, Mitterrand and Berlusconi, the European Commission, IRISI, the 1997 convergence green paper and Ben Ali;
  • the vocabulary of associated/dissociated milieus throughout, plus "R technologies", "meta-transformation", "civic enterprise" and tele-cracy as "the Italian name for industrial populism";
  • the four factors of cognitive capitalism, the "Save Research" movement and the Marcuse disagreement;
  • Seillière and Marine Investment, Chomsky's TINA, Ubu's décervelage, and the geometry-theorem argument;
  • demographic and energy limits (Passet, calories, population doubling times, Lévi-Strauss);
  • the push/pull analysis of TV and IP convergence, and Web 2.0;
  • the long meditation on Mallarmé, Valéry, Husserl's spirit-invested objects, the library, Google and the BnF;
  • Wikipedia;
  • the dismissal of the Lisbon strategy as a "total failure".

The procedural opening (§1) is gone, and the talk's §3 material on Medef/Kessler is moved into the second section.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• The chapter is the most policy-specific text in the book and the most closely tied to Stiegler's institutional practice: INA, IRCAM, IRI, the 1989–92 computer-assisted-reading project and the 1996 Nord-Pas-de-Calais report.
  • Labelled interpretation: the entropy/negentropy distinction carries much of the argument and is asserted rather than derived. See concepts/knowledge-vs-information.md.
  • Labelled interpretation: "we know today [the Lisbon strategy] will have been a total failure" (p. 91) reads as hindsight. Lisbon was widely judged a failure around 2010, so the line may be a later revision for the English edition.

items.title: A Motion Adopted by Ars Industrialis on the Eve of the Tunis Summit (pp. 95–100)
items.text:
Home › Overview › Structure › Tunis motion · prev: ← Chapter 2

The text. pp. 95–100, with notes on p. 112. Note 1 says that the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) was held in Tunis on 16–18 November 2005, and that the motion "had been published in part" by Libération on 14 November 2005. The web version (source) is that partial text. The motion in the book is longer: it is numbered, sets out three conditions, and adds passages on intellectual property, Porto Alegre, a European research programme, the US Federal Communications Commission, Viviane Reding and the French government. The French edition prints the motion at FR p. 163 (Ch. 2, n. 6).

items.title: Abstract (L2)
items.text:
Ars Industrialis's position for the UN summit is set out in one subheading, "The true stakes of the Tunis summit", followed by numbered points.

  • Knowledge, not information. The real stake of the "information society" is the growth of knowledge and intelligence, which the motion calls a common good of humanity. Intellectual property can at most justify temporary limits on that.
  • A missed opportunity. Tunis has missed the chance for a global debate. Society now faces spiritual misery under a consumerist capitalism of exhaustion and desublimation.
  • Spirit, not only religion. The need for spirit must not be met only by religion. The life of spirit happens in work, relationships and communications media. Underinvestment in the value of spirit has fed "regressive and radical spiritualisms".
  • Another summit. The motion calls for another summit, in the spirit of Porto Alegre but "upon a different basis": an industrial politics of technologies of spirit, led by a new form of public power. It has three conditions:
  • treat information technologies and the culture and audiovisual industries together;
  • make television an instrument of knowledge rather than of industrial populism;
  • use digital technology to reinvent television beyond the broadcast model of the 1930s.
  • Europe. Europe should build itself on a long-term public research and industrial programme for the knowledge and culture industries. It should not seek short-term returns, and should look to American federal precedent such as the internet, the FCC, and the state working with universities and the military.
  • Living standards. The standard of living is measured by "the life of its spirit", not by protein consumed.
  • Criticisms. The Beffa report is silent on technologies of spirit. The Lisbon strategy and Viviane Reding's advertising proposals go the wrong way. France needs a "courageous discourse".
  • Close. Europeans can believe again only in Europe's singularity since Greece: a public space of knowledge, now made of cognitive and cultural industries.

items.title: Core claims
items.text:
1. The stake of the "information society", also called "cognitive capitalism" or "society of knowledge", is the development of knowledge and intelligence. The future of capitalism "hangs upon a growth of intelligence and knowledge" (p. 95).
  2. Intellectual property is a key but problematic element: alienation, expropriation, hegemony. Knowledge "has always been defined as that which does not belong to anyone", a common good, so only temporary limits to repay investment are acceptable (p. 95).
  3. Tunis's solutions delay the public character of knowledge. A society of knowledge can only be constituted "in a new form of publicness", a public space serving a social organization better equipped "to discern, critique, improve, create, transmit, and receive forms of knowledge" for the whole world's population (p. 95).
  4. Tunis misses the moment to launch a global debate. It will not pose the principal question: the relations of information, knowledge, technology, industry and society as the stake of transforming contemporary capitalism, which "no longer produces anything but exhaustion, desublimation" and regression (p. 96).
  5. Faced with spiritual misery (Weber's disenchantment; Valéry and Arendt's "life of the spirit (mind)"), people feel a need for spirit. Situating spirit only in religion is a danger. The religious is recognized, but the life of spirit plays out in daily work, relationships and communications, especially television, mobile phones, the internet and the web (p. 96).
  6. Failure to reinvest in the value of spirit "appears to us to have led to the proliferation of increasingly more regressive and radical spiritualisms" (p. 96).
  7. The appeal is international, not merely French or European. It aims to mobilize collective global intelligence around another summit, on a different basis from Porto Alegre and not as a monopoly over intelligence (pp. 96–97).
  8. "Spirit" covers both "available brain time" and the works of spirit (Valéry, n. 2: Regards sur le monde actuel) (p. 97).
  9. Three conditions (p. 97): (1) do not separate the information society from the culture and audiovisual industries; (2) if the information society is to be a society of knowledge, TV must become an instrument of knowledge, not of debasement and industrial populism; (3) digital technologies allow a TV entirely different from the 1930s broadcasting model.
  10. Europe (p. 98): a public action plan on the European plane; a great research programme with large public funds not seeking short-term returns, unlike current European Commission programmes; fundamental research comparable to medicine and physics; public power socializing results with economic actors, as the FCC does in the US. A new public will connecting industry, institutions, artists, media, publishers, territorial collectives and NGOs. Spirit is now "the foremost industrial resource", so new fields of externalities and solvencies are needed.
  11. Habits must change profoundly, which requires a formation of individual and collective intelligence and spirit, a new spirit of capitalism and a renaissance. Living standards are not measured by protein consumed, whose excess leads to physiological ills, depression and demotivation (pp. 98–99).
  12. Chirac's commission to Jean-Louis Beffa (Saint-Gobain) for an industrial-policy report is welcome. No industrial civilization is possible without long-term public and private anticipation, and the US federal state and Asia pursue determined industrial politics; the socialization of the internet was one. But the Beffa report is "silent" on technologies of spirit (p. 99).
  13. Barroso's Lisbon strategy does not go this way. Viviane Reding's recommendation to increase advertising means a further drop in the audiovisual value of spirit and threatens the press's advertising revenue (p. 99).
  14. France must stop invoking cultural exception or diversity and frame an industrial politics of the cultural industries oriented to "an elevation of the standard of social life" against levelling and entropy. It cannot denounce "American sub-culture" while saying nothing of French television (pp. 99–100).
  15. Ministries (research, industry, culture, communication) must act on concrete objects: search engines (Jean-Noël Jeanneney), TV, broadband images, wi-fi. Together with the State and the EU, they must give Europeans hope "regarding their culture" (p. 100).
  16. Europeans can believe only in "the constitution of a public space of knowledge constituting a reason", reason as social motivation and "universal motif of spirit". Today that space is cognitive and cultural industries, the technologies of a new spirit of capitalism. The 20th-century model has left "a capitalism that has lost its spirit", arousing "mistrust, anxiety, and demotivation, that is, irrationality, if it is true that reason is in the first place a motif" (p. 100).

items.title: Section-by-section (L3)
items.text: pp. Part Content (paraphrase) 95 Title (n. 1); "The true stakes of the Tunis summit" Stake = knowledge and intelligence (UNESCO "societies of knowledge", Blair's "economy of knowledge", "cognitive capitalism", "society/revolution of intelligence"). Intellectual property: alienation, expropriation, hegemony; knowledge as common good; only temporary limits. §1: knowledge requires a new form of publicness and a public space for discerning, critiquing and transmitting knowledge, improving "the life of the spirit for the entire population of the world". 96 §2 Tunis misses the moment for a global debate. The general interest must take priority over particular interests; there must be a global politics of industrial technologies of spirit. Consumption capitalism produces exhaustion, desublimation and regression. Spiritual misery; Weber's disenchantment; Valéry and Arendt. Spirit is not only religious; the religious is "distinct and positive" but the motion will not promote "a form of monotheism". The life of spirit is in work, relationships and communications, mass media and the web. Underinvestment feeds regressive spiritualisms. An international appeal for another summit. 97 Another summit; three conditions In the spirit of Porto Alegre but on another basis; not a European social forum and not a monopoly of intelligence. Apprehend the problems at the level of an industrial politics of technologies of spirit ("available brain time" and works of spirit; Valéry, n. 2). A new form of public power over the tools of symbolic exchange; a new industrial model driven by raising everyone's intelligence. Conditions 1–3. Long discussions on these points systematically ignored… 98 Europe and research …and not addressed before Tunis. Public power must support debates with an action plan on the European plane, building Europe on an original, sustainable and strategic project for the knowledge and culture industries. A research programme with large public funds not seeking short-term returns; fundamental research as in medicine and physics; public power socializing results with economic actors (cf. the FCC in the US). Not a new audiovisual public service, but a public will forged from industry, institutions, artists, media, publishers, literary societies, territorial collectives and NGOs; politics presupposes will. A new industrial model: after matter, spirit is the foremost industrial resource and the planet's only chance. New externalities. Behavioural change; the intelligence it requires; a new spirit of capitalism; renaissance; protein. 99 Beffa, US and Asia, Lisbon, Reding, France …hyperconsumptive depression and demotivation. Beffa report welcome but silent on technologies of spirit. US federal industrial politics (the internet; State with university, military, public initiative); Asia. Develop an alternative industrial politics of technologies of spirit for raising intelligence, not for intensifying consumption. Not Barroso's Lisbon; not Reding's advertising increase (deprives newspapers of income). The French government needs a new and courageous discourse beyond cultural exception or diversity: an industrial politics of the cultural industries against levelling and entropy, and no denouncing "American sub-culture" without also addressing French TV… 100 The European public space of knowledge …TV programmes in France. The information society is first a society of screens (TV, computers, PDAs; tomorrow micro- and nanotechnology). Ministries must act on search engines (Jeanneney), TV, broadband images and wi-fi. State, EU and industry: a middle- and long-term project (cf. Beffa) giving Europeans hope in their culture. A Europe its population "can once again believe" in: the public space of knowledge as reason, motivation and "universal motif of spirit". It is no longer only writing but cognitive and cultural industries, the technologies of a new spirit of capitalism, against a capitalism "that has lost its spirit".

items.title: Concepts
items.text: technologies of spirit · industrial populism · spirit · symbolic misery (spiritual misery) · disenchantment · short-termism · knowledge vs information · libidinal economy (desublimation)

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Context. WSIS's second phase was widely judged to have achieved little beyond the internet-governance compromise. Press-freedom groups criticized holding it in Ben Ali's Tunisia. Chapter 2 (p. 64) calls the summit "calamitous and caricatured" and notes it was "entrusted … to the director, Ben Ali". The motion itself ignores the venue issue.
  • Publication. The motion was adopted by Ars Industrialis; Libération printed part of it. The intellectual-property argument, the three conditions, Porto Alegre, the FCC model, Reding and the French government appear only in the book's full text.
  • Labelled interpretation: this is the most "official" register in the book, addressed to policy-makers in the Élysée, the government and the Commission. It contains the book's most explicit claim that knowledge is a common good limited only temporarily by property, which bears on the debate over whether Ars Industrialis challenges capitalist property relations (see reception.md).

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
Home › Concepts · short definitions in the Glossary · cross-reference in the Index

Each concept page gives a definition, where the term appears in the book (with page numbers), related terms, how secondary sources gloss it, and any disagreements among them.

Concept In brief Associated milieu / dissociated milieu (milieu associé / dissocié) Simondon's associated milieu, and Stiegler's contrast between associated and dissociated milieus of symbols and knowledge. Care (soin; prendre soin; epimeleia) Care (soin, epimeleia) as the practices and institutions that keep a technical pharmakon from turning toxic. Disenchantment / re-enchantment (Entzauberung; désenchantement / réenchantement) Weber's disenchantment of the world, and what the book means by re-enchanting it. Economy of contribution (économie de la contribution) The economy of contribution, the model Ars Industrialis proposes to replace consumerism. Grammatization (grammatisation) Grammatization: the discretization of speech, gesture and perception into reproducible marks, from the alphabet to digital code. Hyperindustrial society (société hyperindustrielle) Hyperindustrial society: industrialization extended to services, culture, attention and knowledge. Hypomnemata (hypomnèse, hypomnémata) Hypomnemata: memory aids outside the mind, from Plato's critique of writing to Foucault and digital media. Industrial populism (populisme industriel) Industrial populism: the populism produced by marketing and the program industries rather than by political movements. Knowledge vs information (savoir / information); entropy and negentropy Knowledge against information: why Chapter 2 calls information entropic and knowledge negentropic. Libidinal economy (économie libidinale) The libidinal economy: how consumer capitalism channels desire, and how it exhausts desire into drives. Otium / negotium Otium and negotium: studious leisure against business, and their link to subsistence, existence and consistence. Pharmakon / pharmacology Pharmakon and pharmacology: every technics as both remedy and poison. Proletarianization (prolétarisation) Proletarianization as the loss of knowledge by producers, consumers and knowledge workers. Short-termism (court-termisme) Short-termism as the temporal form of drive-based behaviour in finance, media and politics. Spirit (esprit; la valeur esprit) Spirit (esprit) and Valéry's "value of spirit", the book's measure of what consumer capitalism lowers. Symbolic misery (misère symbolique) Symbolic misery: the loss of individuation that follows from losing a part in producing symbols. Technologies of spirit (technologies de l'esprit); psychotechnologies vs nootechnologies Technologies of spirit, and the contrast between psychotechnologies and nootechnologies. Tertiary retention (rétention tertiaire) Tertiary retention: memory held outside the living being in artefacts, after Husserl's primary and secondary retention. Individuation, transindividuation, disindividuation Individuation, transindividuation and disindividuation, after Simondon.

items.title: Associated milieu / dissociated milieu (milieu associé / dissocié)
items.text: Home › Glossary › associated milieu

items.title: Definition
items.text: Gilbert Simondon (Du mode d'existence des objets techniques, 1958) called a technical object's associated milieu the environment that the object itself conditions and that conditions it in return, in a recursive loop. His example is the Guimbal turbine, cooled by the very river that drives it. Stiegler transposes the idea to social and symbolic milieus. A milieu is associated when its participants contribute to individuating it and individuate themselves in doing so: language, a scientific community, free-software projects. It is dissociated (Stiegler's coinage) when it is individuated by specialists at the expense of everyone else. The culture industries are the paradigm: transmitters and receivers, producers and consumers.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• 2010 Manifesto §3: on the internet, contributors "form what one calls an associated milieu—thereby taking up a concept from Gilbert Simondon". §7: digital infrastructure as an "industrial and technogeographical associated milieu". Its note 9 refers back to Réenchanter le monde (2006) for the concept.
  • Ch. 1: central. Language as the model associated milieu (pp. 34, 49); Simondon's concept and the Guimbal turbine (p. 36); dissociated milieus are "ANTISOCIAL" (p. 36); the internet "structurally constitutes an associated milieu", unlike earlier industrial apparatuses (p. 37); the American revival of associated milieus (p. 45); the polis reconstitutes an "as-sociated milieu" through literal writing (p. 49); public power and the European way of life (pp. 53–55).
  • Ch. 2: Minitel "inaugurated the age of associated milieus founded upon an industrial technology" (p. 61). Tele-cracy is "the perfect accomplishment of the dissociated milieu" (p. 62). Only associated milieus let "the life of the spirit" blossom (p. 67). The knowledge society is "the generalization of associated milieus" (p. 69). Associated milieus are "the a priori condition of any society worthy of the name" (p. 75). Push vs pull in TV/IP convergence (pp. 81–82). The library is an associated milieu par excellence (p. 86). "Societies of authors and readers" against the split of transmitters and receivers (p. 91). N. 3: a human milieu is only ever relatively associated.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: economy of contribution · transindividuation · proletarianization ("the employee of a dissociated milieu") · symbolic misery · technologies of spirit

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Stiegler himself (The Neganthropocene, notes 271 and 449) cites The Re-Enchantment of the World (2014) as the place where he analyses "the recent evolution" of Simondon's associated technogeographic milieus, "which Simondon never had the opportunity to analyse". This is authorial confirmation that the concept is central to the book (Ross file).
  • Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: "dissociated milieu" is credited to Stiegler. The internet is "not structurally dissociated", which makes the contributory economy possible (glossary).
  • Lemmens (2017): clear on the concept; dissociation is still "the dominant situation today" (source).
  • Hui & Halpin (2013): a design programme for social networks as collective individuation (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Stiegler against his 2006–2010 self: later (2018, p. 100) he argues the reticulated web has become "a systemically dissociating milieu, because it is hyper-proletarianizing". The book's hope is thus revised by its author.
  • Labelled interpretation: whether a platform is "associated" turns on who sets the rules (reciprocity, the reader able to write). That is why the 2010 Manifesto ties the concept to free software rather than to "Web 2.0" in general.

items.title: Care (soin; prendre soin; epimeleia)
