items.text: Home › Glossary › care

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Care is attention to and concern for oneself, others and the world, sustained by disciplines and techniques of the self (Greek melete and epimeleia, after Foucault). It is the therapeutic that keeps a pharmakon from becoming toxic. Its opposite is incurie, "carelessness" or negligence. The 2010 Manifesto makes care the axiom of political economy: "to economize means first of all and before anything else to take care" (§2). A politics, and so a political economy, is "firstly and above all a system of care" (§4.2). Culture is what "cultivates a caring relation to the pharmaka".

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Translator's Preface: savoir-vivre as "care for oneself and for sociality".
  • 2010 Manifesto §2 (carelessness of the addicted; care to the heart of political economy), §4.2 (system of care), §5 (a new industrial economy "founded on care"), §7 (care as the "ethics" of contributory business).
  • Ch. 1: traditional societies "take care" of libidinal energy (philia, eros, agape, caritas, mana) (p. 43). Care is the "political question par excellence", understood as socio-therapy, the care taken of individuation (p. 47). The stakes are "(a) founding then (b) caring for" individuation (p. 51). Public power is the care of the social dynamic (p. 54). Consistencies must be treated "with the greatest care" by a libidinal eco-nomy (p. 60).
  • Ch. 2 adds responsibility, attention and the school (pp. 79–91).
  • Prendre soin (2008) systematizes the theme; it does not introduce it.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: pharmakon · economy of contribution · otium/negotium · short-termism (care as the long term) · proletarianization · libidinal economy (addiction as carelessness)

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Stiegler, "Within the limits of capitalism, economizing means taking care" (c. 2008): the source text of the 2010 axiom (source).
  • Cohen (2017): the best secondary account. She links care to Foucault's epimeleia heautou and calls Stiegler's later project a "mystagogy" (source).
  • Ross (2018): culture, education and knowledge are "practices of care" that metastabilize transindividuation (source).
  • Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: the pharmakon is both what enables care and what must be cared for (glossary).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Lotz (2015): the emphasis on "responsibility, care, spirit, and education" shows a position "idealistic and ethical" at its core, a reformist social-democratic ethics in place of political economy (source).
  • Cohen (2017) is sympathetic but corrective. She uses Foucault's aesthetics of existence to temper Stiegler's more prescriptive mode.
  • Labelled interpretation: the play on "economy" in French (économiser, to save or spare, to look after) carries much of the 2010 axiom's force. In English the link between economizing and caring is less evident.

items.title: Disenchantment / re-enchantment (Entzauberung; désenchantement / réenchantement)
items.text: Home › Glossary › disenchantment

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text:
Max Weber's "disenchantment of the world" (Entzauberung der Welt, 1917–19) names the rationalization of modern life. Magic and mystery recede before calculation, bureaucracy and science. Weber also wrote that the spirit of capitalism (The Protestant Ethic, 1904–05) outlives its religious motives. Stiegler's use has three layers:

  1. Disenchantment as libidinal destruction. The industrial capture and destruction of desire is "a chapter of what Max Weber has described much more generally as the disenchantment of the world characteristic of capitalism" (Introduction, p. 2).
  2. Capitalism losing its spirit. Demotivation of producers and consumers "is the concretization of the 'drop in the value of spirit'… the loss of the spirit of capitalism" (Ch. 2, p. 67, per Lotz).
  3. Re-enchantment as a contested slogan. Medef's 2005 summer university used "le réenchantement du monde" to sell the knowledge economy. The book takes the slogan "at its word": real re-enchantment means raising the value of spirit, not producing "knowledge without spirit".

There is also a literal play: savoir/sapere/sapide. A world without knowledge is insipid, without savour (Ch. 1 §3).

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Title. Introduction pp. 2–3; epigraph by Ulrich Beck (what capitalism disenchants are pre-modern traditions, which stopped regenerating after the 1950s). P. 5: Medef's slogan refers to Weber. Capitalism unleashes disenchantment "with a stroke of enchantment": the Protestant spirit, tied to the printing press as a "techno-logy" of spirit. Rationalization (reason as ratio) then lowers the value of spirit, and the present low calls for a sursaut.
  • 2010 Manifesto §4.4: reason replaced by rationalization (Weber, Adorno, Marcuse, Habermas).
  • Ch. 1 "Re-enchanting the world faced with the unhappy destiny of consumption" (p. 33); "The plane that enchants me" (p. 58). The "plane of motifs" is "the plane of enchantment" (p. 58). Enchantment is motivation, which requires incalculable singularities (pp. 58–60).
  • Ch. 2 p. 64 ("on the possibility of 're-enchanting the world'"); p. 71 ("Information society, disenchantment, demotivation…"). Pp. 71–72: talk of "enchantment" is possible because the economy is libidinal; motives are projected onto "the plane that enchants me" (n. 17); cognitive capitalism brings Weber's disenchantment to its climax.
  • Motion p. 96: spiritual misery and Weber's disenchantment.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: spirit · libidinal economy · industrial populism · grammatization (cognitive capitalism as a stage of it, p. 71)

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Stiegler, "Uncontrollable Societies" (2006): extreme disenchantment means capitalism loses its spirit. He rejects Boltanski and Chiapello's "new spirit of capitalism" thesis, and Medef's "re-enchantment" is a symptom (source).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): "extreme disenchantment" as three combined limits of capitalism (source).
  • Lyons (2014) and Hansen (2014): frame the title in Weberian terms. Hansen calls the programme a "re-enchantment of capitalism" (Lyons, Hansen).
  • Context: context-medef-universite-ete-2005.md gives the 2005 Medef theme. It also warns against confusing the book with Maffesoli's Le Réenchantement du monde (2007) or Landy and Saler's The Re-Enchantment of the World (2009).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Rossouw (2015): re-enchantment as a secularized Christian (theological) project (source).
  • Lotz (2015): "new spirit of capitalism" talk veils the real restructuring needed (source).
  • Labelled interpretation: the book does not call for re-sacralization. The Tunis motion explicitly warns against locating spirit only in religion. Its "enchantment" is closer to motivation, desire and meaning sustained by knowledge.

items.title: Economy of contribution (économie de la contribution)
items.text: Home › Glossary › economy of contribution

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text:
The economy of contribution is the industrial model proposed to replace the consumerist model. Its traits:

  1. No separation between producers and consumers. There are only contributors, as in free/open-source software, Wikipedia, smart grids and community-supported agriculture (AMAP).
  2. Its value takes the form of positive externalities: care for self and others, and Sen's capabilities, much of which cannot be monetized.
  3. Its milieus are associated (Simondon), so participants individuate themselves by individuating the milieu.
  4. It aims at de-proletarianization: the reconstitution of savoir-faire, savoir-vivre and theoretical knowledge.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• 2010 Manifesto §3 (named and defined), §6 (free software as de-proletarianization), §7 (generalization: smart grids, AMAP, contributory businesses), §9.3 (fiscal policy for positive externalities; work as distinct from employment). N. 9: the concept was suggested by Franck Cormerais. P. 25: contributory businesses must learn from the failure of the cooperative movements of Charles Gide and Marcel Mauss.
  • Already explicit in 2006: Ch. 1 pp. 36–37 names "the economy of contribution typical of open-source software" (Linux; users as practitioners), grounded in the IP network as an associated milieu since 1992. This economy furnishes "the concepts of a new industrial model" called to replace that of dissociated milieus (p. 36). The internet as associated milieu enables an industrial model resting on the association of addressees and addressors, which produces "a new form of sociality and a new spirit of capitalism (while waiting for the replacement of the latter by another form of society)" (p. 37).
  • Ch. 2 p. 87: Wikipedia is "an extraordinary success" showing that the participatory logic of associated milieus is "an extremely new and powerful dynamic". P. 91 and pp. 92–93: hypertextual "societies of authors and readers", with Web 2.0 as infrastructure anticipating "a new industrial model".
  • Motion p. 95: knowledge as a common good, with only temporary property limits.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: associated milieu · proletarianization · care · pharmakon · otium/negotium · short-termism

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: three traits: no producer/consumer split; non-monetizable value as positive externality; an economy of existences as much as of subsistences. The contributor is neither consumer, nor taxpayer, nor gift-giver in Mauss's sense (glossary).
  • Stiegler–Lemmens interview (2010): a "new industrial model". Stiegler explicitly brackets whether it will still be capitalism. Lemmens presses him on the marginality of free software and on the neoliberal state (source).
  • Hui & Halpin (2013): a Simondonian design programme for social networks along contributory lines (source).
  • Abbinnett (2015): frees labour from "ratio" so that otium becomes a universal good (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Manche (2021): the most rigorous critique. Contribution rests on a teleological, operaist reading of automation. It sidelines profit and accumulation, yields "good vs bad capitalism" reformism, and risks self-exploitation and co-optation by corporate partners (source).
  • Lemmens (2017): accepts the pharmacological frame but criticizes Stiegler's statism (source).
  • Lotz (2015): the book's only example is Wikipedia (p. 87); Benkler's Wealth of Networks says more. Lotz overstates this: Ch. 1 also cites open-source software and Linux (p. 36), and the 2010 Manifesto cites free software, smart grids and AMAP (source).
  • Stiegler's own revision: by The Neganthropocene (2018) he judged the algorithmic web "a systemically dissociating milieu", which qualifies the 2010 optimism (Ross).

items.title: Grammatization (grammatisation)
items.text: Home › Glossary › grammatization

items.title: Definition
items.text: Grammatization is the process by which temporal flows (speech, gesture, perception, calculation) are discretized into reproducible spatial elements, "grammes". The examples are the alphabet's letters, the machine-tool's encoded gestures, the phonograph groove and binary code. Stiegler takes the term from linguist Sylvain Auroux (La révolution technologique de la grammatisation, 1994), who used it for the alphabet's precedence over grammar and logic. He generalizes it to the whole of technical history and links it to Derrida's grammatology. Each stage of grammatization creates new possibilities of knowledge and new risks of proletarianization. It goes with a general organology: the co-evolution of physiological organs, technical organs and social organizations.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Ch. 1 n. 2 defines grammatization as a process of description, formation and discretization of human behaviours that makes their reproducibility possible. §3 (pp. 31–33): critiques of the culture industry lack "a projection into the dynamic of the process of grammatization" and an "organological approach" (note defining general organology). The section "Grammatization and individuation—yesterday, today, and tomorrow" (pp. 47–51; translated earlier by Barker, source) gives the deep history: hydraulic empires' writing as control; Phoenician to Greek literal writing as the citizen's associated milieu; Nora and Minc's comparison of informatics to Sumerian writing (n. 37); the nineteenth-century grammatization of gesture (phonograph, photography, Taylor, n. 38).
  • Ch. 2 p. 62: the internet, like the alphabet, printing, machine-tool and TV, is a stage of grammatization that outstrips its actors' intentions ("epokhal double redoubling", n. 4). P. 71: cognitive capitalism is "a stage of the process of grammatization". P. 77: externalization of memory is grammatization. P. 87: the alphabet as grammatization preceding all science (Auroux, n. 40); the third industrial revolution as a passage from mnemotechnical to mnemotechnological societies. The English bibliography wrongly lists Auroux's book under "Christian Fauré".

items.title: Related terms
items.text: tertiary retention · hypomnemata · proletarianization · hyperindustrial society · transindividuation · pharmakon

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ross (2018): "the primary analytical concept" of the second phase of Stiegler's work. It extends from Palaeolithic "arche-cinema" through gestures in machines and analogue media to binary code, and connects Socrates' pharmakon of writing to Marx's Grundrisse (source).
  • Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: three stages (literal, analogue, digital). The digital is that of hyperindustrial society. The term is borrowed from and "diverted" from Auroux (glossary).
  • Lemmens (2017): grammatization within general organology; the digital as a new pharmakon (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: the conceptual hinge of the book is that grammatization is neither simply loss (Plato, the Frankfurt School) nor simply gain (Serres, the "knowledge society" boosters). It is the condition of both, and that is why Ch. 1 says critics of the culture industry lack it.

items.title: Hyperindustrial society (société hyperindustrielle)
items.text: Home › Glossary › hyperindustrial society

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Against theories of a "post-industrial" society, Stiegler argues that we live in a hyper-industrial epoch. Industrialization now extends beyond material production to services, culture, cognition and everyday life: "life itself", including attention and knowledge, is produced and managed industrially. In Ch. 1 this takes the form of service capitalism. Services take over activities people once performed themselves and control the processes by which ways of life are adopted. The term comes from De la misère symbolique 1: L'époque hyperindustrielle (2004).

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Introduction: "cultural" or "cognitive" capitalism.
  • Ch. 1 "The hyperindustrial epoch as service capitalism" (p. 29): there are "no alternatives" to an ever more industrial world. In hyperindustrial society all forms of life become objects of rationalization, investment and service; "de-industrialization" is only a new division of labour. N. 1 refers to De la misère symbolique 1. L'époque hyperindustrielle (2004). "Hyperindustrial service societies as the destruction of processes of individuation through the control of processes of adoption" (p. 31).
  • Ch. 2 "The re-instrumentation of forms of knowledge and the future of hyperindustrial society" (p. 73): hyperindustrialization is inevitable but has self-destructive limits, and calls for a "renaissance of knowledge" and a "sustainable development of spirit".

items.title: Related terms
items.text: proletarianization · grammatization (the digital stage) · industrial populism · transindividuation (adoption as individuation) · technologies of spirit

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: the digital stage of grammatization corresponds to "hyperindustrial society" (glossary).
  • Stiegler–Lemmens interview (2010/2011): the industrialization of the life of the mind; a "new industrial model" rather than an exit from industry (source).
  • Ross (2018): the setting of the "second phase" of the work (source).
  • Hutnyk (2012): places it in the cognitive-capitalism debate and doubts its novelty (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Against post-industrial theorists (Bell, Touraine), Stiegler's point is that services are more industrial, not less. Lotz reads the corollary, that "the future is still to be sought in an industrial mode of production", as a weakness: industrial production is never put in question (source).
  • Labelled interpretation: the 2006 notion of "service capitalism" predates platform capitalism, but it describes the same mechanism (control of adoption through services). Readers often find it prescient for that reason (Goodreads).

items.title: Hypomnemata (hypomnèse, hypomnémata)
items.text: Home › Glossary › hypomnemata

items.title: Definition
items.text: Greek: memory aids, supports of memory outside the mind. Examples are notebooks, account books, registers and writing in general. In the Phaedrus, Plato contrasts hypomnesis (artificial recall) with anamnesis (living recollection, the true knowledge of the soul). Foucault ("L'écriture de soi", 1983) showed how Stoic and Epicurean hypomnemata served as techniques of the self, a "writing of the self". Stiegler joins the two senses. All mnemotechnics, from the alphabet to digital media, are hypomnemata. They can support anamnesis and self-constitution or replace them, which makes them pharmaka.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Introduction p. 6: hypomnemata supported Foucault's "writing of the self" and also the sophists' control of opinion.
  • 2005 Manifesto: ICTs as "a new form of hypomnemata" (Foucault, Plato), which "conjure new practices… new social organizations".
  • 2010 Manifesto §4: digital hypomnemata as pharmaka; writing as the pharmakon of reference for Western savoir-vivre.
  • Ch. 1 n. 3: hypomnemata are artificial memory supports in all their forms, from Australian tjurunga and incised prehistoric bones through printing and the Bible to electronic assistants and MP3 players. §3: Chinese characters as "the Asian form of the hypomnematon". The future of a society lies in adopting new technologies, "in particular hypomnemata".
  • Ch. 2 p. 64 (spirit always operates through hypomnemata), p. 73 (Mesopotamian control technologies becoming the hypomnemata of Greek individuation), p. 79 (against Plato: the school as appropriation of the alphabetic hypomnesis).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: tertiary retention · grammatization · pharmakon · technologies of spirit · otium/negotium · care

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: both otium and negotium use hypomnemata (glossary).
  • Holmes (2007): notes that the Foucault "writing of the self" link is genuinely Ars Industrialis's own (source).
  • Ross (2018): links Socrates' pharmakon of writing to grammatization (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: the book's core move against Plato is that hypomnesis is the condition of anamnesis, not its contrary, which is a Derridean inheritance. Ch. 2 states it in policy terms: build institutions of appropriation.

items.title: Industrial populism (populisme industriel)
items.text: Home › Glossary › industrial populism

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Industrial populism is a populism produced by the organization of the economy, specifically the culture and program industries and marketing, rather than by political movements. It levels and flatters the lowest common denominator of drives in order to capture audiences and sell their attention. Its emblem is TF1 chief Patrick Le Lay's claim (2004) that what the channel sells Coca-Cola is "available human brain time". The book's subtitle sets the value of spirit against it. The Introduction defines contemporary "cultural" or "cognitive" capitalism as "before all else the destructive organization of an industrial populism" that uses each technical evolution to turn consciousness into a reflex organ (p. 1).

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Subtitle; Introduction p. 1 (definition), pp. 2–3 (Seillière/Le Lay). P. 5: nearly all social life is controlled by the "industry of available brain-time", i.e. industrial populism. P. 7: financier capitalism is "the true underwriter of industrial populism".
  • 2010 Manifesto §9.6: media policy against an industrial populism "induced by the drive-based becoming of consumerism".
  • Ch. 1 p. 50: industrial populism and tele-cratic television as a process of disindividuation (Berlusconi's "tele-cracy").
  • Ch. 2 p. 62: tele-cracy "leads ineluctably to populism". "Enterprises, public power, and industrial populism" (p. 66): evidence from Le Lay; contrast with a knowledge society. P. 69: the model of dissociated milieus "inevitably leads to industrial populism". P. 75: tele-cracy is "the Italian name for industrial populism" (Berlusconi).
  • Tunis motion p. 97: TV must become an instrument of knowledge "and no longer the instrument of debasement and of industrial populism".
  • Already in Stiegler's Libération diary (June 2005): industrial populism produces desublimation, which is "the enemy" (source).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: libidinal economy (drives vs desire) · symbolic misery · spirit · short-termism · technologies of spirit · disenchantment

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire, "Populisme industriel et télécratie": a populism "of a new kind" whose causes are economic. Consumerist societies reach their limits, life becomes drive-based and addictive, and political populism follows secondarily. "Telecracy" is mass audiovisual media short-circuiting political transindividuation (glossary). In 2013 the association used the concept to analyse the Front National (Pharmacologie du Front National).
  • Stiegler, "Uncontrollable Societies" (2006): ties industrial populism to "available brain time" and to the loss of shame (aidos) (source).
  • Ross (2018): reads later "industrially-generated populism" and "post-truth" politics as the continuation of this diagnosis (source).
  • Abbinnett (2015): uses the term as shorthand for the "disorientated life" of consumer culture (source).
  • Context: the exact wording and source of Le Lay's statement is in context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004.md.

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• The secondary literature uses the term but rarely analyses it.
  • Labelled interpretation: in 2005–06 the concept is television-centred (Le Lay, Star Academy). Readers such as a Goodreads reviewer note that the remedies are correspondingly TV-focused (source). Its extension to platforms and social media is a later move by Stiegler (2010 Manifesto §4; The Neganthropocene).
  • The French term differs from the Anglo-American political-science use of "populism". Stiegler's claim is causal: economic organization comes first, political populism second.

items.title: Knowledge vs information (savoir / information); entropy and negentropy
items.text: Home › Glossary › knowledge vs information

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: The central distinction of Ch. 2. Information as a commodity is entropic. Its value decays with time, as with news and market data. Knowledge (savoir) is negentropic. It keeps and intensifies its value, is transmitted and reactivated across generations, and "constitutes time". An economy that converts knowledge into information (Lyotard's performativity, "a doing without knowing") therefore carries an internal contradiction. The "knowledge society" risks becoming its opposite, a reign of ignorance. Savoir covers savoir-faire (know-how), savoir-vivre (knowing how to live) and theoretical knowledge (savoirs théoriques). This three-way division structures the theory of proletarianization.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Introduction p. 3: can there be "knowledge without spirit"?
  • Ch. 1 §3: capitalism tends "to produce entropy and distaste" and liquidates knowledge (p. 33). N. 12: negentropy fights entropy, "the equalization and indifferentiation of all things", and individuation is essentially negentropic.
  • Ch. 2: adaptation is "deeply entropic" (p. 67). Knowledge is critique and therefore "intrinsically contradictory to adaptation" (p. 72). "Knowledge (Savoir) and information" (p. 77) and "Knowledge and memory, or reign of ignorance?" (p. 79): information as commodity is "in its essence entropic"; knowledge is "in its essence negentropic", intensifying (Kant, Thom) and constituting "the time of existence" (pp. 77–79). "Cognitive saturation and 'knowledge management'" (p. 83). Lotz cites p. 23 for knowledge reduced to "controllable, calculative" information, though that page falls in the 2010 Manifesto.
  • Tunis motion: knowledge is essentially "shared and shareable".

items.title: Related terms
items.text: proletarianization · tertiary retention · spirit · short-termism · transindividuation

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ross (2018): entropy and negentropy become the axis of Stiegler's late "neganthropological" phase. This book is an early statement of it (source).
  • Stiegler, 2005 Ars Industrialis presentation: the "cognitive overflow" passage anticipates Ch. 2 (source).
  • MACBA podcast (2019): technics can raise or lower entropy (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: the thermodynamic vocabulary is asserted rather than derived in Ch. 2. Information theory's sense of entropy (Shannon) differs from the economic "decay of value" the chapter has in mind. Stiegler's later work (The Neganthropocene, 2018) tries to make the analogy rigorous through Schrödinger, Lotka and Georgescu-Roegen.

items.title: Libidinal economy (économie libidinale)
items.text: Home › Glossary › libidinal economy

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: The libidinal economy is the organization and production of desire: the channelling of libidinal energy, in Freud's sense of drive energy socialized through sublimation, onto objects. Stiegler's thesis is that twentieth-century capitalism made libido its main energy source. Marketing and the culture industries (Bernays) channel desire towards commodities so as to absorb overproduction. That capture ends by destroying desire. Desire degrades into drives (pulsions), attention is short-circuited, and investment in every sense collapses. The Introduction calls this episode of libidinal economy "a destruction of desire" and "a chapter" of Weber's disenchantment (p. 2). The term echoes Lyotard's Économie libidinale (1974), but Stiegler's use is Freudian and normative: desire, unlike drive, attaches to singular objects and sustains long-term investment.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Introduction pp. 1–2: Benjamin and Freud missed capitalism's reorganization around the consumer "as a very particular form of libidinal economy".
  • 2005 Manifesto: capture of libido as capitalism's energy; its destruction leading "inevitably" to crisis; ruin of sublimation and of the super-ego.
  • 2010 Manifesto §1–3: Bernays; the drive-based consumer and speculator; disinvestment; addiction; contribution "reconstructs a productive economy of desire".
  • Ch. 1 pp. 39–43, "capitalism of drives" (p. 39), is the book's fullest statement. Libido is the socialization of sexual-drive energy into sublimatable objects. It projects consistencies (love, knowledge, art). The libidinal economy economizes by deferring satisfaction (Derrida's différance; Freud's pleasure and reality principles, and after 1920 the life and death drives). Libido, "neither oil nor coal", is what makes capital function, and desire is "one of the productions of libido". Capitalism is "an enormous economy of motivation" whose techniques have become counterproductive, turning motives into de-motivation. Exhausting libido destroys philia and the "we", making capitalism barbarous. Societies traditionally took care of this energy as philia, eros, agape, caritas, mana (p. 43).
  • Ch. 2 p. 71: talk of "enchantment" is possible because the knowledge economy is first a libidinal economy of motives.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: spirit · industrial populism · short-termism · symbolic misery · care · pharmakon · transindividuation

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: libido is "socialized and desexualized" drive energy, invested through artefacts (fetishism), which is why it can be industrialized. Unlimited exploitation exhausts it, so a "renewable" libidinal energy is needed, an ecological problem. Besetzung means both libidinal and financial investment (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): "libidinal dis-economy"; drive-based capitalism; Le Lay; investment against speculation (source).
  • Hansen (2014): reads the programme as "saving libidinal capitalism", a "short-term economy of the drive" to be replaced by a long-term economy of desire. He calls the project curious, even perverse, for seeking to save capitalism (source).
  • Abbinnett (2015): the fall in libidinal energy is "the determining limit of consumer capitalism"; global inequality results from "pathologically disordered forms of libido" (source).
  • Lemmens (2017): accepts the libidinal-exhaustion thesis within a post-autonomist frame (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Marxist objection (Lotz; Hutnyk; Manche): putting desire and consumption at the centre makes labour, capital accumulation and class "evaporate" from the analysis (Lotz, Hutnyk, Manche).
  • Arendtian objection (Roodt): reducing the life of the mind to libido loses what Arendt meant (source).
  • Labelled interpretation: the empirical claim that libidinal energy is being "exhausted" works as a premise in the book rather than a demonstrated finding. Supporters treat it as a structural diagnosis; critics read it as a decline narrative.

items.title: Otium / negotium
items.text: Home › Glossary › otium / negotium

items.title: Definition
items.text: Latin terms. Negotium ("not-leisure") is business: the sphere of subsistence, calculation and exchange. Otium is studious leisure: time freed from necessity for cultivating oneself and others, reading, writing, contemplation and care of the self. In Greek this is skholè, from which "school" derives. Stiegler holds that the two must stay distinct without being opposed. Both use hypomnemata. Otium aims at "consistences" (ideal objects, the objects of sublimation), and its practices are disciplines or techniques of the self. His charge against service capitalism is that it folds otium into negotium: leisure becomes consumption time, and "free" time is sold as available brain time.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• 2005 Manifesto p. 13: industrial technologies of spirit, as new hypomnemata like those of the Stoics and Epicureans or of "the Rome in which the Greek skholè became the Roman practice of the otium", call for new practices. Note 5 cites J.-M. André, L'Otium dans la vie morale et intellectuelle romaine (1966). The manifesto also mentions Foucault's "writing of the self" (hypomnemata in Stoic and Epicurean schools), which is the practice of otium.
  • Ch. 1 develops the related scheme of subsistence, existence and consistence. Man cannot merely subsist; he ex-sists (p. 30). Modes of subsistence and existence must support "the other plane", the plane of consistencies, which "do not exist" and must be cared for (pp. 58–60).
  • Stiegler's Libération diary (June 2005), written in the founding weeks of Ars Industrialis, makes otium explicit. Freedom passes "essentially through otium", and otium is equated with spirit (sacred or profane), linked to Plutarch's "art of living" and to the journal as a practice of self-writing (source).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: spirit · care · hypomnemata · proletarianization (loss of savoir-vivre) · economy of contribution

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: negotium is the calculable sphere of business and subsistence; otium is leisure and existence, oriented to consistences and practised through techniques of the self. Service industries short-circuit otium. See also the entries "Skholè" and "Subsister, exister, consister" (glossary).
  • Cohen (2017): the subsistence/existence/consistence scheme and care of the self (Foucault) (source).
  • Abbinnett (2015): in the contributory economy, freed from "ratio", otium becomes "the global-universal good of prosthetic humanity" (source).
  • Rossouw (2015): the "new otium" as a secularized Christian project (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Abbinnett glosses otium as "the labour of spirit". Labelled interpretation: this is loose, since otium is precisely not labour in the sense of negotium. A charitable reading would say Stiegler distinguishes work (travail, œuvre) from employment, so that otium can be "work" without being employment, as in the 2010 Manifesto §9.3.
  • Rossouw's theological reading against the secular reading of Ars Industrialis remains open.

items.title: Pharmakon / pharmacology
items.text: Home › Glossary › pharmakon

items.title: Definition
items.text: In Plato's Phaedrus, writing is offered as a pharmakon, a drug that is at once remedy and poison. Derrida's "Plato's Pharmacy" (1968) made the ambivalence central. Stiegler generalizes it: every technics is pharmacological. It can support or destroy individuation, and which one depends on the practices, institutions and care that surround it. Without a therapeutic (melete, epimeleia: discipline, care, techniques of the self), a pharmakon becomes toxic. "Pharmacology" is the knowledge and politics of this ambivalence.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Explicitly in 2006: Ch. 1 pp. 47–51. Technologies of spirit are "poison and remedy". The pharmakon (Plato; Derrida, n. 35), reanalysed in Mécréance et discrédit 3, is a question of socio-therapy, of care for individuation. Writing in the Phaedrus is the citizen's tekhnē tou biou and the sophists' weapon. Digital technology is "the hypomnématon (the pharmakon)" that can reconstitute associated milieus (p. 51). Also, implicitly, Ch. 2 p. 79 (anamnesis/hypomnesis).
  • Systematically: the 2010 Manifesto §4.1–4.5 and §6 ("hypomnemata are, as pharmaka, remedies as well as poisons"; psychotechnologies must become nootechnologies). De Beer cites French p. 82 for the pharmakon and technologies of spirit (source).
  • Chronology: the systematic vocabulary of pharmacology is developed in Stiegler's 2007–2010 work (What Makes Life Worth Living, 2010). But the term and the argument are already explicit in Ch. 1 (2006), drawing on Mécréance et discrédit 3 (2006).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: care · hypomnemata · technologies of spirit · tertiary retention · economy of contribution · proletarianization

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: remedy, poison and scapegoat (the third sense is Derrida's). The pharmakon is both what enables care and what must be cared for. "Positive pharmacology" may still prohibit some pharmaka; the example given is nuclear power (glossary).
  • Abbinnett (2015): Stiegler extends Derrida's pharmakon beyond writing to all human–technical interfaces. It "sharpens the aporia" of technological society, between capitalized desire and new cathexes of love and spirit (source).
  • Stiegler–Lemmens interview (2010): a technology is first poisonous and becomes curative only after a second "epochal redoubling" (source).
  • Lyons (2014): foregrounds the pharmakon as the root of the book's "philosophy of hope" (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Hutnyk (2012) turns it back on Stiegler: "stupidity too can be pharmacological", so Stiegler's own decline narrative should be read pharmacologically (source).
  • Manche (2021): pharmacology combined with an operaist reading of Marx's "Fragment on Machines" yields a teleological view of technology (source).
  • Labelled interpretation: Lyons reads the 2014 book through the pharmakon. This fits the 2006 chapters too (pp. 47–51), not only the 2010 Manifesto.

items.title: Proletarianization (prolétarisation)
items.text: Home › Glossary › proletarianization

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text:
Proletarianization is the loss of knowledge (savoir) by individuals when that knowledge is formalized in, and passes into, a technique, machine, apparatus or service. The 2010 Manifesto §6 gives the canonical definition: knowledge "being formalized through a technique, a machine, or an apparatus, can escape the individual". Three waves:

  1. Workers lose savoir-faire (know-how) to machines: Smith and Marx.
  2. Consumers lose savoir-vivre (knowing how to live) to apparatus and services. The TV set "occupying" children is the example, and Ch. 1 §3 has the line "mode de vie" becoming "mode d'emploi" (a way of life becoming a user manual).
  3. Cognitive workers and decision-makers lose theoretical and critical knowledge to information systems. Greenspan admitted he did not understand the system he managed.

Ch. 1 §3 gives the short form: the proletarian is one who loses their knowledge. The producer becomes pure labour power, the consumer pure purchasing power.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Translator's Preface: savoir-faire, savoir-vivre, double proletarianization.
  • Not in the 2005 Manifesto as a term.
  • 2010 Manifesto §5–6: definition; "disapprenticeship"; free software as de-proletarianization.
  • Ch. 1: "The consumer discharged of his existence" (p. 30). §3 (pp. 31–35): generalized proletarianization through service capitalism's control of adoption. "One who has lost his ways of knowing has been proletarianized". The producer loses savoir-faire and becomes labour power (force de travail); the consumer loses savoir-vivre, which becomes a mode of employment, and becomes purchasing power (pouvoir d'achat). Fordism generalizes this, masked by making the producer a consumer. P. 51: machines (Taylor), then appliances, exteriorize knowledge into algorithms, giving proletarianization and loss of savoir-faire, savoir-vivre and contemplation.
  • Ch. 2 pp. 71–72: losses of savoir-faire and savoir-vivre over a few decades, as losses of individuation. P. 74: digital instrumentalization proletarianizes researchers and dissociates cognitive milieus.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: grammatization · hyperindustrial society · economy of contribution · associated milieu · knowledge vs information · care

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ross (2018): "perhaps his fundamental political concept". Socrates is its first thinker; the waves run nineteenth century (work), twentieth (life), twenty-first (theory) (source).
  • Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: Marx's working class was only the first proletarianized class. After 2008 designers and decision-makers are proletarianized by automated systems. The proletarian is "the employee of a dissociated milieu" (Simondon). Proletarianization is "not a fatality" (glossary).
  • Stiegler, April interview (2011): plain-language statement of the consumer's loss of savoir-vivre (source).
  • Lotz (2015): mental life becomes "proletarian" through externalized memory; he notes Stiegler "no longer" speaks Marxist language (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Marxist critics (Hutnyk 2012; Manche 2021; Lotz): redefining the proletariat by loss of knowledge rather than dispossession and wage-labour sidelines class, exploitation and accumulation. Manche's title puts it sharply: "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (Hutnyk, Manche).
  • Sympathetic readers (Ross, Lemmens) reply that Stiegler is returning to an earlier sense found in Marx's Grundrisse (knowledge absorbed into fixed capital) and in Simondon (Lemmens).
  • Labelled interpretation: the concept explains the book's otherwise surprising politics. If the problem is loss of knowledge rather than ownership, the remedy is de-proletarianization through new practices and instruments, which leaves the question of property in second place.

items.title: Short-termism (court-termisme)
items.text: Home › Glossary › short-termism

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Short-termism is the systematic sacrifice of the long term to the short term in investment, management, media and politics. For Stiegler it is not only a financial vice. It is the temporal form of drive-based behaviour: the drive wants immediate satisfaction, whereas desire and knowledge are long-circuited and accumulate over time. Shareholder demands for "two-digit returns" (2005 Manifesto), adaptive corporate strategy, audience-ratings TV and speculative finance express one and the same short-termism. Its opposite is investment, financial and libidinal (Besetzung), and long-term public anticipation.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• 2005 Manifesto: market criteria favour "short-term financial investments"; shareholders want returns "never below 15%".
  • 2010 Manifesto §1: "neo-liberal short-termism" leads to disinvestment. The speculator is "a capitalist who no longer invests". §5: guarantee the short term in order to reach and reverse it in the long term.
  • Ch. 1 p. 40: economic actors draw short-term private profit from dissociation and so have no interest in change, "wrong… regarding their own long-term interests". P. 52: financier capitalism dominates and paralyses the long-term initiatives of industrial capitalism.
  • Ch. 2 p. 66: Medef's "continuous adaptation" is an entropic vicious circle. Industrial policy for technologies of spirit can only be long-term, led by a new public power.
  • Tunis motion: public and private funds should not seek "short-term returns on investment".

items.title: Related terms
items.text: libidinal economy · care · knowledge vs information (information's value decays fast; knowledge lasts) · industrial populism · economy of contribution

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire ("Financiarisation"): finance as a "commerce of promises". Fully realized short-termism destroys the retentions (knowledge) and protentions (investments) of time (quoting For a New Critique of Political Economy, 2009) (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): drive-based consumption mirrors speculative disinvestment, with hedge funds and LBOs as examples (source).
  • Hansen (2014): the "short-term economy of the drive" (source).
  • Ross (2018): the financial crisis as a symptom of increasingly short-term, speculative investment (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Little disagreement on the diagnosis. The critics' question is about agency: who will impose the long term? Stiegler's answer, a "new public power" with industry, is what Lotz and Manche find reformist and Lemmens finds statist (reception.md).

items.title: Spirit (esprit; la valeur esprit)
items.text: Home › Glossary › spirit

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Esprit is the noetic life of human beings: intelligence, attention, memory, judgement and desire as sublimated. Stiegler treats it as both psychic and collective, and as dependent on technical supports. The phrase "la valeur esprit", "the value [called] spirit", comes from Paul Valéry (1939). Valéry compared spirit to a commodity value, like oil or wheat, whose price can fall, and he saw a "drop in the value of spirit" before the war. The book's wager is that spirit is now the main industrial resource ("after matter, spirit has become the first industrial resource", Tunis motion) and the thing being depleted. Spirit in this sense is not religious. The Tunis motion warns against locating spirit only in religion. Nor is it the brain: the Introduction contrasts consciousness, the seat of spirit, with "a brain reduced to an ensemble of neurons".

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Title and subtitle; Translator's Preface (pp. viii–ix: esprit versus "spirit").
  • Introduction pp. 1–3: Valéry; is "knowledge without spirit" possible? P. 7: spirit, which always presupposes technologies of spirit, is "a modality of… psychic and collective individuation" (Simondon). Knowledge is "the treasure bequeathed by those who are dead".
  • 2005 Manifesto: "technologies of spirit", "industrial ecology of spirit", the "life of the mind/spirit" (Arendt). P. 11: "spirit" is meant also in the sense of the English word "mind", despite its metaphysical and theological baggage.
  • Ch. 1: the "enslaved spirit… servile spirit, which serves the service societies" (p. 33; cited by Lotz); capitalism "needs a spirit" (p. 35); "new spiritual devices" (p. 37); capitalism become barbarous is "denuded of spirit" (p. 43); a "debilitated", "rotten" or "servile" spirit cannot found enterprises (p. 46); Weber's spirit of capitalism has been lost through the control of affects (p. 55).
  • Ch. 2 title; p. 67 (demotivation as the "drop in the value of spirit", the loss of the "spirit of capitalism"); p. 68 (spirit as the capacity to imagine and concretize alternatives, per Lotz); p. 69 (spirit cannot be adapted; one learns a theorem by re-living its genesis, methodos).
  • Tunis motion: spirit as both "available brain time" and "works of the mind". P. 96: spirit must not be situated "exclusively on the side of the religious"; underinvestment in the value of spirit has fed "regressive and radical spiritualisms". P. 100: reason as "universal motif of spirit".

items.title: Related terms
items.text: technologies of spirit · industrial populism · libidinal economy (sublimation) · transindividuation · disenchantment (the "spirit of capitalism", after Weber) · otium/negotium · knowledge vs information

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: spirit is what brain activity becomes when it turns external things into memory supports. It is the dynamic of technically mediated transindividuation, "the 'and'" in Simondon's "psychic and collective individuation". When people can no longer use the technologies imposed on them, spirit loses its capital and capitalism loses its spirit (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Uncontrollable Societies" (2006 text): symbolic misery leads to spiritual misery and the fall of the value of spirit. Ross's translator's note on esprit as mind and spirit is a useful comparison with Arthur's choice of "spirit" (source).
  • Trevor Arthur: esprit as a synthesis of psychic, social, intellectual and historical life (source). Lyons credits this preface as the best key to the term (source).
  • Cohen (2017): the best gloss of the Valéry genealogy. She links spirit to Stiegler's subsistence/existence/consistence scheme (source).
  • Abbinnett (2015): reads spirit through Derrida's Of Spirit. Stiegler shares Derrida's suspicion of Heidegger's Geist, but in Abbinnett's reading spirit must pass through epiphylogenetic, written memory (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text:
• Futural versus memorial. Abbinnett contests Beardsworth's Nietzschean, "remorselessly futural" reading of Stieglerian spirit and ties it to inherited, technically retained memory.
  • Empty or full? Lotz calls the positive notion an empty placeholder ("battle against regression", p. 71) (source).
  • Spirit = libido? Roodt (Arendtian) argues the manifestos reduce Arendt's "life of the mind" to libido, as a function of economic forces (source). De Beer, in the same journal issue, embraces the vocabulary in a quasi-spiritual register (source). Rossouw reads re-enchantment as Christianity by other means (source).
  • Labelled interpretation: the English "spirit" carries religious connotations that esprit (also "mind", "wit") does not. This may explain why some English readers hear the book as more spiritualist than French readers do.

items.title: Symbolic misery (misère symbolique)
items.text: Home › Glossary › symbolic misery

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: Symbolic misery is the loss of individuation that results from losing participation in the production of symbols: meanings, works, expressions and affects. The culture industries split producers of symbols from mere consumers. The consumer stops expressing and only receives, and the circuit of symbolic exchange (expression answering expression) breaks. The term comes from Stiegler's De la misère symbolique 1–2 (2004–05; English Symbolic Misery). In this book it works mostly in the background, as the premise behind spiritual misery and the "drop in the value of spirit".

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Implicit throughout. The 2005 Manifesto on the destruction of singular objects of desire and symbolic practices.
  • Ch. 1 §3: malaise, self-disgust and the insipid world (the sapere/sapide pun). P. 39: "absolute spiritual misery" (the Nice case, end of 2005). P. 58: a century of aesthetics in the service of production and consumption yields "profound symbolic and spiritual misery".
  • Tunis motion: "spiritual misery" (misère spirituelle) striking the industrial world.
  • Stiegler's Libération diary (June 2005): the ruin of symbolic exchange as "the great symbolic misery in which desire in general collapses" (source).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: libidinal economy · industrial populism · proletarianization · transindividuation · associated milieu (dissociated symbolic milieus) · spirit

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: the loss of individuation through losing participation in symbol production, increasing since the "machinic turn" of culture and politics. Fighting the Front National means fighting symbolic misery, and so industrial populism (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Uncontrollable Societies" (2006): symbolic misery "leads irresistibly to spiritual misery" (source).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): the producer/consumer split leaves consumers "de-symbolized" (source).
  • Ross (2018): places the Symbolic Misery volumes at the start of the political "second phase" to which this book belongs (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: the term is used more than it is explained in this book. A reader new to Stiegler will need Symbolic Misery vol. 1, ch. 1–2, to see why aesthetic participation is the model for all participation. The Libération diary cites Leroi-Gourhan's "one must participate in order to feel".

items.title: Technologies of spirit (technologies de l'esprit); psychotechnologies vs nootechnologies
items.text: Home › Glossary › technologies of spirit

items.title: Definition (the book's usage)
items.text: The 2005 Manifesto coined "technologies of spirit" for the sector formed when digitization makes the culture industries, program industries, media, telecommunications and cognitive technologies converge. These technologies are spiritual because they work on attention, memory, imagination and desire. They are also hypomnemata. Ars Industrialis is defined as an association "for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit". The 2010 Manifesto sharpens the point into a normative pair. Psychotechnologies serve behavioural control (marketing, audience capture). Nootechnologies serve the life of the mind and de-proletarianization. The same device can be either.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Introduction p. 3: Ars Industrialis's full name. P. 6: radio, TV, computers and the internet are "spiritual instruments" (Mallarmé on the book).
  • 2005 Manifesto (definition; "industrial ecology of spirit"; control societies).
  • 2010 Manifesto §6: "psychotechnologies… must become nootechnologies, that is, technologies of spirit".
  • Ch. 1: "R technologies" are relational technologies (p. 29; n. 5 cites Rifkin, The Age of Access): telecom and broadcast networks, barcodes, chip cards, RFID, wi-fi, Bluetooth, biometrics, nanotechnologies. "R technologies and the new spiritual devices" (p. 37; French "appareils de l'esprit"): in dissociated milieus they serve control, yet they remain technologies of spirit and could support individuation (pp. 37–38). Nora and Minc foresaw the convergence of audiovisual, telecom and computing but not an "industrial politics of technologies of spirit" (pp. 50–51).
  • Ch. 2 p. 61 (convergence in the 1990s), p. 73 (control technologies as the condition of future individuation; "technologies of intellect"). Pp. 84–86: Mallarmé's "The Book, a spiritual instrument"; Husserl's "spirit-invested objects"; digital hypomnemata as "new spiritual instruments".
  • Tunis motion p. 97: "an industrial politics of technologies of spirit" as the basis for another summit.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: spirit · hypomnemata · pharmakon · industrial populism · associated milieu

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire ("Psychotechnique / nootechnique"): the opposition is "normative, assumed as such". Psychotechnics act on or against the mind to control it, and nootechnics foster its individuation. The criterion is reciprocity (the reader can also write) and long circuits of transindividuation (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Within the limits of capitalism…" (c. 2008): calls for a European industrial politics of technologies of spirit (source).
  • Stiegler, 5 Nov 2005 session on cognitive technologies, knowledge management and design methodology (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: critics rarely address the term directly. It inherits the debates on pharmakon and on statism (reception.md).

items.title: Tertiary retention (rétention tertiaire)
items.text: Home › Glossary › tertiary retention

items.title: Definition
items.text: Tertiary retention is memory retained outside the living being, in artefacts: tools, writing, recordings, databases. Husserl distinguished primary retention (the just-past held in the present of perception, as when a note's sound lingers in a melody) from secondary retention (recollection). Stiegler adds tertiary retention, the technical, "epiphylogenetic" memory that both stores the past and conditions the other two. What we can perceive and remember is overdetermined by the recording and selection technologies of an epoch. Marketing and the program industries operate by controlling tertiary retentions, and through them protentions (expectations and desires).

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
The term appears explicitly in the Introduction's n. 2 (p. 101): the psychic apparatus distributes itself into prostheses and technical apparatuses that support "what I have elsewhere called tertiary retentions", which Ars Industrialis calls hypomnemata. Elsewhere the idea runs under other names:

  • 2005 Manifesto and 2010 Manifesto: hypomnemata and "mnemotechnologies".
  • Ch. 2 "Knowledge (Savoir) and information" (p. 77) and "Knowledge and memory, or reign of ignorance?" (p. 79). Memory is externalized from the human origin; living memory exceeds its "retentional finitude" by exteriorization (p. 79); the mnemotechnical → mnemotechnological transition. "Instruments of knowledge and the criteria of selection" (p. 87): memory as retention is selection, and industrializing it defines new criteria of selection (p. 88; Lotz: memory and imagination become objects of investment).

items.title: Related terms
items.text: hypomnemata · grammatization · knowledge vs information · pharmakon · proletarianization

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire ("Attention, rétention, protention"): tertiary retentions are hypomnesic sediments in artefacts that overdetermine secondary retentions, which in turn overdetermine primary ones (glossary).
  • Ross (2018): marketing and cultural tertiary retentions aim to control protention, which leads to "hypercontrol" and then "uncontrollability" (source).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): money is itself a tertiary retention and protention (source).
  • Manche (2021): a clear standard exposition; the concept is introduced in Technics and Time 3 (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: Ch. 2's anti-Platonic argument (writing is memory's condition, not its death) is the clearest application in the book. Its target is Michel Serres's view that externalizing memory to machines frees us for pure knowledge. For Stiegler, there is no knowledge outside its retentional supports.

items.title: Individuation, transindividuation, disindividuation
items.text: Home › Glossary › transindividuation

items.title: Definition
items.text: From Simondon (L'individuation psychique et collective). Individuation is the never-finished process by which an individual becomes who it is. It is always at once psychic (an "I") and collective (a "we"). Stiegler adds a third, technical strand, because individuation passes through artefacts and memory supports. Transindividuation is the co-individuation of "I"s that produces a "we": shared meanings, knowledges and institutions, metastabilized in symbols and techniques. Disindividuation is the breakdown of this process. It happens when psychotechnologies short-circuit transindividuation: they impose ready-made identifications, saturate attention, or split producers of meaning from consumers.

items.title: Where it appears
items.text:
• Translator's Preface: individuation ("one becomes who he is") and transindividuation ("we become who we are").
  • Ch. 1 p. 30: service industries short-circuit transindividuation; n. 7: individuation is not individualization. §3 (pp. 31–33): individuation is adoption, and service capitalism destroys individuation by controlling adoption (primary and secondary identification). P. 34: Simondon (IPC p. 18) on the individual as an element in a vaster individuation, with language as the model of participatory psychic and collective individuation. P. 47: "Grammatization and individuation". P. 57 (quoted by Lotz): hyper-solicitation of attention "short-circuits transindividuation", causing dis-identification and disindividuation. N. 49: the double sense of "disaffected".
  • Ch. 2 p. 71: spirit is a matter of motives, so of psychic and collective individuation. P. 81: "The risk of disindividuation as the growth of ignorance rather than knowledge". Individuation is always psychic and collective; knowledge exists only as shared and public.

items.title: Related terms
items.text: spirit (as the "and" of psychic and collective) · associated milieu · grammatization · symbolic misery · proletarianization · hyperindustrial society

items.title: How secondary sources gloss it
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Vocabulaire: spirit is the dynamic of technically mediated transindividuation (glossary).
  • Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011): psychotechnologies short-circuit transindividuation (source).
  • Hui & Halpin (2013): "collective individuation" as a design goal for social networks, against individualist user models (source).
  • Ross (2018): care and knowledge "metastabilize" transindividuation (source).
  • Lotz (2015) quotes p. 57 as the book's central formulation of the existential crisis (source).

items.title: Disagreements
items.text: • Labelled interpretation: Stiegler's adaptation thesis (individuation = adoption, from Technics and Time 3) is a distinctive addition to Simondon. It turns the theory into a theory of culture and marketing: whoever shapes adoption shapes individuation.

items.title: Evaluation of sources
items.text:
Home › Source evaluation · see also reception.md

Each source in sources/ is rated on five criteria:

  • Accuracy: against the book itself (see STRUCTURE.md).
  • Coverage: which parts of the book it treats: P = Preface, I = Introduction, M05 / M10 = Manifestos, C1 / C2 = Chapters, T = Tunis motion.
  • Depth: how far the source goes, from 1 (notice) to 5 (sustained analysis).
  • Stance: interpretive bias.
  • Reliability: high / medium / low.

The files themselves hold the condensed account and fuller notes.

items.text: Issue Positions Our assessment Is the remedy empty? Lotz: "empty placeholders". Lyons: "philosophy of hope" but no concrete answers. Lemmens interview: a "new industrial model" with policy planks Both reviewers under-weight the 2010 Manifesto §9 policies and Ch. 2's "practical consequences". Those are concrete but sectoral (education, media, R&D instruments) rather than an account of political agency Marx Lotz, Hutnyk, Manche: class and accumulation sidelined. Ross, Lemmens: return to the Grundrisse and the knowledge sense of proletarianization A real disagreement of frameworks; see concepts/proletarianization.md Spirit Roodt: reduced to libido. De Beer: spiritual depth. Abbinnett v. Beardsworth: memorial v. futural. Rossouw: theological The book's own definition is noetic and transindividual and explicitly not only religious (Tunis motion) Digital networks 2010 Manifesto: associated milieu. Stiegler 2018: "systemically dissociating" The author revised his view; read the 2010 text historically Authorship / founders EN Wikipedia: three co-authors. Catalogues and association: five founders Five (Collins, Crépon, Perret, B. Stiegler, C. Stiegler) Tunis motion Lyons, blurbs: "at the summit", "account of the summit". Association: press motion on the eve The association's account is correct

items.title: F. Ranked reading list
items.text:
Ordered by value for someone reading the book now. Primary texts first, because their accuracy is not in question.

  1. primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005: the draft of Ch. 2. Read it before or alongside the chapter.
  2. primary-parallel-stiegler-uncontrollable-societies-nja-2013: the best contemporaneous statement of spirit, Medef and industrial populism.
  3. review-lotz-marx-and-philosophy-2015: the best page-located review, and the sharpest critique of the book itself.
  4. lit-ross-neganthropocene-introduction-2018: places the book in the corpus; the author's own later revision.
  5. glossary-arsindustrialis-vocabulaire-2013: house definitions. Mind the dating.
  6. lit-manche-proletarianisation-not-capitalism-2021: the strongest critique of proletarianization and contribution.
  7. lit-cohen-dare-to-care-2017: Valéry's esprit and care.
  8. review-roodt-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012: the Arendtian challenge to "life of the mind".
  9. lit-lemmens-digital-pharmakon-general-intellect-2017: a sympathetic critique of statism.
  10. primary-parallel-stiegler-pharmacology-of-desire-2011: the libidinal-economy thesis at full strength.
  11. lit-abbinnett-politics-of-spirit-2015: the Derridean reading of spirit.
  12. review-debeer-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012: French page anchors.
  13. review-lyons-critical-inquiry-2014: the sympathetic Anglophone reception.
  14. context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004 and context-medef-universite-ete-2005: needed to follow the Introduction.
  15. lit-hutnyk-proletarianisation-2012, lit-hansen-saving-libidinal-capitalism-2014, lit-hui-halpin-collective-individuation-2013: further angles.
  16. Everything else is reception colour or bibliographic support.

items.title: Ars Industrialis: what the association's own site says
path: Ars Industrialis: what the association's own site says

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Name. "Association internationale pour une politique industrielle des technologies de l'esprit".
  • Self-description ("qui sommes-nous ?"). The page opens with a quotation from Demy's Les Demoiselles de Rochefort ("Nous sommes des sœurs jumelles…"). The founders describe themselves as "au départ quatre philosophes et une juriste", "cinq" at the initiative of the association. They are worried by the "désarroi" in industrial countries, especially France. Their working hypothesis is that a decisive element of the contemporary malaise (in Freud's sense) is a mutation in the technologies of spirit, the "hypomnémata" of our time (after Foucault's "L'écriture de soi"). They want to be a "force de proposition, et non seulement de réflexion". Thought and the life of the spirit consist first in combating stupidity (bêtise), beginning with one's own, and the "forces of regression" that encourage it.
  • The founders (from the inaugural minutes and the Tunis motion): George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard Stiegler (philosophers) and Caroline Stiegler (jurist).
  • Public sessions were held at the Théâtre de la Colline (Paris), usually on Saturday afternoons, roughly quarterly. Up to the book's publication (Oct 2006) and just after: 18 June 2005 (inaugural); 24 Sept 2005 (knowledge vs information society: the Tunis summit); 5 Nov 2005 (cognitive technologies and digital libraries); 25 Feb 2006 (suffering and consumption); 20 May 2006 (politics and television); 14 Oct 2006 (public impotence and political power); 16 Dec 2006 (sustainable investment); 20 Jan 2007 (participatory democracy); May–June 2007 (formation and destruction of attention). A parallel seminar, "Trouver de nouvelles armes. Pour une polémologie de l'esprit", ran at the Collège international de philosophie for about four years.
  • 2020. A convocation signed by Bernard Stiegler calls an extraordinary general assembly on 27 February 2020 to amend the statutes and found the "Association des Amis de la Génération Thunberg". It refers to the Internation group's work, presented in Geneva on 10 January 2020 to Antonio Guterres and Greta Thunberg. The site footer reads "arsindustrialis.org – 2008-2012". The site is now essentially an archive and links to "Épokhè".

items.text:
• This is the authoritative source for the founders and the session chronology, and it settles the co-founder question (five people, including Caroline Stiegler). Compare media-wikipedia-stiegler-ars-industrialis-2026.md.
  • everybodywiki ("Ars industrialis") claims the association was renamed in 2017. The association's own 2020 convocation points to a 2020 statutory change instead.

items.title: Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"
path: Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"

items.title: Established facts
items.text:
• Speaker. Patrick Le Lay, then chairman and CEO (PDG) of the TF1 television channel. He died in March 2020.
  • Publication. The remark appeared in an interview printed in Les Dirigeants face au changement (Paris: Éditions du Huitième Jour, 2004). This volume is a "baromètre 2004" by the partners of the consultancy EIM (Executive Interim Management). It mostly contains interviews with French business leaders (the catalogue record says 21) and has a preface by Ernest-Antoine Seillière, then Medef president. French Wikipedia also gives the title as Les Dirigeants français et le changement (June 2004). The page is inconsistent on this point, and the form used by Acrimed, Stiegler and the Swiss teaching sheet is Les Dirigeants face au changement.
  • How it became public. Acrimed reports an AFP dispatch of 9 July 2004, followed by a Libération item (10–11 July 2004) headlined "Patrick Le Lay, décerveleur". French Wikipedia cites L'Expansion/L'Express of 9 July 2004 as the earliest dated coverage, and Le Nouvel Observateur. In a September 2004 Télérama interview, reported by Le Monde on 8 Sept 2004, Le Lay said the Medef had invited him to a discussion about change, that it was not an official interview, and that the phrase was "un peu caricaturale et étroite".
  • Exact wording (as reproduced by Acrimed). Key sentences:
  • "à la base, le métier de TF1, c'est d'aider Coca-Cola, par exemple, à vendre son produit"
  • "Or pour qu'un message publicitaire soit perçu, il faut que le cerveau du téléspectateur soit disponible."
  • "Nos émissions ont pour vocation de le rendre disponible"
  • "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible."
  • "Rien n'est plus difficile que d'obtenir cette disponibilité." French Wikipedia also gives his remarks that audience share "se joue chaque jour" and that television is "une activité sans mémoire". Stiegler's 2005 talk, the precursor of ch. 2, quotes further lines from the same interview on reactivity (Star Academy). I have not checked whether the printed book keeps all of them.
path: Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"

items.title: Stiegler's use
items.text: In the 24 Sept 2005 Ars Industrialis talk (see primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md), Stiegler quotes Le Lay at length. He calls this business model "industrial populism" and says selling "available brain time" is the very opposite of a knowledge society. He also cites Le Lay on knowing audiences "to the second" and on Star Academy as "réactivité maîtrisée", and he links this to Bradbury and Truffaut's Fahrenheit 451. The Tunis motion (14 Nov 2005) defines "esprit" as both the "temps de cerveau disponible" that TV channels want and the source of "œuvres de l'esprit". French Wikipedia also says Stiegler called the remarks "effroyables de cynisme et de vulgarité" in Le Monde diplomatique (June 2005, "De la misère symbolique 2. La 'catastrophe' du sensible"). Stiegler also appears in the 2010 France 3 documentary Le Temps de cerveau disponible (Jean-Robert Viallet and Christophe Nick; see media-plandetudes-fiche-temps-de-cerveau-2010.md).
path: Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• The date is often given loosely as "2004", and the publication varies between "a book" and "an interview". The precise form is an interview in an EIM book, publicised by AFP on 9 July 2004. Some English sources misdescribe it as a TV statement or a speech.
  • The Medef link is real but is often missed: the volume was prefaced by Seillière, and Le Lay said the Medef asked him to take part. This is why Stiegler can join "re-enchantment" (Medef 2005) and "available brain time" (Medef-prefaced book, 2004) into one critique.
  • Wikipedia's sourcing for the book title is internally inconsistent, as noted above.
path: Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"

items.title: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")
path: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

items.title: What could be established
items.text:
• The theme. The Medef (the French employers' federation) held its 2005 université d'été under the banner "Réenchanter le monde". Three sources support this. (1) Ars Industrialis's own presentation of its 24 September 2005 session says the Medef summer university "a mis son programme de rencontres sous le signe de la nécessité de 'réenchanter le monde'" (node/1460). (2) Olivier Ezratty, a tech consultant who attended the 2005 edition as a spectator, lists the sequence of Medef summer-university titles: "Réenchanter le monde" (2005), "Concilier l'inconciliable" (2006), "Jouer le jeu" (2007), "Voir grand" (2008). (3) The French publisher's blurb, quoted on bookseller and reader sites, says that in 2005 the Medef held its summer university "sous la bannière du 'réenchantement du monde'".
  • Who chose and framed it, according to Stiegler. Stiegler's 24 September 2005 talk (node/1933; see primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md) attributes the theme to Ernest-Antoine Seillière, Medef president until July 2005. He says Denis Kessler, a leading Medef figure, presented the theme by calling for an "âge d'une augmentation de la valeur esprit", that is, a greater role for knowledge in the economy. According to Stiegler, Kessler cited a Tony Blair speech proposing to redirect EU Common Agricultural Policy money towards knowledge technologies. Stiegler also cites Seillière's preface to the EIM volume Les Dirigeants face au changement (2004), the same book that contains Patrick Le Lay's "temps de cerveau humain disponible" remark (see context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004.md). Stiegler suggests the preface may have been written by advisers or by Kessler. The book's Introduction repeats this material (English edition pp. 2–3, per the existing primary-parallel file). A French excerpt of the Introduction quoted on the Charybde blog (see review-hugues-charybde27-2024.md) adds details. The theme served to promote the views of a Medef leadership "qui était alors en train de changer" on cognitive capitalism and knowledge industries. Kessler "en présentant cette université d'été" referred to Blair's proposal at a time when Britain held the EU presidency (second half of 2005). Seillière had himself wanted this summer university "juste avant de quitter la direction du Medef". The excerpt also sets out the book's question: is the Medef's re-enchantment a "sursaut de la valeur esprit", or a project for an industrial production of "connaissances sans esprit"?
  • Leadership. Laurence Parisot succeeded Seillière as Medef president in July 2005, so the August 2005 summer university was held under her new presidency on a theme reportedly set by her predecessor. Her 2005–2013 tenure is confirmed by Wikipedia. According to a third-party transcription recorded in review-flammarion-4e-de-couverture-2006.md, the French edition is dedicated "A la mémoire de Simon Nora" and "A Laurence Parisot". If that is correct, the book is pointedly addressed to the new Medef president.
  • Speakers. Ezratty recalls being impressed by the speakers in 2005 and names only Erik Orsenna and Canada's ambassador, who spoke on state reform in Canada.
path: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

items.title: What the Medef meant, as far as can be told
items.text: Every account available here comes through Stiegler or through readers repeating him. As he presents it, the Medef used "re-enchantment" as a positive slogan for the knowledge economy, the "société de la connaissance" of Blair and the Medef. Under that slogan, human capital and knowledge would replace the West's lost "technological rent" (Seillière's preface: "Ce début de siècle sonne la fin de la rente technologique pour l'Occident"). Stiegler and Ars Industrialis took the slogan "at its word" and turned it around. The same industrial milieu that wants re-enchantment also sells "available brain time", and that contradiction is the book's starting point. Stiegler set the slogan against Weber's "disenchantment" and Valéry's "baisse de la valeur esprit" (1939).
path: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis, presentation of the 24 Sept 2005 session: the Medef university placed its programme "sous le signe de la nécessité de 'réenchanter le monde'".
  • Ezratty (2008): "'Voir grand' fait ainsi suite à 'Réenchanter le monde' (2005), 'Concilier l'inconciliable' (2006) et 'Jouer le jeu' (2007)."
  • Kessler, as reported by Stiegler: "l'âge d'une augmentation de la valeur esprit".
path: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Kessler's and Seillière's statements are given here through Stiegler's citation, so they should be cited as "according to Stiegler".
  • Ezratty's blog is a reliable first-hand record of the sequence of titles, but it is a personal blog.
  • Do not confuse this event with other 2005–2007 "réenchantement" uses: Jean Staune's science and spirituality writing, Michel Maffesoli's Le Réenchantement du monde (2007), and Joshua Landy and Michael Saler's The Re-Enchantment of the World (Stanford, 2009). These are unrelated to the Medef event or to Stiegler's book.
path: The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

items.title: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion
path: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

items.title: The summit (established)
items.text:
• What it was. The UN World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) ran in two phases: Geneva (December 2003) and Tunis, 16–18 November 2005. Tunisia proposed the summit, and the ITU adopted a resolution on it at its 1998 Minneapolis plenipotentiary conference (ITU French booklet). The ITU organised it under UN auspices.
  • Outcomes. The Tunis Commitment (dated 18 Nov 2005) and the Tunis Agenda for the Information Society. These documents reaffirm Geneva's principles, address financing and the "digital divide", define Internet governance, and create the Internet Governance Forum (IGF), a non-binding multi-stakeholder forum. The US kept control of the DNS root zone and ICANN. Calls from Brazil, South Africa and China for multilateral (ITU) oversight ended in a vague compromise on "enhanced cooperation" (Wikipedia). Commentators said the summit made no notable progress on governance.
  • Attendance. Wikipedia gives about 13,500 participants in total (c. 6,200 from NGOs, 4,800 from the private sector, 980 media). The ITU booklet gives no figures.
  • Controversy. Tunisia under Ben Ali was criticised for its internet censorship and its treatment of journalists. RSF had protested the choice of host as early as 2002, quoting Robert Ménard: "il est tout simplement scandaleux de tenir un tel sommet dans ce pays". During the summit, according to Wikipedia, Ménard was refused entry, a Libération journalist was stabbed and beaten, a Belgian TV crew was forced to hand over footage, and a civil-society session ("Expression Under Repression") was obstructed.
  • Vocabulary. UNESCO's preferred term was "knowledge societies" (plural, "sociétés du savoir"). The WSIS and EU term was "information society". Ars Industrialis exploited this distinction, and ch. 2 opens with it.
path: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

items.title: The Ars Industrialis motion: how it came about (from arsindustrialis.org)
items.text:
• 18 June 2005, inaugural session (Théâtre de la Colline): knowledge societies and the Tunis summit were already on the agenda as the next topic (see media-arsindustrialis-seance-inaugurale-2005.md).
  • 24 September 2005, session "Société de savoirs et société de l'information: les enjeux du Sommet de Tunis". It was moderated by Catherine Perret, with Jean-Max Noyer (Paris XI), Serge Regourd (Toulouse) and Stiegler (president). Its stated aim was to draft a public motion "en tant que personne morale" before Tunis. Stiegler's talk there is the precursor of ch. 2 (see primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md and media-arsindustrialis-presentation-tunis-seance-2005.md).
  • 5 November 2005, session on cognitive technologies and digital libraries, with contributions by Philippe Aigrain, Jean-Max Noyer, Stiegler and Alain Giffard. The page links to the motion text (see media-stiegler-technologies-cognitives-2005.md).
  • 14 November 2005: the motion "Le véritable enjeu du sommet de Tunis" was published in Libération, two days before the summit opened. It was signed by George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard and Caroline Stiegler, "fondateurs d'Ars Industrialis" (full analysis in primary-arsindustrialis-tunis-motion-2005.md).
