It calls Tunis "le rendez-vous manqué" and asks for "un autre sommet". It criticises the Beffa report on industrial policy, commissioned by the French presidency, and the EU's Lisbon strategy (Barroso). It also demands that television become an instrument of knowledge rather than "industrial populism".
path: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Tunis Commitment (French text): "Nous reconnaissons le rôle principal et les responsabilités des gouvernements dans le processus du SMSI."
  • Ars Industrialis motion: "Le sommet de Tunis est le rendez-vous manqué de ces enjeux".
path: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• A common error, also in the Critical Inquiry review: the motion is described as a "transcription of a group motion at the Tunis Summit". It was not adopted at the summit. It was a press motion by a small Paris association, published in Libération on the eve of the summit. The English title in the book ("A Motion Adopted by Ars Industrialis on the Eve of the Tunis Summit") is accurate.
  • Some bookseller blurbs say the English edition includes "an account of the organisation's 2005 summit in Tunis". That is misleading: Ars Industrialis held no summit in Tunis.
path: WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

items.title: Vocabulaire d'Ars Industrialis (Petit, 2013)
items.text: Primary-adjacent: written inside the association (the page states it was drafted by Victor Petit and published in Pharmacologie du Front National, 2013). It is the association's own house glossary of 48 entries, so it reproduces Stiegler's positions rather than evaluating them. The single-page version is at /vocabulaire; individual entries live at arsindustrialis.org/vocabulaire-<slug>. No page numbers (web text); the entry name is given instead.

items.title: Condensed account (by concept)
items.text:
• Spirit (entry "Esprit"). Opens with Valéry (La liberté de l'esprit, 1939): life is a power of reciprocal transformation with a milieu, and human life also creates a "supplement" of values, the valeur esprit. Note 24 quotes Valéry's comparison of a value called "spirit" with the values of oil, wheat or gold. This spiritual capital is made of material things (books, paintings, instruments), but those things count as capital only if people know how to use them. When people can no longer use the technologies of spirit imposed on them, spirit loses its capital and capitalism loses its spirit. Note 26 says capitalism suffers from having no spirit and contrasts this with Boltanski and Chiapello's "new spirit". Spirit is neither an immaterial soul nor brain matter. It is what brain activity becomes when it turns external things into memory supports (tertiary retentions), so it is psychic, social and technical at once. Spirit is finally defined as the dynamic of technically mediated transindividuation: the "and" in Simondon's "psychic and collective individuation".
  • Libidinal economy ("Économie libidinale"). Libido, a Freudian concept, is the socialised and desexualised energy of the drives, turned into objects of investment through sublimation. It is always channelled through artefacts (fetishism), which is why it can be industrialised. Twentieth-century capitalism made libido its main energy and channels it towards consumer goods so that overproduction is absorbed. Unlimited managerial exploitation of libido destroys desire, so a "renewable" libidinal energy is needed, which makes this an ecological problem. A healthy market economy combines investment with sublimation. Related entries: "Désir/Pulsion" (consumerism reduces desire to drive) and "Investissement" (Besetzung means both financial and libidinal investment).
  • Industrial populism ("Populisme industriel et télécratie"). Today's populism is "of a new kind" because it comes from economic organisation rather than from properly political causes. When consumerist societies reach their limits, life becomes drive-based and addictive, and the resulting regression produces political populism secondarily. "Telecracy" is when mass audiovisual media short-circuit political transindividuation, with television acting as marketing's "secular arm". The entry adds claims about children's screen exposure and synaptogenesis.
  • Symbolic misery ("Misère symbolique"). This is the loss of individuation that comes from losing participation in the production of symbols. It has grown since culture's and politics' "machinic turn". The National Front is to be fought by fighting symbolic misery, which in turn means fighting industrial populism.
  • Proletarianization ("Prolétarisation"). It means depriving a subject (producer, consumer or designer) of savoir-faire, savoir-vivre, or the knowledge to conceive and theorise. The entry reads Marx as saying the working class was only the first class to be proletarianised. In the 20th century the consumer's savoir-vivre was proletarianised too: marketing turns "mode de vie" into "mode d'emploi". After 2008, designers and decision-makers are proletarianised by automated decision systems. The process is "not a fatality" but a pharmacological question, and generalised de-proletarianisation is the stake of the economy of contribution. The proletarian is "the employee of a dissociated milieu" (Simondon).
  • Associated vs dissociated milieu ("Milieu"). "Associated milieu" comes from Simondon (technical individuation, the Guimbal turbine). "Dissociated milieu" is explicitly credited to Stiegler. A milieu is associated when individuals contribute to individuating it, and dissociated when it is individuated by experts at their expense. Culture industries dissociated symbolic milieus by splitting senders from receivers, and service economies deepened this. The internet is "not structurally dissociated", which is what makes contributory economy possible.
  • Pharmakon. The word means remedy, poison and scapegoat. Every technical object is pharmacological. The pharmakon is both what enables care and what must be cared for. The entry cites Derrida's "Pharmacie de Platon" (note 55) and develops a "positive pharmacology", which may nonetheless prohibit some pharmaka (the example is nuclear power). Economising means taking care.
  • Psychotechnics / nootechnics. This is a normative opposition, "assumed as such". Psychotechnics act on or against the mind in order to control it, whereas nootechnics foster the mind's individuation. The same technology can be either (pharmacology). What makes a technology a nootechnics is reciprocity, where the reader can also write, together with long circuits of transindividuation.
  • Otium/negotium. Negotium is the calculable sphere of business and subsistence, and otium the sphere of leisure and existence. They must stay distinct without being metaphysically opposed. Both use hypomnemata. Otium aims at "consistences" (ideal objects, sublimation) and involves disciplines or techniques of self (Foucault's writing of the self). Service industries now short-circuit otium and fold it into negotium. Related entries: "Skholè" and "Subsister, exister, consister".
  • Short-termism ("Financiarisation"). Finance is a "commerce of promises". The entry quotes Stiegler (Pour une nouvelle critique de l'économie politique, 2009): fully realised short-termism destroys the retentions (knowledge) and protentions (investments) of time.
  • Grammatization. This is the discretisation of temporal continua (gestures, speech, calculation) into reproducible spatial "grammes". Stiegler borrows and diverts Sylvain Auroux's term (note 33) and links it to Derrida's grammatology. The entry gives three stages: literal, analog and digital. The digital stage is that of "hyperindustrial society".
  • Tertiary retention ("Attention, rétention, protention"). Primary and secondary retention are Husserlian. Tertiary retentions are hypomnesic sedimentations in artefacts, and they overdetermine secondary retentions, which in turn overdetermine primary ones.
  • Economy of contribution. It has three traits: producer and consumer are no longer separated; the value produced is not fully monetisable (it is a positive externality); and it is an economy of existences as much as of subsistences. The contributor is neither consumer, taxpayer nor gift-giver. The amateur is its ideal type ("Amateur"). The entry rejects the "creative economy" as hyperconsumerist.
  • Transindividuation. The term is derived from Simondon's "transindividual". In Stiegler's version, the diachronising co-individuation of "I"s produces the synchronising transindividuation of a "we". The preindividual milieu is "intrinsically artefactual", and technics is the "third strand" beside the psychic and the social. When technologies serve proletarianisation they short-circuit transindividuation.
  • Le Lay. In the "Marketing" entry (note 44), Le Lay's "temps de cerveau disponible" remark illustrates the "cynical lucidity" of the culture industries.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "Lorsque les hommes ne savent plus se servir des technologies de l'esprit qui leur sont imposées, c'est alors l'esprit qui a perdu son capital, c'est aussi bien le capitalisme qui a perdu son esprit" (entry "Esprit").
  • "La misère symbolique est la perte d'individuation qui résulte de la perte de participation à la production de symboles" (entry "Misère").
  • "ce populisme est, en sa nature profonde, d'un genre nouveau, en ceci qu'il procède d'une organisation économique bien plus que d'une causalité proprement politique" (entry "Populisme industriel").
  • The consumer's way of life is turned by marketing "en mode d'emploi" (entry "Prolétarisation").

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Reliability: high as a statement of the association's vocabulary. It is not neutral, since it is advocacy and self-description. It postdates Réenchanter (2006) and includes later developments (pharmacology, 2008 crisis, telecracy, "mécroissance"), so it should be used carefully as a gloss on 2006 usage. In particular, the systematic "pharmacology" vocabulary was developed mainly from c. 2007–2010 (Ce qui fait que la vie vaut la peine d'être vécue, 2010), so its prominence here may over-systematise the 2006 book (to verify against the text).
  • Stance: a Simondon–Freud–Derrida–Valéry–Foucault synthesis, presented normatively (the psycho/nootechnics opposition is openly "normative").
  • Weak points: empirical claims about screens and synaptogenesis are asserted without discussion. The economic entries (contribution, finance) lean on French heterodox economists (Orléan, Giraud, Moulier-Boutang, Azaïs et al.).
  • Usefulness: it gives the best compact French definitions for nearly every slug. The "Esprit" entry reconstructs the Valéry "valeur esprit" source that gives the book its title.

items.title: Abbinnett, "The Politics of Spirit in Stiegler's Techno-Pharmacology" (2015)
items.text: A peer-reviewed article. Page numbers below are those of the accepted manuscript (pp. 1–13), not the journal's pagination. Abbinnett later expanded this material into The Thought of Bernard Stiegler (Routledge, 2018).
path: Abbinnett, "The Politics of Spirit in Stiegler's Techno-Pharmacology" (2015)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Aim (abstract, pp. 1–3). Abbinnett traces a notion of "reflexive freedom" from Technics and Time 1–2 to the pharmacology of What Makes Life Worth Living and For a New Critique of Political Economy. His thesis is that the pharmakon "sharpens the aporia" of technological society. Because human culture can be reduced neither to "the disorientated life of industrial populism" nor to idealist reflexivity, a "new politics of difference and autonomous desire" becomes possible.
  • Pharmakon (pp. 2–3). He starts from Derrida's "Plato's Pharmacy". Stiegler extends the pharmakon beyond Derrida's "orthographic economy" to the totality of human–technological interfaces. It becomes the antagonism between the toxic reduction of life to "capitalized desire" and forms of cathexis (love, spirit) made possible by techno-hybridisation. He quotes WMLWL p. 4: the pharmakon is "at once what enables care to be taken and that of which care must be taken".
  • Proletarianization and libidinal economy (pp. 3–4). The global economy is a regime of "technologically intensified desire". Inequality results from "pathologically disordered forms of libido", and the desire to consume is not confined to speculators or the bourgeoisie. Retaining "fidelity to Marx" means grasping the crisis of subjectivity, or spirit.
  • Spirit and its genealogy (pp. 7–11). It runs from originary technicity and epiphylogenesis (TT1, with epimetheia as anticipation of catastrophe "touched with the hope that human spirit may yet be sufficient") through the informatic reduction of memory (TT2) and Simondon's concretisation. Stiegler shares Derrida's suspicion (Of Spirit) of Heidegger's essentialist Geist, but finds a "Hegelian residue" in Derrida's orthographic culture. Abbinnett resists Beardsworth's Nietzschean, "remorselessly futural" reading of Stieglerian spirit ("Thinking Technicity", 1998). He holds that a politics of spirit must pass through epiphylogenetic, orthographic memory.
  • Conclusion (pp. 11–13). The fall in libidinal energy is "the determining limit of consumer capitalism". The same virtual technology that disperses the self is the condition for spirit's return as noesis. Sublimation (Freud's Project) is the basis of social cathexis. Stiegler's economy of contribution would free labour from "ratio" so that otium, "the labour of spirit", becomes "the global-universal good of prosthetic humanity" (citing WMLWL pp. 59–61 and NCPE pp. 65–66).
path: Abbinnett, "The Politics of Spirit in Stiegler's Techno-Pharmacology" (2015)

items.title: Short quotations (Abbinnett)
items.text:
• The pharmakon shows that culture cannot be reduced "either to the disorientated life of industrial populism, or to idealist notions of reflexivity" (abstract).
  • Global inequalities are "the outcome of pathologically disordered forms of libido" (p. 4).
  • "'otium' (the labour of spirit) emerges as the global-universal good of prosthetic humanity" (p. 13).
path: Abbinnett, "The Politics of Spirit in Stiegler's Techno-Pharmacology" (2015)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: Derridean and Heideggerian, sociologically framed. Sympathetic, but anticipates Marxist objections and tries to answer them. Valuable as a reading of spirit through Derrida's Of Spirit, which none of the other sources do. It also records the Beardsworth versus Abbinnett disagreement over the temporality of spirit (futural versus memorial).
  • Weaknesses: dense and sometimes loose. It glosses otium oddly as "the labour of spirit", whereas Stiegler and Ars Industrialis oppose otium to the negotium of labour. It conflates "biopolitical capitalism" with Stiegler's own "psychopower". Some typos (e.g. "Steigler").
  • Relevance to the book: it uses "industrial populism" as a key term but does not cite Réenchanter. It is useful for the spirit, pharmakon and otium slugs.
path: Abbinnett, "The Politics of Spirit in Stiegler's Techno-Pharmacology" (2015)

items.title: Cohen, "Dare to Care" (2017)
items.text: An article in the boundary 2 Stiegler special issue. Page numbers are the journal's.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Spirit / Valéry (pp. 150–152). Cohen reads the phrase "the life of the spirit" as a sign of Stiegler's admiration for Valéry, especially "La liberté de l'esprit" (1939), "to which Stiegler regularly returns". In Valéry, spirit is a "bizarrerie" that estranges humans from the "initial and normal conditions of life". Cohen recasts this in Simondonian and Leroi-Gourhanian terms: the life of the spirit emerges transductively when technical exteriorisation opens the possibility of a psychic and collective individuation. He cites the Ars Industrialis glossary entry "Esprit" (as "Stiegler 2014b") for the claim that the "and" designates spirit. He adds Simondon's definition of "spirituality" as respect for the relation between the individual and the preindividual (L'individuation psychique et collective, pp. 105–6).
  • Subsistence, existence, consistence (pp. 151–152, nn. 3–4). Desire infinitises its object and so opens the plane of consistence. Stiegler's tropes of raising and lowering map onto movement between subsistence, existence and consistence. This is useful for "valeur esprit" as rising or falling.
  • Care / epimeleia (pp. 158–162). Stiegler's Taking Care and Foucault's late lectures both turn on epimeleia, care of self. Stiegler's notion of the philosophical pharmakon is a practice in which repetitions "take care of me" (the soin motif).
  • Critique (p. 165). Stiegler's "general organology" rarely attends to lived experience. It privileges the technological and "relegates vitality to subsistence". His reading of Foucault is "unnecessarily limited", missing the late "aesthetics of existence". Cohen proposes the motto "Curare Aude, Dare to Care".

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Cohen, p. 150: "The phrase 'life of the spirit' signals Stiegler's admiration for the work of Paul Valéry."
  • Cohen, p. 165: Stiegler "privileges the technological aspects of organology and often relegates vitality to subsistence".
  • Cohen, p. 165: "Curare Aude, Dare to Care."

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: Foucauldian, biopolitical and medical humanities. Sympathetic but corrective.
  • Value: the best secondary gloss found on the Valéry genealogy of "esprit" and the subsistence/existence/consistence scheme, both of which are central to the subtitle "la valeur esprit". It also gives a good account of how care (soin, epimeleia) links Stiegler and Foucault.
  • Limits: it focuses on the later "mystagogy" lectures (2014) and does not discuss industrial populism or Réenchanter.
  • Reliability: good, as a peer-reviewed article in a major journal with careful citations.

items.title: Hansen, "Saving Libidinal Capitalism" (c. 2014)
items.text: A short online review of For a New Critique of Political Economy (2010) and What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2013), both translated by Daniel Ross. The review has no page numbers.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Pharmacology. Technical developments both disable and enable. Hansen places the idea alongside Plato, McLuhan and Derrida, and says Stiegler adds political commitment. "General organology" is the holistic account of organic, technical and social individuation.
  • Limits of capitalism. Consumerist capitalism has become "toxic". A second limit is the destruction of desire, attention and care through "a short-term economy of the drive". A third is the exhaustion of mental, libidinal, geophysical and biological resources.
  • Proletarianization. Hansen links it to the falling rate of profit: capital proletarianises the consumer in order to seize her libidinal energy.
  • Libidinal energy. It is "essentially renewable". The way out is de-proletarianisation, moving from object-bound drive to long circuits of transindividuation. Digital pharmaka can "reenchant the world".

items.title: Short quotations (Hansen)
items.text:
• "a short-term economy of the drive"
  • Stiegler's project aims "to reenchant capitalism itself" (Hansen's characterisation)
  • "tap the potential of digital pharmaka to reenchant the world"

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Value: a leading media theorist (Hansen, a Whiteheadian and phenomenological media theorist) frames the post-2006 programme explicitly as re-enchantment of capitalism, which directly echoes the title of the 2006 book.
  • Stance: sympathetic but wary. He calls the project "curious" (even "perverse") for seeking to save rather than abolish capitalism, and judges Stiegler's Marx "piecemeal". This sits between the Marxist critiques (Hutnyk, Manche) and the sympathetic expositions (Ross, Lemmens).
  • Reliability: moderate; a short review.

items.title: Hui and Halpin, "Collective Individuation" (2013)
items.text: A chapter in the Unlike Us Reader. Page numbers follow the reader's pagination. The work came out of the authors' research at IRI (Institut de recherche et d'innovation, Centre Pompidou), which Stiegler directed.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Social networks as atomism (pp. 104–108). The "social graph" ontology of nodes and links goes back to Moreno's sociometry in the 1930s. Digital platforms such as Facebook industrialise social relationships by treating users as "social atoms" optimised for marketing data. Time and attention are "chopped into smaller pieces". No group is formed through a common project that would invest "attention, libidinal energy, and time". Following Stiegler (États de choc), such atoms are "disindividuals" (p. 108).
  • Pharmakon (p. 110). Decentralisation alone (Diaspora, StatusNet) does not escape the atomist ontology. With Stiegler (Ce qui fait que la vie vaut la peine d'être vécue), the technology of decentralisation is "always a pharmacon": both democratic (2011 protests) and an instrument of control.
  • Collective individuation (pp. 111–113). With Simondon (L'individuation psychique et collective), individuation is always psychic and collective, and each individual is both agent and milieu. The alternative is to start from the collective: groups formed around a common project, as in Ushahidi in Haiti or tsunami mapping in Japan, where individuals individuate through the collective. They propose platforms built around collective projects (goals, tasks, merging and splitting groups). "A project is also a projection", that is, protention.
  • Conclusion (pp. 115–116). Social networking may play the role the novel played for early capitalism (Lukács). It carries an "unredeemed promise" of global friendship.

items.title: Short quotations (Hui & Halpin)
items.text:
• "these constructed social atoms are not actually 'individuals', but disindividuals" (p. 108)
  • "the technology of decentralization is always a pharmacon, something that is simultaneously positive and negative" (p. 110)
  • "Decentralization is not, and never will be, enough." (p. 110)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: Simondonian and Stieglerian, with an engineering bent (Halpin worked at the W3C). It applies the concepts to platform design rather than explicating them.
  • Value: a concrete gloss on how the associated milieu and contribution ideas of the Ars Industrialis manifestos translate into a design programme. The term "associated milieu" itself is not used, but the "collective project" plays that role. It also illustrates the pharmacological ambivalence of networks that the later Stiegler emphasises (see lit-ross-neganthropocene-introduction-2018.md).
  • Limits: short, programmatic, and not exegetical. It does not mention Réenchanter.

items.title: Hutnyk, "Proletarianisation" (2012)
items.text: An article in New Formations. Page numbers follow the journal's pagination.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Proletarianization (pp. 127–129). Hutnyk opens with Stiegler's "Within the limits of capitalism, economizing means taking care" (Ars Industrialis, n.d.). He calls Stiegler's Marxism "unorthodox" and notes that Stiegler calls proletarianisation Marx's greatest contribution. He quotes the Ars Industrialis Manifesto 2010 definition at length (p. 128): knowledge, once formalised in a technique, machine or apparatus, "escapes" the individual. Workers lose savoir-faire. In the 20th century consumers lose savoir-vivre to devices such as the television set, which creates "available brain time" (an allusion to Le Lay). Intellectual workers of "cognitive capitalism" lose the "life of the spirit" as critical, self-formalising authority. Hutnyk observes that Stiegler's notion is both narrower than Marx and Engels's (focused on knowledge loss) and more generalised (nearly the whole middle class).
  • Television, attention and care (pp. 129–137). He reconstructs the "battle for intelligence" in Taking Care of Youth and the Generations: the audiovisual industries destroy the intergenerational transmission of attention, and the result is "care-less-ness". He calls this rendering "alarmist and patronising" (p. 130), resting on thin statistics, "Euro-" centred, and close to a familiar conservative complaint about declining standards and youth.
  • General intellect (pp. 136–137). He contrasts Stiegler's account of retentional devices with Marx's General Intellect, which is both deskilling and the basis of the "composite worker".
  • Critique (pp. 145–148). In focusing on loss of skill and knowledge, Stiegler and Ars Industrialis underplay the two further moments of Marx's concept: immiseration through sinking into wage labour (now brain labour), and the class mobilisation that follows. Stiegler has "very little to say about class or social conflict" (p. 147) and ignores reproductive labour. He condemns "delinquents" rather than seeing stupidity itself as possibly pharmacological. Transindividuation can also be carried by "ruinous" media and may be proto-revolutionary. His model of time (long vs short circuits) is too undifferentiated.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Ars Industrialis Manifesto 2010, quoted p. 128: proletarianization is "the process through which an individual or collective knowledge, being formalized through a technique, a machine, or an apparatus, can escape the individual".
  • Hutnyk, p. 130: "this rendering of the problem is alarmist and patronising."
  • Hutnyk, p. 147: Stiegler "has very little to say about class or social conflict".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: Marxist and autonomist (Plan C), sympathetic but sharply critical, much like Manche (RP 2021) but earlier and more polemical.
  • Accuracy: quotations are carefully sourced. The critique of Stiegler's empirical claims about children and television is fair. Reading Stiegler as a conservative "decline" theorist arguably neglects his pharmacological insistence on positive potentials and on technics as originary.
  • Relevance to the book: it does not discuss Réenchanter, but it quotes the 2010 Ars Industrialis manifesto, which is reprinted in the English edition, and so serves as a critical gloss on that manifesto's proletarianisation paragraph and its "available brain time" motif.
  • Reliability: good on sources. The interpretation is strongly partisan.

items.title: Lemmens, "The Digital Pharmakon and the (Dis)Empowerment of the General Intellect" (2017)
items.text: An open-access journal article. The web text has no page numbers, so sections are named instead. Two published comments respond to it (DOIs 10.1007/s10699-015-9469-0 and -9470-7).
path: Lemmens, "The Digital Pharmakon and the (Dis)Empowerment of the General Intellect" (2017)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Cognitive capitalism and the general intellect (sections 1–3). Lemmens surveys the post-operaist reading of Marx's "Fragment on Machines" (Negri, Hardt, Moulier-Boutang, Lazzarato), in which the general intellect has migrated into living labour and digital networks favour the autonomy of the multitude. Against this he sets Berardi's gloomy "semiocapitalism", with libidinal exhaustion and psychopathologies of the "cognitariat", which "only seems to perceive the negative side".
  • Grammatization (section "Pharmacology of the Digital"). For Stiegler, digital network technologies are a mnemotechnological transmutation as decisive as writing or printing, a "third phase" of grammatization (Auroux).
  • General organology and libidinal economy. There are three organ systems: psychosomatic, social and technical. Their relations are transductive and form "circuits of desire": "every organology constitutes a libidinal economy". Technical organs can bind drives (sublimation) or unbind them (desublimation).
  • Pharmakon. Technologies compensate for the défaut originaire and have both autonomising and heteronomising potential. Lemmens notes the affinity with Feenberg's "technical ambivalence". Autonomy exists only in relation to technical heteronomy, adopted "with care", which requires a therapy, a "sociotherapy", in short a politics.
  • Associated vs dissociated milieu. Digital networks can create long circuits and new social autonomy if they are collectively appropriated so that they become "an associated milieu instead of a dissociated milieu, the latter being the dominant situation today". They are better suited to this than radio and TV because they are multilinear and allow reading and writing.
  • Proletarianization. Against Hardt and Negri, and closer to Berardi, Stiegler holds that the general intellect is being proletarianised, producing "systemic stupidity". Cognitive capitalism destroys cognition. Yet the situation is pharmacological: Free Software, P2P, Wikipedia and similar projects are first steps of deproletarianisation, carried by the hacker ethic (Himanen).
  • Critique (section "Class-Based Pharmacology"). Stiegler lacks "a class-based analysis". It is "unrealistic if not totally illusory" to trust governments and public institutions to promote alternatives (citing La télécratie contre la démocratie, 2006). Lemmens calls for a "compositionalist" pharmacology aimed at recomposing the general intellect.
path: Lemmens, "The Digital Pharmakon and the (Dis)Empowerment of the General Intellect" (2017)

items.title: Short quotations (Lemmens)
items.text:
• "every organology constitutes a libidinal economy"
  • "What is lacking in Stiegler, however, is a class-based analysis of this pharmacological situation"
  • Digital networks must become "an associated milieu instead of a dissociated milieu, the latter being the dominant situation today"
path: Lemmens, "The Digital Pharmakon and the (Dis)Empowerment of the General Intellect" (2017)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: sympathetic Stieglerian combined with post-autonomist Marxism. It sits between Ross (exposition) and Manche and Hutnyk (Marxist critique): it accepts the pharmacological framework but criticises Stiegler's statism. This bears directly on the book's 2005/2010 manifestos, which appeal to public power and European industrial policy.
  • Reliability: high on exposition and peer-reviewed. It is good for the associated-milieu, organology and libidinal-economy concepts, and it places Stiegler clearly within the cognitive-capitalism debate.
path: Lemmens, "The Digital Pharmakon and the (Dis)Empowerment of the General Intellect" (2017)

items.title: Manche, "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (2021)
items.text: An open-access article in Radical Philosophy. The web version has no internal page numbers, so references below use the article's note numbers.
path: Manche, "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (2021)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Proletarianization. Manche treats it as a "noetic" process, a generalised loss of knowledge that amounts to "becoming stupid". Stiegler introduces the term in Technics and Time 3 and develops it from Symbolic Misery (2004) onward into a three-part loss: savoir-faire, savoir-vivre and savoir-théoriser. She lists Réenchanter le monde (2006) among the works that develop it. The three losses map onto three eras (19th-century industrial capitalism, 20th-century Fordist consumerism, and today's digital/automatic paradigm) and are cumulative. Proletarianisation occurs when the cycle of exteriorising and reinteriorising knowledge breaks (note 30 quotes Automatic Society: "exteriorization without return").
  • Tertiary retention / pharmakon. She gives a standard account: Husserl's primary and secondary retentions are extended to tertiary retentions (externalised, intergenerational memory), and Plato's Phaedrus is read via Derrida, with technics as pharmakon and hypomnēmata.
  • Economy of contribution. It is meant to counter automation's effects on individuation by rewarding contributions to collective knowledge, through a conditional "contributive income". Manche traces this to Gorz's "second cheque" and to the French intermittents du spectacle regime (citing Corsani and Lazzarato). Stiegler also wants an unconditional minimum income for "fragile" people. The Plaine Commune "contributive learning territory" involves corporate partners (Orange, Dassault Systèmes).
  • Short-termism. It is mentioned only within the automation and investment debate, not as a stand-alone concept.
path: Manche, "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (2021)

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "Proletarianisation is the problem, not capitalism." (Manche, final section; this is her reconstruction of Stiegler's stance)
  • Stiegler, cited by Manche (note 1, Ballast 2019): "what I'm interested in is to put down capitalism, for good. Or to do something else in the meanwhile."
  • Stiegler, cited (note 28, States of Shock): "the proletariat is not the working class, but the non-working class".
path: Manche, "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (2021)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Stance: Marxist critique. Manche holds that Stiegler's Marx comes via the Franco-Italian (post-)operaist reading of the Grundrisse "Fragment on Machines". In her view this produces a teleological view of technology and automation-unemployment forecasts that the economic evidence does not bear out. It also sidelines the profit motive and capital accumulation and yields a "good vs bad capitalism" reformism, which risks self-exploitation and co-optation by corporate partners.
  • Value: the most rigorous critical piece found on proletarianisation and contribution. It is a useful counterweight to sympathetic readings (Ross, Lemmens, Ars Industrialis). It bears on the book's 2005/2010 manifestos, which explicitly seek to "save capitalism from itself" by re-founding its spirit (check the manifesto text).
  • Accuracy: its exposition of Stiegler's concepts is careful and conventional. The critique targets the later work (Automatic Society, L'emploi est mort) more than the 2006 book.
path: Manche, "The problem is proletarianisation, not capitalism" (2021)

items.title: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)
items.text: Ross's Introduction to the open-access volume, with a note of how Stiegler's essays in it cite The Re-Enchantment of the World. Page numbers follow the printed book.
path: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)

items.title: Condensed account (Ross, Introduction)
items.text:
• Phases of the work (pp. 7–24). Ross divides Stiegler's work into three "conversions of the gaze":
  • a technological phase: the existential, carceral origin and the Technics and Time project of exteriorisation and the default of origin;
  • an organological and pharmacological phase, prompted by 11 September 2001 and the rise of the National Front, in which Stiegler decides to write in direct relation to "questions of political economy";
  • a neganthropological phase (entropy, the Anthropocene, platform capitalism). Réenchanter le monde (2006) belongs to the second phase. Ross notes that Anglophone philosophy rarely reads beyond Technics and Time 1–3, whereas media-studies readers take up the "direct, visible, legible" second-phase works without their philosophical underpinnings (p. 22).
  • General organology (pp. 19–20). It has three strands: psychic and somatic organs, social organisations, and technical organs. Because we are neotenic and "perpetually unfinished", we must produce artificial organs, learn to practise them, and institute intergenerational social organisations that metastabilise "forms of knowledge that are these practices and these cares".
  • Grammatization (p. 20). It is "the primary analytical concept" of the second phase. Stiegler takes it from Sylvain Auroux and extends it from the discretisation of speech into alphabetic writing to every spatialisation that makes temporal or perceptual flows discrete and reproducible: from Palaeolithic "arche-cinema", through workers' gestures in machines and radio and cinema, to binary code. It links Socrates' pharmakon of writing (Phaedrus) to Marx's Grundrisse (knowledge absorbed into fixed capital).
  • Proletarianization (pp. 20–21). Ross calls it "perhaps his fundamental political concept": the deprivation of knowledge, first thought by Socrates. In the 19th century work-knowledge is lost, in the 20th life-knowledge (through the culture industry and marketing, which target youthful attention and intergenerational transmission), and in the 21st rational and conceptual knowledge (through computation).
  • Protention (pp. 21–22). Marketing and cultural tertiary retentions aim to control protention (expectations, desires, beliefs), which decides behaviour where it is not reduced to drives. The libidinal economy harnessed to production depletes libidinal energy, unbinds drives and makes the productive economy insolvent. This leads from control societies to "hypercontrol" and then "uncontrollability", with passages à l'acte (acting out).
  • Care (p. 24). Culture, education and knowledge are "practices of care" that metastabilise transindividuation.
  • Contemporary challenges (pp. 9–12). Ross's list includes the financial crisis as a symptom of increasingly short-term and speculative investment, and "industrially-generated populism" leading into the "post-truth" age and the "Trumpocene". He presents these as continuations of the diagnosis of industrial populism.
path: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)

items.title: Stiegler's own citations of the book in this volume
items.text:
• Note 271 (endnotes section) refers readers to The Re-Enchantment of the World (Bloomsbury 2014), with Automatic Society 1, for "the recent evolution" of Simondon's associated technogeographic milieus, "which Simondon never had the opportunity to analyse". Note 449 likewise lists the book among his commentaries on Simondon's associated milieu. This is an authorial pointer that the book is a key place where Stiegler develops the associated/dissociated milieu concept.
  • In the body (p. 100; and pp. 208–9 in the chapter "What is Called Caring?"), Stiegler partly revises the 2006 hope. He says that for ten years he had stressed, via free software, that digital networks could form "networks of associated milieus". He now argues that the algorithmic web has become "a systemically dissociating milieu, because it is hyper-proletarianizing" (p. 100). The web associated milieu (since 1993) is traversed by two contrary tendencies: contributory de-proletarianisation, and extreme proletarianisation that turns contributors into functions of the system (pp. 144–146).
path: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Ross, p. 20: grammatization is "the primary analytical concept emerging from this general organology, in this second phase of Stiegler's work".
  • Ross, p. 21: proletarianization is "perhaps his fundamental political concept".
  • Stiegler, p. 100: the reticulated milieu "becomes a systemically dissociating milieu, because it is hyper-proletarianizing."
path: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Reliability: high. Ross is Stiegler's principal translator and a close collaborator, and the reconstruction is lucid and well documented. Stance: insider and sympathetic, Derridean and Simondonian, with no external critique.
  • Value for the book: it places Réenchanter within the "second conversion" (post-2001, post–Le Pen 2002). It provides authorial confirmation that the book is a reference text on the associated milieu, and it documents Stiegler's later self-correction about the internet as an associated milieu. This matters when glossing the 2005/2010 manifestos' optimism about digital networks.
path: Ross, Introduction to Stiegler's The Neganthropocene (2018)

items.title: Rossouw, "Bernard Stiegler's aestheology and the new otium of the people" (2015)
items.text: An article in LitNet Akademies, the English version of an Afrikaans text.
path: Rossouw, "Bernard Stiegler's aestheology and the new otium of the people" (2015)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Thesis. Stiegler's political ideal, a "new otium of the people", is read as "the pursuit of Christianity through means other than Christian". Art and the aesthetic stand in for religion, a move Rossouw compares to Schiller's turn to art after the French Revolution. For Stiegler, the central crisis of Western modernity is "of a theological nature": a loss of faith in the social order and its future.
  • Otium / negotium. Negotium is business and subsistence; otium is education, art, intellectual work and contemplation. The industrialisation of leisure lets negotium dominate otium. Rossouw sketches a history of otium: Cicero's otium for the common good, Augustine's prayer, and medieval clerical and aristocratic privilege. Stiegler's new otium is cultivated through disciplines and practices, forms attention, creates community, commemorates tradition, offers shared time, and is open to all.
  • Subsistence, existence, consistence. In this triad, the "consistent that does not exist" plays God's role in Christianity.
  • Proletariat / hyper-industrial. The proletariat extends "from producers in the industrial society to consumers in the hyper-industrial society". Disindividuation and loss of participation lead to symbolic misery. The keywords include "re-enchantment" and "new proletariat".
  • Critique. Rossouw names two questionable moves: "Christianity is used to authorise art", and "the aesthetical is interpreted as the ground of politics".
path: Rossouw, "Bernard Stiegler's aestheology and the new otium of the people" (2015)

items.title: Short quotations (Rossouw)
items.text:
• "the central crisis of Western modernity is of a theological nature"
  • "the pursuit of Christianity through means other than Christian"
path: Rossouw, "Bernard Stiegler's aestheology and the new otium of the people" (2015)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text: • Stance: a theological-political critique by a South African philosopher who knows the French corpus well (Stiegler's student milieu). It offers a distinctive reading of re-enchantment as a secularised Christian project, which is relevant to the book's Weberian and Valéryan register of "spirit" and "re-enchantment".
path: Rossouw, "Bernard Stiegler's aestheology and the new otium of the people" (2015)

items.title: Stiegler interviewed for April (2011)
items.text: Nature of source. A 12 min 19 s video, with a transcript published by April. The account follows the transcript.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text: Stiegler presents the Ars Industrialis analysis five years after the book: - 20th-century consumerism was a response to the contradictions of productivist capitalism that Marx analysed. Workers lost their savoir-faire. Consumers now lose their savoir-vivre. - Generalised proletarianisation: people operate systems without understanding them. Examples: Alan Greenspan's testimony after 2008, engineers ignorant of their discipline's history, Fukushima. - Free software and hackers are a "deproletarianising" industrial model that has effectively won. - Simondonian individuation and co-individuation through shared knowledge. - Employees work from fear and from reward or punishment, not motivation. Traders such as Kerviel act from addiction. - Ars Industrialis proposes contributive economies as a therapeutics of the digital pharmakon, which could otherwise serve a police state (British surveillance; states' worries about the internet after Tunisia). - Participation is distinguished from contribution.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• On free software: "c'est un modèle industriel déprolétarisant".
  • "ce sont les consommateurs qui perdent leur savoir-vivre".
  • "Ils ne connaissent plus de choses, ils savent faire des choses."

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• It does not discuss the book, the Medef or "valeur esprit". It is useful as Stiegler's own plain-language statement of ch. 1's consumer and proletarianisation thesis (loss of savoir-vivre). It also shows the later shift to "contribution" and free software, which the 2005 founding minutes had left open ("pas de point de vue arrêté sur le libre"). The "Tunisia" mention here refers to the 2011 revolution, not the 2005 summit.
  • It is self-presentation for a sympathetic audience. The transcript is reliable as a record.

items.title: Announcement and argument for the 24 September 2005 session
items.text: Nature of source. This is the announcement and argument page for the session, read in full. It links to Stiegler's talk text (node/1933, analysed in primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md) and to a Japanese translation of it.
path: Announcement and argument for the 24 September 2005 session

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Purpose. The session will not just inform members about the UN summit (16–18 Nov 2005). Ars Industrialis, acting as a legal person, will draft a public motion to intervene in the European political, economic and industrial debate. The summit is treated as an occasion to raise the "politique industrielle des technologies de l'esprit".
  • Terms. The page notes the vocabulary: "société de savoir" (UNESCO) and "société de la connaissance" (attributed to "Anthony Blair" and the MEDEF). It equates this with "cognitive capitalism", where all questions about hypomnémata now converge. Tunis should therefore address an industrial politics of hypomnémata, that is, a politics of spirit.
  • The paradox. People speak of knowledge societies at the very moment when the "avilissement des esprits (devenus du temps de cerveau disponible)" is openly claimed by part of industry in the name of economic "realism". Meanwhile the Medef summer university was placed under the sign of "réenchanter le monde". The page links this to Weber's disenchantment and the "spirit of capitalism", and then to Valéry's 1939 "baisse de la valeur esprit".
  • First hypothesis. The issue needs ambitious theory, made concrete in a long-term European policy carried out by "une nouvelle forme de puissance publique".
  • Format. The session is moderated by Catherine Perret, with Jean-Max Noyer, Serge Regourd and Stiegler. A further session on 5 November will cover search engines, databases and digitised collections. Proposed working groups: suffering and consumption; property and the economy of free software; the future of television; information society and industrial policy; search engines.
  • Method. Industrial competition imposes "unsustainable" rates of socialisation of ICTs, which produce informational inflation and the "cognitive overflow syndrom" (saturation). The association wants to use digital tools without a "pratique maniaque".
path: Announcement and argument for the 24 September 2005 session

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "l'université d'été du MEDEF a mis son programme de rencontres sous le signe de la nécessité de 'réenchanter le monde'".
  • "l'avilissement des esprits (devenus du temps de cerveau disponible)".
path: Announcement and argument for the 24 September 2005 session

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• This is the earliest dated document found that joins the Medef slogan, Le Lay's "available brain time", Weber and Valéry in a single argument. It amounts to the seed of the book's Introduction.
  • Its "cognitive overflow" passage anticipates ch. 2's "cognitive saturation" section.
  • It is unsigned, but it is clearly the official voice of the association.
path: Announcement and argument for the 24 September 2005 session

items.title: Ars Industrialis inaugural session (18 June 2005): minutes
items.text: Nature of source. These are written minutes (compte rendu) of the founding public meeting. They are not a transcript: Stiegler's words are paraphrased by the note-taker.
path: Ars Industrialis inaugural session (18 June 2005): minutes

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
The heading names the five founders: "Georges" [sic] Collins, Marc Crépon, Bernard Stiegler, Caroline Stiegler and Catherine Perret.

  • Why the association exists. Stiegler gives three reasons. First, the founders were already preparing a joint seminar at the Collège international de philosophie, "Trouver de nouvelles armes. Pour une polémologie de l'esprit" (from October 2005), and felt that theory had to be joined to political work. Second, they share a diagnosis of industrial societies. Third, the association aims to widen that sharing to other "singularities". The urgency comes from a first deadline: the Tunis summit on "information societies" that autumn, where Ars Industrialis wants to be a "force de proposition".
  • The manifesto. It is presented as provisional, a conceptual base and "platform for discussion" rather than a doctrine. Its concepts are "weapons" for thinking a new epoch of capitalism defined by generalised digitisation. The association wants to be a place of "translation" between disciplines and languages, and a process of psychic and collective individuation and transindividuation, that is, a new "discipline".
  • The diagnosis. Capitalism is in a crisis that is moral and psychic and concerns the libido. To understand it, one has to understand the libidinal organisation of society under generalised digitisation and the techniques that manipulate desire. Having lost its symbolic efficacy, capitalism now targets the drive (pulsion) rather than the libido. It substitutes a "drive-based economy" (économie pulsionnelle) for a libidinal economy. This is a dangerous passage to the limit and produces new pathologies, felt as an explosive suffering and malaise. The idea anticipates ch. 1's "capitalism of drives". The resulting suffering is described as "désublimation généralisée". Every society is a process of sublimation, offering something beyond the calculable that makes life worth living. That possibility is now compromised, which raises the question of a new "belief" affirming that there is a "high and low".
  • Questions from the floor dealt with desire vs drive and the status of the manifesto. Crépon spoke on the association as a space of sharing.
  • Second part. Knowledge, information and media societies were announced as the topic of the Tunis summit and of a future meeting. The speakers noted, "documents à l'appui", the "langue de bois" of knowledge management discourse. The floor asked about free software, which is not in the manifesto. The answer: the association has no fixed view yet but may open a working group.
  • Third part. Philippe Aigrain presented the website as the association's "organe moteur", built around members' personal pages. Catherine Perret set out practical rules. Stiegler mentioned contacts in England, Italy, Spain, Belgium, Japan, the US and Taiwan.
path: Ars Industrialis inaugural session (18 June 2005): minutes

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• The manifesto's concepts "sont en même temps des armes pour penser notre temps et tenter d'agir sur lui".
  • On the crisis: its "caractère moral et psychique qui a à voir avec la libido".
  • "A une économie libidinale, il substitue une économie pulsionnelle."
  • Suffering understood as the effects of a "désublimation généralisée".
path: Ars Industrialis inaugural session (18 June 2005): minutes

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Valuable for dating. The core vocabulary of ch. 1 (libidinal economy, desire vs drives, desublimation, belief) and the knowledge-society theme of ch. 2 were already in place on the founding day.
  • It confirms the five founders: four philosophers and a jurist, according to the site's "qui sommes-nous" page (see context-ars-industrialis-association.md). This contradicts accounts listing only three co-authors or co-founders. The spelling "Georges" Collins varies across sources; the motion and most sources spell it "George".
  • The minutes are unsigned. Paraphrase is not Stiegler's own wording.
path: Ars Industrialis inaugural session (18 June 2005): minutes

items.title: "Souffrance et consommation" (25 Feb 2006)
items.text: Nature of source. The session page: argument, list of speakers and documents. The talks were posted as WMA audio downloads, with no transcript.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text: The argument: if libido is capitalism's fundamental energy, capitalism is an epoch of libidinal economy, and 20th-century consumption is its typical organisation, then consumption now tends to become addictive and so generates psychic and social suffering. The session examined both the addictive dimension inherent in desire and the conditions in which it becomes destructive of desire, with a view to a new organisation of desire. It referred to the trial of Emmanuel and Patricia Cartier, accused of infanticide, framing them and their children as victims of extreme addictive consumption. That is the argument's hypothesis, not established fact. Speakers: Stiegler (president), Marc Valleur (psychiatrist, head of the addiction service at the Marmottan centre) and Jean-Pierre Klein (psychiatrist, art therapy). Preparatory reading: an extract "L'individu désaffecté" from Stiegler's Mécréance et discrédit t. 2, which Galilée was due to publish in March 2006. The working group included George Collins, Caroline Stiegler (listed as "juriste"), Danielle Rapoport and others.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text: • "la consommation tend à devenir essentiellement addictive et comme telle à engendrer souffrances et désordres psychiques et sociaux."

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text: This shows that the "consumer" and "capitalism of drives" themes of ch. 1 were being worked out in public with clinicians eight months before the book (October 2006). It also gives independent confirmation that Caroline Stiegler was a jurist.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Stats when read: average 3.5/5 from 24 ratings; about 194 readers list the book; 3 written reviews. The page's counts do not fully add up.
  • Editions listed: Flammarion (Oct 2006, c. 172 pp.) and Flammarion "Champs" paperback (Oct 2008, c. 176 pp.).
  • Blurb (truncated on page): it opens with Valéry's 1939 "baisse de la valeur esprit" and states that only 45% of French people then listened to the radio and that TV did not yet exist. It contrasts this with today's connected devices competing for attention.
  • Reviews: (1) Charybde2 (Feb 2024): the same text as the Charybde blog note (see review-hugues-charybde27-2024.md). (2) Khalil_Livres (June 2024): summarises the book as a critique of the declining "valeur esprit" tied to passive TV consumption, and as a plea for individuals to regain the capacity to shape their lives with the support of public policy. (3) Kadjagoogoo (May 2017): a YouTube link only, no text.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text: • Khalil_Livres (quoting or paraphrasing the book's theme): "Une menace contre le désir est une menace contre l'humanité tout entière."

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text: There is little reception here. The French readers who engage are sympathetic and summarise rather than criticise. The useful datum is the edition history (2006 first edition; 2008 "Champs" paperback). That history explains why some sites, for example Unidivers in a search snippet, give 2008 as the publication date. That date is the paperback, not the first edition.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
When read: 3.56 average from 34 ratings, 6 written reviews. Distribution: 5★ 5, 4★ 13, 3★ 12, 2★ 4, 1★ 0. (A second Goodreads ID, 19255433, belongs to an unrelated teacher-training book. Don't confuse them.)

  • James Davies (2023): short but hard, with long, digressive sentences. The argument is repeated but evolves: technology shapes minds and social life. Optimistic and pragmatic. The Tunis-motion proposals about television feel dated in the internet era.
  • Solal (2026, in French): the author is "not anticapitalist" and is Eurocentric, but many analyses are worth keeping, especially on TV, internet, phones and games. Recommended despite the opening jargon.
  • Attasit Sittidumrong (2023, in Thai): reads the book as a critique of a "consciousness industry" eroding critical thought and links it to Arendt's Eichmann-type functionary. "Re-enchantment" is the remedy, but the solutions are too abstract.
  • melancholinary (2019): first Stiegler. The vocabulary is impenetrable but the core ideas are simple. Values the pharmakon and the libidinal critique of neoliberalism.
  • Michael (2025): "timely" for the AI moment. Worth reading aloud in a group.
  • Peter Zomer (2024): "gorgeously difficult". Prescient on screen addiction and on citizens becoming consumers. Part I's psychoanalytic analysis is strong, Part II's solutions abstract. Notes that Ars Industrialis never got the traction hoped for.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• Davies: "Stiegler doesn't slow down much to flesh out his concepts."
  • Zomer: "Gorgeously difficult. This guy has something to say."
  • Michael: "it could not be more timely concerning our AI present".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text: Reader reception is consistent: difficulty and jargon, strong diagnosis, weak or abstract remedies, and a sense of prescience about attention and AI. The Thai reviewer's Arendt link is a reader's association. The Arendt reference is more explicit in other Ars Industrialis texts and in the Roodt (2012) article cited on the P2P wiki. Zomer's "Part I / Part II" probably maps to ch. 1 and ch. 2. Davies's point about TV-centred proposals is fair: the 2005 motion is explicitly about television. These are low-authority, self-selected reviews and should be used only as reception evidence.

items.title: Heulot, "Réenchanter le monde, le programme de Bernard Stiegler" (Rennes, 2014)
items.text: A four-session popular philosophy workshop in Rennes. The society published a presentation and a bibliography for it.
path: Heulot, "Réenchanter le monde, le programme de Bernard Stiegler" (Rennes, 2014)

items.title: Condensed account (presentation text)
items.text:
• The workshop starts from the present crisis, which it dates back to Ford in the 1910s. It presents Stiegler as thinking the causes of the disenchantment of the world, in which a financial and economic rationality wholly given over to marketing leads to global catastrophe.
  • Its themes: reason turned against itself; a capitalism that extends its power while destroying itself; desire replaced by drive, leaving people "disaffected and dismissed from their existences".
  • Re-enchantment requires thinking industrial technology as a pharmakon, both poison and remedy, so as to "re-found society" and fight "against the reign of ignorance". These are the French titles of Ch. 1 and Ch. 2. The "valeur esprit" must become an object of technical, financial and political investment.
  • Guiding questions: what is this disenchanted world, what is the diagnosis, what are the causes, what remedies, what can still be hoped for?
  • The bibliography gives the book as Flammarion Champs-Essais, alongside De la misère symbolique, La télécratie contre la démocratie, Ce qui fait que la vie vaut la peine d'être vécue, Pharmacologie du Front national, Mécréance et discrédit 1–3, Pour une nouvelle critique de l'économie politique, and Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment.
path: Heulot, "Réenchanter le monde, le programme de Bernard Stiegler" (Rennes, 2014)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Value: evidence of French practitioner reception. A community philosophy workshop of four sessions took the book as its organizing text in 2014. It independently confirms the French part titles "refonder la société" and "contre le règne de l'ignorance".
  • Stance: sympathetic and pedagogical. Like Lyons, it frames the book through the later pharmakon vocabulary.
  • Reliability: accurate as far as it goes. A short announcement, depth 1.
path: Heulot, "Réenchanter le monde, le programme de Bernard Stiegler" (Rennes, 2014)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text: In a new-media art mailing-list thread titled "what is to be done?", Holmes replies to a post asking what to do about a process that shaped our sense of the metaphysical but is now run by machines. He says such a post needs proposals, and that Western philosophy offers little to respond with. He then turns to Stiegler, whom he is reading at that moment, and gives a compact summary. Advanced capitalism is above all cultural, built on devices that externalise memory and creativity. Such devices are indispensable, but their industrial production must be shaped so that people can keep "individuating" in tension with society. Holmes connects Stiegler's "writing machines" to Foucault's "writing of the self". Europe should redirect these technologies to protect singularity. Without such a change, Stiegler expects disenchantment with democracy to spread, possibly to violent outbursts. Holmes notes that Stiegler's latest book, Réenchanter le monde: La valeur esprit contre le populisme industriel, opens with a chapter called "What is to be done?". He asks the original poster how they would answer it.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "There is, effectively, nothing in the Western philosophical tradition that will help respond."
  • "So I am quite curious what you think is to be done."

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• This is very early English-language reception, three months after the French publication and seven years before the translation, by a well-known practitioner-critic in the tactical-media and net-art scene. It shows the book circulating among art and media activists.
  • The summary is accurate in outline. The book's intro is indeed "Que faire ?" / "What Is to Be Done?", and the Europe and individuation framing matches. The prediction of violent outbursts reflects Stiegler's warnings in this period (e.g. after the 2005 banlieue riots), but Holmes does not cite a page. The Foucault "writing of the self" link is genuinely Ars Industrialis's: the "qui sommes-nous" page cites "L'écriture de soi".
  • It is an informal list post and not a review.

items.title: INA clip, "Bernard Stiegler rises against consumerism" (2012)
items.text: A 1 min 38 s clip from France Télévisions' Mots de minuit, catalogued by INA with a short description.
path: INA clip, "Bernard Stiegler rises against consumerism" (2012)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text: Philippe Lefait interviews Stiegler about États de choc (2012). The description calls Stiegler co-founder of Ars Industrialis and says that, as early as 2005, the association predicted "the collapse of the consumerism and contemporary capitalism system".
path: INA clip, "Bernard Stiegler rises against consumerism" (2012)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text: It is relevant only as an example of how French media framed Ars Industrialis after 2008: as prophets of the end of consumerism, dated to 2005. It says nothing about Réenchanter le monde. The "predicted in 2005" framing is a media gloss, though it agrees with the inaugural session's diagnosis of a libidinal crisis of capitalism.
path: INA clip, "Bernard Stiegler rises against consumerism" (2012)

items.title: Son[i]a #285, Bernard Stiegler (MACBA, 2019)
items.text: A podcast interview in which Stiegler speaks at length on the programme that this book founded. The episode page gives a description and a timeline of topics.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Stiegler is introduced as head of IRI (Centre Pompidou), founder of Ars Industrialis, and theorist of the "proletarianisation of knowledge".
  • His framing: technology as a starting point for thinking about living together. Technics can raise or lower entropy, which makes it poison or cure (pharmacology).
  • His proposal: a new model of knowledge and a large-scale contributory economy building collective intelligence against the Anthropocene, robotics and the quantification of life.
  • Timeline headings include "Contributory economy: work vs proletarianization", "Refounding Knowledge", "Digital pharmakon", "The need of an economic peace", "Macroeconomics and Neganthropic bifurcation" and "Degrowth is the wrong question".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Relation to the book: late (2019) and in the vocabulary of entropy and neganthropology. Still, "Refounding knowledge" and "degrowth is the wrong question" restate positions already in the 2006 book: Ch. 2's knowledge-against-information argument, and the Introduction's call for "new, qualitative growth" rather than mere reduction.
  • Reliability: primary voice. The description and timeline give themes, not specific arguments.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
The page defines Ars Industrialis as a "cultural and political international association" for a new "industrial politics of the spirit", inspired by Stiegler. Its "Definition" section is labelled "Via Deepseek" and its bibliography "Suggested by DeepSeek". Claims made:

  • Founded 18 June 2005 on Stiegler's initiative by a group of "philosophers and jurists".
  • Stiegler is described as "then director of the Department of Cultural Development at the Centre Georges Pompidou and former director of IRCAM".
  • The founding manifesto draws on Arendt's "life of the mind", glossed in brackets as "(vita activa)".
  • Technologies of spirit capture libidinal energy for consumption. They are explained through Foucault's biopower and Stiegler's "psychopower".
  • Pharmakon; proletarianisation as loss of savoir-faire and savoir-vivre; disindividuation; economy of contribution, with Wikipedia as the model of contributor-consumers; care; nootechnologies and hypomnemata.
  • A second manifesto appeared in 2010.

Bibliography: Mingant (InMedia 2012), Roodt (2012, Arendt/Stiegler), Abbinnett (2017), Bradley (boundary 2, 2015), Duchesne Winter (2019, Sumak Kawsay), and Stiegler (2014).

items.title: Short quotations
items.text: • "Ars Industrialis was established on 18 June 2005 on the initiative of Bernard Stiegler".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• AI-generated content, openly flagged. No inline sources for individual claims.
  • Anachronism or error: in June 2005 Stiegler was still director of IRCAM (2002 until 1 Jan 2006, per French Wikipedia). He became director of cultural development at the Centre Pompidou on 1 January 2006. So "then director of the Department of Cultural Development … former director of IRCAM" is wrong for June 2005.
  • Conceptual slip: "life of the mind (vita activa)". Arendt's The Life of the Mind and her vita activa (in The Human Condition) are different, even contrasting, notions. The manifesto's "vie de l'esprit" alludes to the former.
  • "18 June 2005" matches the inaugural session date on arsindustrialis.org. That date is the first public meeting, which may differ from the legal registration date.
  • The conceptual summary (psychopower, pharmakon, contribution) is broadly accurate for Ars Industrialis as a whole (2005–2015). But some of it, especially "nootechnologies" and the developed "economy of contribution", belongs mainly to the association's later work (2008 onwards). It should be checked against the 2006 book before being attributed to it. The Wikipedia example does appear in ch. 2 (cf. English edition p. 87, per the Lotz-based note in the Colline file).

items.title: Swiss teaching sheet on Le Temps de cerveau disponible (2010)
path: Swiss teaching sheet on Le Temps de cerveau disponible (2010)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text: A teaching guide for upper-secondary and teacher-training use. It covers the 57-minute documentary directed by Jean-Robert Viallet and produced by Christophe Nick, broadcast on France 3 on 17 March 2010 and on TSR2 on 26 Sept 2010. The film traces TV entertainment from the 1980s to reality TV and argues that programmes exploit drives and transgression to sell "available brain time". It calls the film an effective indictment, "notamment grâce aux réflexions du philosophe Bernard Stiegler". It also faults the film's shortcut conclusion about "social war". A box presents Stiegler as founder of the IRI at the Centre Pompidou and convenor of Ars Industrialis, and links to his pages on arsindustrialis.org. The lesson plan asks teachers to put Le Lay's sentence back in its context, an interview for the book Les dirigeants face au changement, using Acrimed's full reproduction (article1688). It also asks them to return to "le discours de Stiegler sur les pulsions, de vie et de mort", and asks what a "promesse sadique" is. The further reading includes Stiegler's La Télécratie contre la démocratie (2008).
path: Swiss teaching sheet on Le Temps de cerveau disponible (2010)

items.title: Short quotations
items.text: • The film is an effective indictment "notamment grâce aux réflexions du philosophe Bernard Stiegler".
path: Swiss teaching sheet on Le Temps de cerveau disponible (2010)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• This is evidence of the pedagogical afterlife of the Le Lay and Stiegler pairing. The "available brain time" critique reached schools via the documentary, not via Réenchanter le monde itself, which the sheet does not cite.
  • It is accurate on the Le Lay source (interview in Les dirigeants face au changement). It relies on Acrimed.
path: Swiss teaching sheet on Le Temps de cerveau disponible (2010)

items.title: Stiegler, "Cognitive technologies" (Ars Industrialis, 5 Nov 2005)
items.text: Nature of source. A written contribution (c. 2,600 words) posted for the session. The session page (node/1461) also lists contributions by Philippe Aigrain, Jean-Max Noyer and Alain Giffard, and links the Tunis motion.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• Origin of the concept. Stiegler says he placed "cognitive technologies" at the basis of the Costech laboratory he founded at the Université de technologie de Compiègne in 1993. The aim was to distance it from cognitive science, which modelled cognition on an idealised Turing machine with infinite memory and ignored the role of tools and prostheses. His axioms are that every memory is finite and every machine is concrete. He compares this with Californian "situated cognition".
  • Memory theory. As in Technics and Time 1, human knowledge appears with a third, external and technical memory ("epiphylogenetic") alongside genetic and somatic memory. "Tertiary retention" makes possible mnemotechnics, such as alphabetic writing as the condition of geometry, law and philosophy. Cognitive technologies are the latest hypomnémata. Together with the "cultural" technologies of communication, which are now merging with them through digitisation, they form the "technologies of spirit" of the Ars Industrialis manifesto. The example given is Mesopotamian catalogues as early "directories".
  • Practical experience. He cites projects he worked on: a computer-assisted reading station for the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which was not completed because the BnF withdrew; an audiovisual reading station for the INA legal deposit; hypermedia documentary formats for digital TV; and aids for blind users.
  • Method. Today "use" is prescribed by user manuals and marketing so as to maximise return on investment, which is almost the opposite of epistemic activity. Design should instead rely on circles of practitioners, whose knowledge forms a Simondonian "preindividual fund". It should treat feedback as the co-evolution of the instrument within a whole cognitive arrangement. This requires public power to accompany the time needed to build such arrangements.
  • Axioms. "Lire, c'est écrire": perception requires motor action. Cognitive technologies are hypomnémata produced by grammatisation (discretisation of the continuous), and every grammatisation also produces disindividuation. "Désindividuations et nouvelles formes d'individuation" are the political stake, "l'objet d'une lutte politique et économique".

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "toute mémoire est finie et ... toute machine est concrète" (axioms; ellipsis mine).
  • "lire, c'est écrire".
  • "Désindividuations et nouvelles formes d'individuation sont l'enjeu politique des formes contemporaines d'hypomnémata".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• It is useful background for ch. 2's sections on knowledge management, instrumentation vs instrumentalisation, and the call for a "knowledge editorial industry". The practical "specific, hierarchical, reversible" design principles of the 24 Sept talk are grounded here in Stiegler's own engineering projects.
  • It is one of the few places where Stiegler explains the concepts behind the book in a talk setting and in a practitioner register (design methodology). It is self-presentational: the claims about Costech's priority and the BnF project come from Stiegler himself.

items.title: Wikipedia coverage
items.text: Is there a dedicated article? No. Neither Ars Industrialis nor the book has a standalone Wikipedia article. Both are covered inside the Stiegler biographies.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
• English Wikipedia, "Bernard Stiegler". "In June 2005 Stiegler founded a political and cultural group, Ars Industrialis", whose manifesto calls for an "industrial politics of spirit". It names co-founders George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler, and mentions an updated 2010 manifesto. No inline citations for these sentences. The bibliography lists Réenchanter le monde (2006) "with Marc Crépon, George Collins & Catherine Perret" and the Bloomsbury 2014 translation. It does not name the translator and has no description of the book. IRCAM directorship is given without dates. Pompidou directorship of cultural development from 1 Jan 2006, and IRI created April 2006 (cited to the IRI site).
  • French Wikipedia, "Bernard Stiegler". "En 2005, avec Marc Crépon, [George Collins, Catherine Perret, Caroline Stiegler] il fonde l'association Ars Industrialis", with a cited mission phrase "pour une politique industrielle des technologies de l'esprit". IRCAM director 2002 to 1 Jan 2006 (cited). The book is listed under "En collaboration" without a note. No mention of the 2020 transformation of the association, and no description of the book or of the Medef context.
  • French Wikipedia, "Temps de cerveau humain disponible". A well-referenced article (L'Expansion, Nouvel Obs, Le Monde, Acrimed, Communication & langages) on Le Lay's 2004 remark. It records Stiegler's reaction in Le Monde diplomatique (June 2005) and his role in the 2010 documentary. It is inconsistent about the source book's title (see context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004.md).

items.title: Short quotations
items.text: • EN: "In June 2005 Stiegler founded a political and cultural group, Ars Industrialis".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Authorship of the book. EN Wikipedia lists three co-authors (Crépon, Collins, Perret) and omits Caroline Stiegler. The FR article lists four. Library catalogues (e.g. Philharmonie de Paris) credit "Bernard Stiegler et Ars Industrialis [Marc Crépon, Georges Collins, Catherine Perret et Caroline Stiegler]", and the Ars Industrialis site and the Tunis motion name the same five founders. The EN bibliography's three-name list is an error or omission. Mirrors of the 2006 Wikipedia text spread it further.
  • "Founded June 2005" is consistent with the inaugural session of 18 June 2005, but it is uncited.
  • The articles are adequate for basic facts and say nothing about the book's argument. Don't use them for content.

items.title: Ars Industrialis 2005 Manifesto (web version)
items.text: The association's own English web version of the 2005 Manifesto, with the French original. The book reprints the manifesto at pp. 11–16 of the English edition. The web English is not Trevor Arthur's translation, so its wording differs from the book's.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
1. Threat. The "life of the mind/spirit" (Arendt) risks total subjection to the market. Firms exploiting the culture industries, program industries, media, telecoms and finally cognitive technologies drive this. Digitization makes these sectors converge, and the converged sector is named the technologies of spirit. Thesis: convergence has so far intensified control, but these technologies can and must open a new age of spirit.
  2. Industrial politics = industrial ecology of spirit. Under market criteria alone the technologies of spirit serve societies of control (Burroughs → Deleuze). That means short-term financial return, and new social practices are blocked. Properly used, they could found a new epoch of civilization and avert a widely sensed chaos.
  3. Desire destroyed. These technologies of "soul" and "consciousness", now joined by bio-technologies, aim to control modes of existence at every stage of life. Control of desire destroys the singularity that existing requires, and it destroys libidinal energy (Freud). Twentieth-century capitalism made libido its main energy source, channelled into commodities to absorb excess production. The capture of libido has ended up destroying it, which leads "inevitably" to an unprecedented global crisis.
  4. Super-ego and sublimation. The ruin of desire is the ruin of sublimation and of the constitution of the super-ego. It brings geopolitical, political, social and psychic disorders on top of economic ones, under a model that sets production and consumption against each other.
  5. Singularity vs calculation. Desire forms in symbolic practices supported by techniques. Objects of desire are singular. Industrial fabrication of desire categorizes singularities and makes the incalculable calculable. Yet singularity is not outside technics; art aims at "a number that averts counting" (Claudel). ICTs are hypomnemata (Foucault's "writing of the self"; Plato's hypomnesis). Like ancient hypomnemata they call for new practices and new social organization, not just user manuals and marketing for 15%-plus shareholder returns.
  6. Self-destructive capitalism. "This capitalism is self-destructive." The association will fight the tendency by inventing practices of spiritual technologies that rebuild objects of desire and experiences of singularity.
  7. Boost desire, not consumption. The political-economic task is to revive desire, not consumption. The general interest is a question of the symbolic, so a new form of public power is needed. It would join firms, public bodies, foundations, associations, economists, artists, scientists, philosophers and investors.
  8. Scope. Based in Paris, European first, international in aim.
  9. Objectives and programme. Symposia, publications, motions and studies. A Paris meeting series: European policy on industries of spirit; Google's digital-library initiative; research; the Tunis WSIS (Nov 2005); marketing and advertising; art in industrial society; European languages and idiomatic difference; psychological disorders and public health; intellectual property; US, Latin American, Chinese and Japanese perspectives.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "This capitalism is self-destructive."
  • The goal is "giving a boost to desire, and not simply giving a boost to consumption".

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
