items.title: Reader reception (same pages)
items.text:
• Babelio: 3.5/5 from 24 ratings. Short reader notes stress the Medef riposte, the critique of "temps de cerveau disponible", and the call for an "industrial ecology of spirit".
  • SensCritique (reader "Denaya", 19 Aug 2011): the writing is "souvent inintelligible", with sentences that are too long, badly built and obscure.
path: Flammarion back-cover text (2006) and booksellers' summaries

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• The blurb confirms that the Introduction starts from Valéry and the Medef slogan. It shows that the 2006 edition includes the Manifesto.
  • Promotional text. Reliable for framing, not for content.
path: Flammarion back-cover text (2006) and booksellers' summaries

items.title: Hugues, Charybde 27 (2024)
items.text: A bookseller's blog reading note. It quotes several long passages from the book without page numbers; they are not reproduced here.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
1. The book is a "philosophical and political manifesto" against the hold of the capitalist imaginary on real and digital life. Valéry's 1939 "baisse de la valeur esprit" is extended to reality TV, the selling of audiences, and consumers treated as conditioned nervous systems.
  2. Biographical context: Stiegler's late turn to philosophy, his prison years, Derrida's support, Ars Industrialis, the IRI, and the Centre Pompidou.
  3. Occasion of the book: the Medef's 2005 summer university, which used the slogan "Réenchanter le monde". The book takes the slogan at its word and asks whether employers want a revival of spirit or "knowledge without spirit".
  4. The diagnosis is set within Weber's disenchantment thesis.
  5. The opening section quotes employer and media figures: Ernest-Antoine Seillère, Denis Kessler, and Patrick Le Lay's "temps de cerveau disponible". It also has the Medef's "knowledge economy" talk and Benjamin and Freud material. Hugues locates all of this in the introductory part of the book, which corresponds to EN Introduction "What Is to Be Done?", p. 1.
  6. On ecological and social crisis, the book cites Laurence Tubiana ("Toubiana" in the note) and Robert Lyon. It calls for "qualitative growth" instead of endless consumption and for a new framework to stop the fall of the value of spirit.
  7. A closing passage built on the anaphora "Nous savons…" lists what "we know" about the need to raise consciousness and intelligence. Hugues locates it at the end of the book's opening part, but he gives no page.
  8. Verdict: a "rare and invigorating" reading of contemporary imaginaries. Its concepts are tools ("munitions") against capitalist manipulation, and it was early in seeing the climate emergency.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "Un formidable manifeste philosophique et politique de 2006"
  • "une lecture rare et tonique de ce qui est à l'œuvre dans nos imaginaires"

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Valuable for the Introduction's content: the Medef/Seillère/Kessler/Le Lay framing, the Valéry opening, Tubiana and Lyon, and the "Nous savons" passage. It agrees with de Beer, who also cites Robert Lyon. There are no page numbers, and where in the book the quoted passages fall is inferred.
  • Stance: enthusiastic, left-ecological and bookseller-activist. Uncritical.
  • Reliability: accurate paraphrase as far as can be checked. Read 18 years after publication, it projects later climate concerns onto the book, though Tubiana is in fact cited.

items.title: Lotz, Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015)
path: Lotz, Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015)

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
1. Framing. The book is a short presentation of the motives and assumptions of Ars Industrialis, the group Stiegler co-founded in Paris about a decade earlier. It aims at solutions to capitalism's "dead end". Lotz says Stiegler "no longer" thinks this in Marxist language and instead grounds it in the co-belonging of technics and humanity (the "prosthetic"). Ars Industrialis wants "technologies of spirit" and a politics drawn from analysing consciousness industries. Knowledge is the central concept.
  2. Contents. Manifestos of 2005 and the 2010 update; two articles by Stiegler; the brief Tunis motion. The Introduction is "the most telling and most transparent text", outlining the central claims.
  3. Core thesis as Lotz reads it. Contemporary capitalism centres on the control, discipline and production of "brain time" by industries that take over the whole mental apparatus. Psychic desires are channelled to consumption (p. 1) and the consumer is manufactured (p. 2). This produces stupidity and short-circuiting, a "total absence of thought" (p. 68), and destroys knowledge and memory as mental life becomes proletarian through externalized memory. Knowledge is reduced to calculable information (p. 23). Memory and imagination become objects of financial investment (p. 88). Own judgement (p. 70) and critical judgement (p. 72) become harder. Lotz likens this to extending Arendt's Eichmann analysis to a whole culture. Capitalism replaces intelligence with "brains without consciousness" and reflex/drive systems (p. 4). Hyper-solicitation of attention short-circuits transindividuation and causes disindividuation, loss of attention, civility and "politeness" (p. 57). Youth have "lost the feeling of existing" (p. 58). The result is demotivation of producers and consumers, the "drop in the value of spirit" and the loss of the spirit of capitalism (p. 67).
  4. Remedy as Lotz reads it. Spirit = the capacity "of imagining and concretizing alternatives" (p. 68). Lotz finds this content empty ("battle against regression", "conquest of the best over the worst", p. 71). The new culture rests on collective intelligence (p. 75) and new instrumentation (p. 73), so the future is still industrial (p. 82). The only example given of cooperative knowledge instruments is Wikipedia (pp. 87, 92). Consumerism cannot last, "in contradiction with the future" (p. 23).
  5. Critique.
  6. Abstraction: little concrete analysis of social relations, power, political opportunities, or the capital/labour relation.
  7. He calls for political economy (p. 7) without linking it to his concept of technology.
  8. Labour control "evaporates" into control of consumer behaviour, and the production/consumption dialectic and the role of money and capital are not analysed.
  9. The frame is a subtle return to Kant/Enlightenment and reformist social democracy: idealist and ethical (responsibility, care, spirit, education).
  10. No account of ecological transformation or of a political movement.
  11. "New spirit of capitalism" (p. 6) and "new industrial model" (p. 6) veil the real restructuring needed. "Politics of decentralization" (p. 63) and socialization of technology (p. 24) are noted. Benkler's Wealth of Networks tells us more.
  12. Verdict. Post-Technics and Time writings are "at times repetitive". This volume works well as an introduction to Stiegler's last decade. Its value lies in extending culture-industry critique to technological and media systems.
path: Lotz, Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015)

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "the focus of his book seems to be located in his claim that the center of our contemporary capitalist world should be seen in the control, discipline, and production of 'brain time'"
  • "Overall, Stiegler's reflections remain extremely abstract and empty of any concrete content."
path: Lotz, Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015)

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Accuracy: good on the diagnosis, and the page references are consistent with the verified contents (e.g. pp. 57–58 fall in Ch. 1's last sections, pp. 66–92 in Ch. 2). One slip in framing: Lotz calls the 2010 text an update of the 2005 Manifesto. It is a new manifesto, though it does revisit 2005.
  • Coverage: whole book, with the most citations from Ch. 2.
  • Depth: medium. It is a ~1,200-word review.
  • Stance/bias: Marxist (journal and reviewer). It judges Stiegler by the absence of a capital/labour analysis and a revolutionary subject. This is fair as external critique, but it underplays Stiegler's own claim that proletarianization is about knowledge (savoir-faire/vivre/theoretical). That claim is his explicit rewriting of Marx's concept. It also does not discuss the economy of contribution, which the 2010 Manifesto (pp. 17–28) puts forward as the concrete alternative.
  • Reliability: high as a record of page-located claims. Its critical judgements are partisan but well-argued. See EVALUATION.md.
path: Lotz, Marx & Philosophy Review of Books (2015)

items.title: Lyons, Critical Inquiry (2014)
items.text: A short review in Critical Inquiry, online first and then in print (CI 41.4, 2015, pp. 900–902).

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
1. Thesis. In the Western capitalist world, the "value of spirit" (mind, intelligence, attention, care for oneself and others) is shrinking. Stiegler blames television, social media and "communicational technologies" for an "industrial populism".
  2. Status of the book. It is the first collective publication of Ars Industrialis, the group founded in 2005 by Stiegler, his partner Caroline and colleagues.
  3. Structure. As Lyons describes it: two manifestos (the 2005 original and its 2010 revision), then two long diagnostic essays by Stiegler on hyperindustrial neoliberalism, the loss of savoir-vivre and a "reign of ignorance", then a transcribed group motion from the Tunis Summit on the crisis of information societies. He gives no page numbers apart from the total of 136 pp.
  4. Lineage. The diagnosis starts from Paul Valéry's pre-war reflections. It echoes Weber's "disenchantment", but argues that neo-capitalist consumption now produces a new and "poisonous" enchantment.
  5. Libidinal economy. Desire has given way to instant gratification, and productive sublimation has given way to manipulated libidinal economies.
  6. Pharmacology. Following Plato, Stiegler treats technology as a pharmakon, both poison and remedy. Harmful technologies can therefore be reclaimed, for example by turning social media toward real community. This is why Lyons calls the book hopeful rather than paranoid.
  7. Other sources. Simondon, Freud and Marx are drawn on, often without explanation.
  8. Translator's preface. Lyons calls it a useful key. It explains that "esprit" covers personal and collective individuation, memory, and reflective and critical faculties.
  9. Verdict. The range of topics overwhelms the reader. The prose drifts by association and relies on "slippery" outward reference and philosophical shorthand. Lyons doubts it suits newcomers. The essays "barely graze the surface", and the manifestos start discussion rather than supply solutions. Even so, the collected texts are "invaluable" as critical stimulation.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• "The value of spirit in the Western capitalist world is dwindling, fading, nearly lost."
  • "Not content to mourn and wallow, Stiegler's is a philosophy of hope."
  • "these texts are collectively invaluable as critical stimulation, wary yet optimistic"

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Accuracy. The structural description matches the verified EN contents: preface, introduction, two manifestos, two chapters, Tunis motion. Lyons does not mention the Introduction ("What Is to Be Done?") separately. The translator's first name is spelled "Trever" in one place.
  • Depth. This is a short notice-length review, thematic rather than section by section. It gives no page references, so it is of little use for section summaries apart from the general themes (Valéry, Weber, pharmakon, libidinal economy).
  • Stance. Sympathetic and literary/media-theoretical. The pharmakon reading is foregrounded. Lyons offers no political-economic critique, which contrasts with Lotz (Marx & Philosophy), who finds the book abstract and reformist. Both reviewers agree that it lacks concrete proposals.
  • Reliability. Accurate but general. Best used for the book's reception tone and for the role of the translator's preface.

items.title: Roodt, Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe (2012)
items.text: This is a critical article on the Ars Industrialis manifestos, which appear in the book as the "Ars Industrialis 2005 Manifesto" (EN p. 11) and the "2010 Manifesto" (EN p. 17). It does not cite Réenchanter le monde itself: it uses the web versions of the manifestos (2008 English translation and 2010). It is included because it is the most sustained critique found of the manifestos' key concept.

items.title: Condensed account
items.text:
1. The claim she examines. The founding manifesto commits members to an "industrial politics of spirit". Its opening makes clear that "spirit" refers to Hannah Arendt's "life of the mind", which it says is under worldwide threat. Stiegler also calls his own project "a struggle for the life of the spirit" (citing Mécréance et discrédit 3, p. 120).
  2. Her reconstruction of Stiegler and the manifestos. Digital media deliver spirit over to global capitalism by fabricating desire, or "libidinal energy", and directing it toward consumer goods. Because singularisation happens through libidinal energy, fabricated desire yields false singularities and narrows the possibilities of existence. Technology is also the means of liberation: new techniques for making objects of desire outside the market would free libido and open new forms of individual and social life, which is the new politics of spirit.
  3. Arendt's distinctions. Arendt separates mind from psyche or soul: the passions are undergone and belong to necessity, whereas thinking, willing and judging are self-reflexive and free. She also separates the free activity of mind from political freedom, which arises only in collective action.
  4. Three disagreements. (a) Stiegler equates mind with libido, collapsing Arendt's mind/psyche distinction. (b) He treats the freedom of mind, or its absence, as a function of economic forces. (c) He assumes a direct path from liberated mind to new forms of collective existence and political action, whereas for Arendt action is never the necessary outcome of mental operations.
  5. Style of thought. Stiegler is a synthetic thinker who links technology, politics, economy, culture, psyche and spirit, and therefore calls for resistance on every front. Arendt is a thinker of distinctions, and her hope lies in the ever-present human capacity to begin something new together, not in schemes to redeem spirit.
  6. Verdict. Stiegler's analysis of technics, his critique of consumption and his call for care for the world should not be dismissed. But the manifesto's appeal to Arendt does not hold, and the Ars Industrialis project cannot be derived from Arendt's view of mind or of action.

items.title: Short quotations
items.text:
• (Her English abstract) the new politics of the spirit "cannot be reconciled with either Arendt's view of mind or her conception of political action"
  • (abstract) Stiegler's critique "should not be discarded out of hand"

items.title: Notes for evaluation
items.text:
• Coverage. Manifestos only (2005 and 2010), via their web versions. Useful for the section on the 2005 Manifesto's Arendt reference and on the 2010 Manifesto's libido and pharmacology vocabulary.
  • Stance. Arendtian and political-theoretical, and analytically careful. She concedes common ground (critique of consumer society, care for the world).
  • Possible oversimplification. "Stiegler equates spirit with libido" compresses his more layered account (libido as the energy of sublimation, spirit as the noetic and transindividual). Supporters would say she does not engage his Freud and Simondon apparatus. She is explicit, though, that she judges only the manifesto's presentation.
  • Disagreement. Directly contrary to de Beer in the same issue, who embraces the spirit vocabulary.
